strings: Create, customize, and build a theme: defineTheme, palette generation, token overrides, component style overrides, custom variants, responsive adaptations, and production builds.
Build an npm package that adds components, templates, themes, docs, and codemods to Astryx apps, and look up every field of every file it holds.

In global mode: users can install your integration for their computer, beside the global CLI. It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs it. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

An integration is a way to share things with Astryx users: a package you own and maintain, built on a framework Astryx gives you. Publish one, many, or any mix, and people install it in one step. It works with the Astryx CLI alongside Core. See each kind under `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks`.
For example, ship a carousel as an integration. Any app that installs it can find it with `astryx search carousel`, and the CLI uses it like any Astryx Core component.
An integration can also replace a built-in template or doc. To start, install `@astryxdesign/cli` and open `astryx docs authoring/quick-start`.
Every field of every file you write for an integration is in `astryx docs authoring/field-reference`.

Every integration runs `astryx integration check --strict` in its own build: it is required, not optional, so a doc, prop, or link that stops matching the code fails your build instead of your users' apps. See `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.
Add components, templates, themes, docs, and codemods, and configure how it behaves.

In global mode: every kind your package adds also applies outside projects when users install it for their computer, beside the global CLI; inside a project, only if the project installs it. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.
These are everything you can add to an integration. Mix them however you like. You are not limited to any one thing.
One component, or a whole library of them.
Components together with themes and templates.
Only docs, if that is all you need.
Agent guidance, so the AI agents in an app follow your library.
Codemods that update app code across your breaking changes.
Each kind below is its own guide. Open one to learn, in depth, how to add it and how to keep it healthy as your package grows.
Ship codemods that `astryx upgrade` runs to migrate app code, and know which of them an app runs.
Add components to an integration, document their public contract, and make them work in every app that installs the package.

In global mode: components from an integration installed for the computer show up outside projects; inside a project, only components from integrations the project installs. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.
Choose a stable component name and generate its source, doc, package export, and integration entry.
Keep the component doc import and package exports map aligned, then verify the packed package.
Write and maintain the default component doc, then adapt it when one family owns several exports or a member needs its own file.

A component's `.doc.mjs` is part of the integration's public contract, not optional commentary. Astryx uses it for CLI output and search, and people and agents read it to decide whether the component fits and how to use it.
Change the source and its `.doc.mjs` together.
Update the doc whenever the public name, import, behavior, props, defaults, examples, or accessibility requirements change.

`integration verify` checks the doc shape and packed import, and `doctor integration components` compares each props table with the component's TypeScript props (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components/describe-the-component/check-the-props`). Neither can prove the prose still matches the component.
Every component doc has one stable identity and enough usage guidance for a reader to choose it correctly. Pick the shape below that matches your module.
After every source or doc change, read the component back. This output is what people and agents receive.
Compare each props table with the component's TypeScript props, then fix the doc or the code.
Adapt a single-component doc when one module exposes several public components or hooks that belong to one family.
Write the default component doc: explain when to use the component, document every public prop, and add focused examples.
Move one member of a component family into its own sibling doc without duplicating it in the parent.
Use a component replacement only when an integration must intentionally own a Core component identity.
Confirm that an app discovers the component, its package, its public import, and its documentation.
Set how your integration behaves in an app: agent guidance, the command your users run, debug and gap reports, and more as it grows.

In global mode: installed for the computer, beside the global CLI, your package's manifest is read as it is in a project and applies in folders outside any project; peer ranges are checked against the global CLI's release. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

Beyond the things you ship, an integration can set how it behaves in an app: the guidance it gives the AI agents working there, the command its users run the CLI with, and the record it keeps of each CLI run. Open one below to set it up.
Add a few lines of guidance that apps put in front of the AI agents working in their code.
Name the command your users run the CLI with, so every command the CLI prints in their apps starts with it.
Receive a record of each CLI run in apps that use your package, and handle the gap reports they send about it.
Write docs that ship with your package and that people and agents find by search or one level at a time.

In global mode: docs from an integration installed for the computer show up outside projects; inside a project, only docs from integrations the project installs. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.
Add a doc topic to your package and write its sections.
Check the docs tree, links, overlaps, doc fields, read size, and CLI peer.
The tokens a doc writes for links, Astryx commands and package-manager steps, which the CLI shows each reader in their own package manager.
Take over a topic or guide, or merge sections into it.
Link one doc to another so the link keeps working when the doc moves.
Give your package its own docs section and place guides in it.
Write short sections that people and agents find by search.
Templates are ready-made UI pages or page sections built with Astryx. Apps copy them into their code and adapt them to their product.

In global mode: templates from an integration installed for the computer show up outside projects; inside a project, only templates from integrations the project installs. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.
Make sure your template works when an app copies it: write the template file, set up its styles, fonts, icons, and images, then package and test it.
Publish a package that works the first time: include everything the template needs, check the package before you publish, and try the template in a real app.
Make sure the published package contains and exposes everything the copied template imports.
Prove the template works the way apps use it: installed from the packed package, copied, built, and rendered.
Catch missing files, exports, and CLI requirements before you publish, and know what still needs the app test.
Make sure the template's styles, fonts, icons, images, and video still show up after an app copies it.
The copied file does not bring sibling assets with it (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/build-the-template/write-the-template-file`). Give every asset exactly one owner:
How the copied source reaches it
The value is small, editable, and belongs to the starting point
The asset should stay centrally maintained with the package
Import a stable public package path
The app must provide product-specific content or branding
Use an explicit placeholder or app public URL and say what to replace
Do not make a template look self-contained while it relies on an undocumented package file or app convention.
Keep text in the app's typeface unless the template truly needs its own, and ship every font file it uses when it does.
Keep icons consistent and accessible by rendering them through Astryx, and ship custom product icons from your package.
Make sure every image and video still works after the copy, or becomes a clear placeholder the app replaces.
Keep the copied UI on the app's theme: use Astryx props and tokens first, keep editable styles in the file, and ship shared CSS from your package.
Astryx copies just this one file into an app, so write it to work on its own there: where it lands, what it can import, and what it exports.
Write the doc that helps people and agents find, choose, and trust your template: its name, description, readiness, preview, and any Core replacement.
Describe a smaller composition, choose its preview shape, and connect it to component examples only when that relationship is real.
Help people find a page: give it a category for `astryx search` and template listings, and flag a sparse starting shell as a scaffold.
Use a template replacement only when an integration intentionally changes the default source returned for one Core template id.
Understand what the template doc controls, keep it accurate as the UI changes, and check how Astryx lists the template.
Help others build apps faster and share a consistent visual language by turning your UI idea into a full page or page section.
Write templates people trust: what good means, the rubric that scores it, and how to grade one with an agent.

A good template does more than render. It gives an app a clear product starting point that is easy to understand, safe to change, and complete after Astryx copies it out of the package. A rubric scores that quality so you can grade as you build.
Its purpose and primary task are clear before someone reads every detail.
It composes Astryx components instead of rebuilding their behavior with raw HTML or custom styles.
Its hierarchy, spacing, interactions, and reading order still work at narrow widths and in every supported color mode.
Its source, imports, styles, fonts, icons, images, and media still work from the copied location.
Its metadata makes the template easy to find and accurately explains when to use it.
Its example content is realistic enough to expose overflow, empty-space, and hierarchy problems.

Grade the first runnable version, again after each source, doc, dependency, or asset change, and in full before every release. Grade the source, doc, copied file, and rendered app together; none of them is enough alone.
Read every scoring rule in `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/write-good-templates/template-grading-rubric`.
Fix publication blockers first, then every reasonable deduction.
Repeat the full grade on the packed package in a clean app (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/build-the-template/package-and-test/test-template-in-app`).
To have an agent grade and improve the template, use `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/write-good-templates/grade-template-with-agent`.
Keep each scorecard with its package revision and rubric version.
Grade and improve with an agent
Give an agent the rubric and evidence it needs to find problems, produce a reproducible scorecard, and improve the template.
Use a shared set of heuristics to score template quality consistently across Astryx usage, icons, CSS, layout, metadata, images, and code quality.
Author a theme in your integration; apps install, apply, and extend it like any theme.

In global mode: outside projects, the theme list includes themes from integrations installed for the computer, and `theme add` there only shows them; inside a project, it lists only themes from integrations the project installs. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

A theme contribution has editable `defineTheme` source plus a built module and production CSS. `integration add theme` scaffolds the source and declares the package exports; `theme build` writes the built outputs. An app installs the package, runs `theme add`, applies the theme from its generated app module, and customizes it with `extends` instead of copying source.

These guides cover the whole path: scaffold the source, generate its palette, define and build the theme, ship fonts and assets, run `integration verify`, and document how apps add and extend it. Applying a theme, including mode and SSR, works the same for every theme; see `astryx docs use-a-theme`.
Scaffold a theme in your package — blank, or forked from an existing theme.
Point theme tokens at the palette, keep light-dark() to colors, and avoid Core internals.
Document a theme by extending the core theme topic, so an app reads it in `astryx docs theme`.
Name the fonts in the theme, then export an optional font stylesheet that `theme add` imports with the built theme.
Turn a few seed colors into full light and dark color ramps, saved in the theme folder.
An app installs the integration and applies or extends your theme, the same as any theme.

Every file an integration author writes, field by field: the integration manifest, astryx.config, codemods, identity, and each doc type. The guides that use them are the rest of `astryx docs authoring`.

People can install your integration next to their global Astryx install, where it works in every folder outside a project; inside a project, only the project's own integrations work. A checklist, with the exact commands to try it.
Find a CLI message and how to fix it.
Find the message the CLI printed while you build, verify, or install an integration, and apply its fix.
Create a new integration package or add Astryx to one you already publish.
Test, publish, and upgrade your package.
Pick the check for each problem, learn what fails and what only warns, and run every check in CI.
Publish your package to npm under the right release tag, checking it before and after.
Test an integration in an app
Install your packed package in an app and run the commands its users will run.
Update your package for each Astryx release, and help apps upgrade with it.
Version your package, declare its peers, and keep apps on older CLIs working.
What browsers Astryx targets, which modern platform features it depends on, and how to support older browsers for your own audience.
Show dates in the Persian, Hebrew, Islamic, Buddhist, Japanese, lunisolar, and other calendars while values stay Gregorian ISO dates.

`Calendar`, DateInput, DateRangeInput, and DateTimeInput show the Gregorian calendar unless the application chooses another one. Values never change with the calendar: they stay Gregorian ISO dates. `astryx docs internationalization/i18n-calendars` has the short version.
Choosing a calendar, which calendars need Temporal, server rendering, the lunisolar calendars, and week numbers.
Commands, programmatic APIs, and output contracts. Building an integration is under `astryx docs authoring`.
Use the CLI in any folder: install it once for your computer, and every project still gets the release that matches its Core. See `astryx docs global`.
The programmatic API: functions, the JSON output envelope, error codes, and response types.
To run the whole CLI from your own command-line tool, with its arguments, folder, and command name, use the host entry: `astryx docs cli/host-entry`.
Every fixed list of values, such as error codes and response types.
Stable, append-only machine-readable error codes on the --json error envelope (envelope.code). Codes never change or get removed; branch on these, not on prose.
Fallback for any error without a more specific code.
A top-level command name was not recognized (e.g. `astryx bogus`).
A subcommand under a command group was not recognized (e.g. `astryx theme bogus`).
An unknown option was passed, --json was given to a command without JSON output.
An argument or option value is invalid: wrong type, out of range, an unknown choice, an extra argument, or a conflicting combination.
A required argument or option value was omitted.
`--lang` was given a value outside its choices (en, zh, dense).
`--detail` was given a value outside its choices (full, compact, brief).
The running Node.js version is below the supported minimum.
`@astryxdesign/core` could not be located (not installed / not in a monorepo).
The installed `@astryxdesign/core` loaded but is too old for this input — it lacks a capability the CLI must call to emit correct output (upgrade core).
No component matched the requested name.
No hook matched the requested name.
No docs topic matched the requested name.
A docs topic exists but the requested section within it does not.
A `--category` filter value did not match any known category.
No template matched the requested name.
A template id matched more than one template (narrow with --type/--package).
A component name is owned by more than one package (narrow with --package).
A theme slug is owned by more than one package (narrow with --package).
No theme matched the requested slug (theme add).
An integration manifest already declares a different path for the requested contribution root.
A package export already maps a generated contribution subpath to a different target.
No package matched the requested name.
An unrecognized `--agent` value was passed to init.
An unrecognized `--features` value was passed to init.
A `--codemod` value did not match any registered codemod (upgrade).
A codemod or post-codemod hook failed during an upgrade run; the error carries a `receipt` that lists the files the run already changed.
A required codemod change remains blocked by a protected consumer file.
A working-tree protection declaration could not be read or parsed.
A generic discover/lookup query matched nothing in any package.
A component exists but has no typed `.doc.mjs` file.
No showcase exists for the requested component.
No source file could be located for the requested component/template.
A required input file did not exist.
Refused to overwrite an existing file.
A path escaped its allowed root, or a name contained traversal markers.
Writing output files failed (and was rolled back).
A theme definition or contributed theme descriptor is invalid.
A theme file could not be loaded / parsed into a defineTheme result.
A palette generation request or one of its constraints was invalid.
The current `@astryxdesign/core` version could not be detected.
A `--from`/`--to` value was not a valid semver string.
A required external dependency (e.g. jscodeshift) is missing.
GitHub CLI (`gh`) is not installed or not authenticated.
No blog post matched the requested slug in the feed.
A network fetch (RSS feed or post text) failed.
A layout expression failed to parse (syntax error, with line/col).
A layout expression parsed but failed validation (unknown component/prop/enum/block).
Recorded in the debug log, never printed: a command exited non-zero without reporting an error code.
Recorded in the debug log, never printed: the process was ended by a signal (Ctrl-C, SIGTERM) before the command reached a terminal path.
Nothing could answer this run, and nothing was written: the project's own CLI could not start and nothing else could answer, or the Core a command needs outside a project could not be installed.
The command needs a project (an app with Astryx installed, or an integration package) and was run outside one. Nothing was written.
The `type` discriminant present on every --json success envelope. Consumers switch on it to narrow `data`.

The install receipt: the `mode` (`default` | `features`), the features run, agent-doc files written, any soft `docsError`, whether theme guidance was emitted, the template outcome (`workflow` | `created` | `skipped`) plus its path, and whether the next-steps were emitted.
The removal receipt — returned when --remove-agents is set: `data.removed` is true when a managed agent-docs block was found and removed, and false when there was none to remove.

The computer-level agent text receipt — returned when --user is set: `data.files`, one `{path, action, reason?}` per path acted on, the skill file first and then each link to its folder (action `written` | `linked` | `unchanged` | `removed` | `absent` | `kept`; `reason` only on `kept`: `edited` when a person changed the text, `not-astryx` when Astryx did not write it), `data.command` (the command the text names), and `data.warnings`.

The component catalog grouped by component group (each component's group field): `detail` (the level: names | compact | full) and `components`, the grouped map of names entries ({name, package, and optional canonical import for integrations}), brief entries ({name, package, description, import}), or a full ComponentDoc per entry with its package.

The component specialization of the shared `BatchResponse` and `BatchRow` types. An explicit programmatic selector array, or two or more CLI selectors, returns one ordered receipt: `count` plus `results`, one row per selector including duplicates. Every row carries `selector` and `status` (found | not_found | ambiguous | error). A found row carries `result`, the same {type, data} response as one selector. An ambiguous row carries `code`, `error`, and `candidates` ({package, component, kind, installed}). Other failed rows carry `code`, `error`, and optional `suggestions` ({name, reason}).

One component's authored ComponentDoc plus ownership fields (package, the owner; import, the specifier; sourceAvailable, whether source exists) and parentDoc (present when the component is documented inside another component's doc, naming that doc). The envelope's package names the same owner.
Just one component's props table (ComponentPropDoc[]). The envelope's package names the npm package that owns the component.
One component's source file, as {component, source}. The envelope's package names the npm package that owns the component.
One component's showcase example, as {component, aspectRatio, source}. The envelope's package names the npm package that owns the component.

One component's example blocks, as {component, showcase, examples, related} of BlockEntry ({name, package, displayName, description, isShowcase, category}); each block names the package that owns it, and the envelope's package names the component's owner.

All reference-doc topics as DocsListEntry[] ({topic, description, package, replaces?, replacedPackage?}), in read order; meta.namespaces lists the docs tree's top-level namespaces, and meta.notLoaded each package whose docs did not load.

One topic's full ReferenceDoc (the JSON read of a topic, --full, --dense, or a topic with one section), with token-ref blocks inlined and each section naming the package that wrote it, plus links ({up, previous, next}: the commands that open the level it sits in and its neighbors there). A topic or guide that took another's place carries replaces and replacedPackage, the package whose topic or guide it replaced.

One topic's section index, the text read of a topic with more than one section (and --index): the topic's name, title, and description, plus sections, each {id, title, package, summary} (pass the id as the section argument; package is the npm package that wrote the section; summary is the section's one-line summary), and links ({up, previous, next}: the commands that open the level it sits in and its neighbors there); replaces and replacedPackage when the topic or guide took another's place.

One ReferenceSection of a topic, found by key or title, with token-ref blocks inlined, plus links ({up, previous, next}: the commands that open its topic index and the sections before and after it). The envelope's package names the npm package that wrote the section.

One node of the docs tree, read by its route: its id, kind, package, title, summary, and breadcrumb, plus a namespace's slots with their children (one level down, each naming its package, and a guide an integration replaced its replaces and replacedPackage) or a typed doc's content, and links ({up, previous, next, related}: the commands that open its parent, its neighbors, and the docs it names).
The feed URL plus every post parsed from the RSS feed, each with slug, title, description, date, type, authors, link, and plaintext URL.
One post's metadata plus the feed URL and the post's full plaintext body.

What the project has, the integrations it loads and the official packages it declares, official packages first (package, the npm package and always equal to name; name, category, components, version, a list per other kind they add, and latest when a source knows it); meta.available lists what the project could add, the official packages first, each with its package and the command that adds it, and meta.sources reports each source, the official list last; when it lists no integration it carries meta.configured to tell "nothing configured" from "nothing discovered".

One package, for an @scope/name or @scope/name@version query: its package (the npm package the result is about), what the shown version adds, whether the project has it, and, when a source knows the package, its versions, latest release, and the command that adds it.
The validated ComponentDoc for one installed component, for an @scope/name/Component query, plus package, the npm package that owns the component.
One item that is not an installed component, for an @scope/name/<item> query: its kind, name, package, version, and whether the project has the package. The envelope's package names the same package.
The echoed query plus every matching item and package across all packages, each with its kind and whether the project has it, even when only one matches; total is set when --limit cut the list.

The echoed query, `matchCount` (total matches, before `limit`), and results, a ranked SearchResultEntry[] bounded by `limit`: each {domain, name, package, score, reason, description, command} (package is the npm package that owns the result), plus import (components, hooks), title, parent (the command that opens the level above), and, for a hit on one section, section (docs), or displayName and kind (templates). The result for a deprecated component also carries deprecated {replacement, description}: the name of the component to use instead and the modernization route, from its doc. When a search with no `type` could not obtain @astryxdesign/core, `meta.partial` is {skipped, reason}: the domains it skipped (component, hook, template) and why.

The how-to-build-a-page playbook, emitted when no query is given: `playbook: true`, a title, the ordered steps (title, commands, optional returns), the on-system rules, and related lookups. Commands are bare subcommands for the caller to render with its own invocation.

The template to start from and its kit: query, hasResults, matchCount (never a cap), directMatch, start {name, package, command, basis, reason, alternatives, ...} (the start and each alternative name the package that owns the template), pages (search's closest templates), blocks and domain as SearchResultEntry[] (each naming its package), frame and foundation (Core component names), and hint {reason, commands} when thin.
The names of swizzlable components discoverable from cwd's @astryxdesign/core. The envelope's package is @astryxdesign/core.

An eject receipt: component name, owning package, output directory, files-copied count, the copied file names (relative to the component folder; owner modules copied beside it start with ../), whether any file uses StyleX, and, when the owner has an issues URL, feedback ({issuesUrl, ghCommand?}): where to report the gap that led to swizzling. The envelope's package names the same owning package.

The fixed gap category values and human-readable labels; when a loaded integration names its own issues URL, meta.destinations lists every destination ({to, default, issuesUrl}) and meta.ask tells an agent to ask the person.

An aggregate receipt: overall status, the selected package, issuesUrl (or null), deliveries in handler order, each {handlerType: project | integration | fallback, handler, audience, status, url, message}, and filedCount/routedOnlyCount totals; without --to, when a loaded integration names its own issues URL, destinations and ask as on gap-report.categories.
The effective discovered TemplateListEntry[] for pages and blocks. A winning replacement entry includes optional `replaces`, naming the Core id omitted from the default list.

The resolved template's source, exactly as a copy writes it, plus its description, kind, the component names it composes, and demoMediaReplaced (how many Astryx demo media references were replaced with placeholders for you to swap for your own media), and demoContentReplaced (how many Astryx docs-only demo content elements were replaced with a Text placeholder for your own content).
A layout skeleton (structural tags with spatial annotations) plus the template's description and the components it composes. The envelope's package names the npm package that owns the template.

A scaffold receipt: template id, output directory, written file name, file count, demoMediaReplaced (how many Astryx demo media references were replaced with placeholders), demoContentReplaced (how many Astryx docs-only demo content elements were replaced with a Text placeholder), notes (setup notes naming what the template needs that the project lacks — missing packages, missing StyleX compiler; empty when satisfied), missingPackages (external package names the template imports that are not in the project), and installCommand (a ready-to-run install command with the detected package manager and workspace version ranges; null when nothing is missing, or when several lockfiles leave the package manager undetermined). The envelope's package names the npm package that owns the template.

A write receipt for the no-build-step CDN starter page: the path (relative to cwd), the Astryx version every CDN URL was pinned to, whether it was written, and the reason it was not. `exists` when a file was already there, which is a success.

The hook catalog grouped by category: `detail` (the level: names | compact | full) and `components`, the grouped map of hook names, brief entries, or a full HookDoc per entry. The envelope's package is @astryxdesign/core, the only package that ships hooks.
One hook's full authored HookDoc. The envelope's package is @astryxdesign/core.
Just one hook's parameters table (HookParamDoc[]). The envelope's package is @astryxdesign/core.

A theme build receipt: name, tokenCount and componentCount (override counts), sizeKB, the written outputs {css, cssDts, js, dts, and variantsDts when applicable}, warnings (defects to fix), and notices (advisories about a correct theme, such as a named font it does not load).
The --check receipt: theme name, an upToDate flag, the stale outputs (each {path, reason: missing | outdated}), and the full list of checked paths. Writes nothing.

Several themes built in one invocation: `count` plus one {file, receipt} per theme in argument order, where receipt is that theme's theme.build (or theme.build.check) envelope, or null when it produced no CSS.

Every bundled, installed package, and local theme as a ThemeListEntry[]. Each entry has slug, displayName, description, maintained, owner package or local root, source, added, and default fields. Optional meta.unmigratedCopies names earlier descriptor-less copies, their missing descriptor, and the upgrade command; those copies are not data entries.

The app theme record after add, remove, or use. It includes every added theme and its built imports, the default slug, generated module path, and the command change. After add, the envelope package names the npm package that owns the added theme; a local theme has none.

A local source-fork receipt with the resolved slug, displayName, source theme maintained flag, source-selector package, outputDir, source entry, exportName, and every file written, including the descriptor. The written local descriptor always uses maintained: false.
A write receipt for the annotated theme template: the path (relative to cwd), whether it was written, and the reason it was not. `exists` when a file was already there, which is a success.
The whole themeable surface: the echoed filter, componentCount, and targets, one per theming target — {key, className, component, props, states}, where props and states are its legal override keys.

An author-reviewable OKLCH palette response: recipe (`astryx-oklch-v1`), status (`candidate`), familyCount, stopCount, modes, candidate (`TonalPaletteCandidate`), and generationReceipt. The generationReceipt contains schemaVersion (1), recipe, generatorVersion (`palette-generator-v1`), candidateFormatVersion (`palette-typescript-v1` or `palette-json-v1`), candidateSha256, optional preview, resolved request, and diagnostics. File-write fields are output, receipt, preview, written, and reason (`exists` or null).
Every available codemod, oldest→newest, as {name, package, title, version, optional}; returned for --list without running anything.

The copied-composition receipt for --registry: applied, ok, the counts (found, current, wouldUpdate, updated, wouldMerge, merged, wouldRefreshReceipt, receiptsRefreshed, conflicts, missing, invalid, failed), and items.

A short-circuit outcome with no codemods run (up_to_date, no_codemods, or config_fixable), each carrying the agent-docs summary. no_codemods and config_fixable carry cliBehindCore ({cliVersion, command}) when the installed Core is newer than the CLI, which then has no codemods for the releases after its own version.

The run receipt: from/to versions, codemod count, integrations processed, the agent-docs summary, sourcePathFound (false when the resolved source directory does not exist, so no source file was read), and (apply mode) filesChanged, transformsApplied, and per-codemod errors. regenerate lists generated files to rebuild, each with its codemods, commands and messages. When the installed Core is newer than the CLI, it also carries cliBehindCore ({cliVersion, command}): codemods for the releases after cliVersion did not run.

(same, refuse, or own; absent on a group), subcommands?), jsonSupported, globalMode ({docs, summary}: what a run may do beyond its command, such as the hand-off to the project's own CLI, the daily update check, and the agent skill file, and the docs topic that explains it), and the flat responseTypes index.

Help, in one of two shapes. A bare `astryx --json` returns the root manifest: name, version, commands (the command names), jsonSupported, and manifest (the full payload `astryx manifest --json` returns). `--help --json` on any command, or `astryx help [command] --json`, returns that command's help: command, description, usage, options (each flags, description, and defaultValue and choices when set), and subcommands (each name and description). data.manifest marks the first shape; data.usage marks the second.

A contribution-writer receipt: kind, name, optional root {path, created}, integration-manifest path, every affected project-relative path, written, and dryRun.

The packed-package check: name, version, packable, tarball {filename, fileCount, size, unpackedSize} or null, inventory {manifest, roots [{kind, path, expectedFiles, missingFiles, complete}], expectedFiles, packedFiles}, contributions {local, packed}, each null or {themes [{slug, exportName}], components, templates [{id, type, name}], codemods [{version, id}], docs, agentDocsAppend}, and issues [{code, severity, message, fix?, file?, line?}] (the issues validation finds in the source and, prefixed packed_, in the packed tree, with the fix and the place when the check knows them).

The validation result: validated (false when nothing was validated: with no package.json the issues list carries one no_package error so the command exits 1, and with a package.json but no integration manifest the issues list is empty and proves nothing), the package name and version (both null when validated is false) plus issues, an AstryxIntegrationIssue[] of {code, severity: warning | error, message, fix?, file?, line?} (fix: the change that resolves it; file and line: where, relative to the package), and notes when there are any: {code, message, next?} information beside the issues (text output marks a next note [next minor]); a note fails nothing by default, and one with next: true counts as a warning under integration check --next, fails integration check --strict --next, and fails --strict from the next minor release. Notes include invalid_cli_command for a malformed cliCommand and cli_peer_version when the running CLI is outside the @astryxdesign/cli peer range of the package, and the package layout findings added after the last minor release, each with its fix in the message (duplicate_component_doc, symlinked_root, unreadable_file, invalid_package_json, no_provider_id, source_without_component_doc where a doc and its source still pair), and doc_name_mismatch and unknown_block_component, until they become warnings in the next minor release. For the commands a topic writes, runner_command (written with a package runner), plain_command (written bare), package_manager_command (written for one package manager) and doc_token (a token that does not parse) notes each give the file, line and the token to write. A doc_target_not_found note names a doc whose replaces or extends names no topic and no guide of the CLI docs or the docs of the package (such as a namespace), and a doc_section_unplaced note a section whose before or after names no section of what it extends (it is added at the end), and a duplicate_guide_replacement note two docs of the package that replace one guide; they become warnings in the next minor release. When the manifest loads, docTypes checks each doc against its published authoring type: status (checked | skipped), reason, typescript, docs, findings (all warnings, each naming the field and a fix), unchecked, and fixtures (test fixture docs not checked). When the manifest loads, docNames lists the component doc names it could not judge: status (checked), findings (always empty; a doc name the module its import names provably does not export is a doc_name_mismatch note, with its fix in the message) and unchecked ({file, name, reason}: a doc whose name differs from the name it is listed under and whose source exports cannot all be read, such as a re-export from another package). When the manifest loads, blockComponents lists the component names templates give in exampleFor or componentsUsed that could not be judged: status (checked), findings (always empty; a name neither the package nor Core has, and the template does not import, is an unknown_block_component note, with its fix in the message) and unchecked ({file, name, reason}: a name the template may reach through anything other than named imports and re-exports from Core, React, StyleX, local helpers or the entry of the package itself, such as an import from another package, a default or namespace import, an alias of or member read off an imported binding, require() or a dynamic import(), or a local module that cannot be read, or any name Core would have to resolve when Core is not installed). Since 0.7.3 each import apps cannot use is also a note (its fix in the message), listed only and failing --strict from the next minor. So are the examples a package ships: component_without_example (a published component no block shows with exampleFor and isShowcase: true, or names in alsoShowcaseFor), template_category (a category written as a path, such as components/X), showcase_not_standalone (a showcase importing server-only code or reading process.env past NODE_ENV) and template_asset_not_packed (a new URL(…, import.meta.url) asset missing, or left out by npm pack --dry-run). When npm cannot list the files, an asset no files entry can reach is still a note and any other is listed in exampleAssets ({status: checked, findings: [], unchecked}, only when it lists any) as {file, asset, reason}. publicImports ({status: checked, findings: [], unchecked}) lists each import the check could not judge as {file, specifier, reason}; never counted or failed on. For the package being authored, olderCliNotes ({file, kind: template | namespace, field, message}) lists each descriptor field a CLI before 0.7.4 refuses, such as stability on a template or namespace doc; it is present only when it has entries, and is never counted or fails a check.

validated (false when no integration manifest was found, so nothing was inspected), the integration identity, structural issues, and non-blocking Core template-id conflicts as {id, severity: warning, integrationPackage, integrationType, integrationName, coreMatches, message, command}.

Every source check of an integration package in one result: validated (false when no integration manifest was found, so nothing was checked), the package name and version, strict, next (true with --next), and checks, one entry per check (validate, components, templates, docs), each with check, errors, warnings, skipped, failed, and response, the envelope that check returns on its own. Check a project's Astryx setup and get a pass/warn/fail report per check. Use it as a CI gate or before debugging a broken install.

Runs a series of diagnostics: Node version, @astryxdesign/core install and version alignment with the CLI, installed themes and wiring, astryx.config validity, whether every integration astryx.config names loads (a failed one fails the run), integrations linked from package.json without a config entry, core peer dependencies, integration provider identity and contribution issues, agent docs, the detected package manager, and the health of the docs the CLI reads (authoring and CLI docs, the docs tree, doc size), and returns a structured report. Theme checks run when the generated app module exists; without one, doctor reports that the CLI manages no themes and names theme add, and the `themes` check counts a theme as wired when package.json `astryx.theme` names one or when the source of the app (JavaScript, TypeScript and CSS files, outside dependencies and build output; type-only imports do not count) imports the built module or stylesheet of a discovered theme, the same imports theme add writes, or passes one to Theme (followed through module-scope variables, defineTheme extends, re-exports and installed packages; only a theme whose package is installed, or a local theme, counts), naming the file; a theme passed to Theme that cannot be traced, such as a prop or a variable declared inside a component, is reported as unconfirmed (info), not as missing. Earlier descriptor-less copies are a non-failing upgrade warning. It never installs, writes, or mutates. It imports astryx.config, executes every added theme source while validating private inputs, and loads every recorded built theme module to prove its runtime imports work, including themes from installed packages. Local theme source also runs during build-freshness checks. Stylesheets are parsed without execution. Config and theme top-level code therefore run, so use doctor only with project code you trust. Outside a project it checks the computer instead: the Node version (`node-version`), the release that answered (`answering-release`), the newest release the computer knows of (`newest-release`), the astryx commands on the search path (`cli-on-path`), the integrations installed for the computer (`computer-integrations`: each one used outside a project, and a warning for one skipped because its peer range excludes the answering release or that fails to load), and the computer-level agent text (`computer-agent-text`): present and matching this release, present but different, edited, absent, or turned off, and where it is linked, with `astryx init --user` as the fix for the stale and absent cases. The agent-text check is always info. The newest-release check also runs inside a project: it names a newer release when the computer knows of one; inside a project whose release is older it names the install and upgrade commands; outside one, when the CLI installed for the computer is older, it names the command of the package manager that installed it, after the Node the newest release needs when the computer runs an older one. It is always info and installs nothing. The `cli-on-path` check also runs inside a project: it lists every astryx command on the search path in order, passes when the first is a release that hands each project run to the release of that project, and warns when the first is another program or a release that predates the hand-off, naming `npm install -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest`. Inside a project, `computer-integrations` lists, as info, the integrations installed for the computer that the project does not install, with its install command; they are not used there. It never fails a check because the folder has no project, and installs nothing. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, it checks the computer instead (the Node version, the version that answered, the newest version it knows of, the astryx commands on the search path, the integrations installed globally, and the agent guide for the computer) and never fails a check because the folder has no project. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs global/who-answers`.
Directory to diagnose. A directory outside any project, a missing one included, gets the computer checks.

A finished build to check before you deliver it: a project folder, a build output folder, or one built `.html` file, relative to `cwd`. Adds two checks after the others. `built-astryx-usage` fails when the path holds no value import from an Astryx package (any `@astryxdesign/*` package or an integration the project installs), no component imported from one, and no Astryx styles in built CSS or HTML. `built-astryx-purity` warns with the source check of `astryx docs is-my-code-good`: raw elements Astryx has a component for, raw SVG and icon-library icons, inline styles, classes, `stylex.create` and imported stylesheets, each with its file and line, in `.tsx` and `.jsx` files and JSX in `.js` source, found by parsing it; it is info, not inspected, when the path holds no source with JSX, such as a bundle. It reads at most 20,000 files, each up to 5 MB, skipping installs and version control; when either limit leaves source unread and nothing was found, the purity check is info, not fully inspected, and when the file limit ends the read before any Astryx turns up, `built-astryx-usage` warns that the rest went unread instead of failing. Given one built `.html` file, it also reads the local stylesheets and scripts that page links, finding a root-relative link from the nearest folder above the page that holds it; a linked file that is not there makes `built-astryx-usage` warn instead of fail. An empty folder fails with nothing checked, like a missing path. A source tree counts as using Astryx through an import, a re-export (`export … from`) or a stylesheet `@import` of an Astryx package; a type-only import or re-export (`import type`, `export type`, or a list whose names are all `type`) does not count, since the build erases it. `--built` goes with `doctor` alone; a `doctor integration` check refuses it. A path that does not exist fails `built-astryx-usage` with nothing checked, and the purity check is left out. The integrations that count are the dependencies the nearest package.json above the path declares whose installed copy, found the way the CLI autolinks (a hoisted workspace copy included), has an integration manifest. The files under the path, and that configuration, are only read, never run. Without it, doctor runs exactly as before.

Generate candidate tonal palette data without filesystem effects.

Runs the versioned astryx-oklch-v1 authoring recipe. The returned candidate contains exact hex values for review; it does not modify a theme, write files, perform semantic mapping, or make accessibility claims. Stop numbers remain stable across layouts, and requested decimal stops are emitted explicitly. Anchor policies are intentional: exact preserves the chosen color at its stop; bounded permits movement within maxDeltaE; flexible treats it as guidance. An anchor needs a mode and stop. Stops apply to every family in one request. The candidate always exposes standalone black and white values for direct theme authoring. Generated TypeScript exports them as `black` and `white`, so they can be assigned directly to semantic theme tokens. Those names are reserved and cannot be used as tonal family IDs. Sets a project up with NO prompts, so it behaves identically for humans, agents, CI, and piped I/O. By default it writes the agent-docs cheat sheet, including guidance from configured integrations, at the project root (the nearest package.json that declares an @astryxdesign package, else the nearest package.json, searching no higher than the repository root): to AGENTS.md, to the project's Claude Code file (CLAUDE.md, else .claude/CLAUDE.md; when CLAUDE.md exists, a block in .claude/CLAUDE.md is removed, unless the project ignores CLAUDE.md, in which case a .claude/CLAUDE.md the project commits keeps a copy), and as a one-line import of AGENTS.md in GEMINI.md unless GEMINI.md already imports it. In the home folder, or in a settings folder in it outside a project, it writes none: every folder of the home folder whose name starts with a dot is a settings folder, and such a folder itself never counts as a project, even with a package.json; a folder below it with a package.json does. The managed block is Astryx-owned: it is written, refreshed, and removed whatever ignore rules or generated markers say, and the text around it is never changed. It then prints getting-started guidance; `features` / `all` print only the chosen features' guidance instead (the theme feature also writes the annotated theme template). With `removeAgents` it removes the managed agent-docs block, at the project root and in `ctx.cwd`, instead of installing. Outside a project it writes the same files but prints no getting-started steps and no step that adds a theme to an app, since those set up a project the folder does not have. With `user` it sets up the computer instead of the folder: it writes the computer-level agent text, one skill file at `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, linked into the skill folders of agents that read only their own (`~/.claude/skills` always; Kiro, Windsurf, Letta, Xcode's coding assistant, and `~/.config/agents/skills` when that folder exists), with a managed copy for Continue, whose scanner skips links,, telling agents anywhere on the computer that Astryx is there and when to use it; with `user` and `removeAgents` it removes the file and the links it made and records that the text is turned off. The CLI installed for the computer refreshes the file in the background after each upgrade; package install scripts, project setup, and upgrade never write it. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, it writes the agent docs and prints no getting-started steps; `user` writes only the agent guide for the computer, in the home folder, and touches nothing in `cwd`. Check integration component names, replaces declarations, and documented props.

Loads one local or installed integration, compares its component names with Core, and returns non-blocking conflicts with the exact package-qualified component command required to keep an intentional overlap. Each component's replaces is checked too: its findings are issues, errors for a package that declares the CLI range that turns replacement on and warnings otherwise. A `{@link}` in a component doc's text that names no doc is an `invalid_doc_graph` warning, since it prints as written. Each component doc's props are compared with the component's TypeScript props, read with the project's own `typescript` (or, where `typescript` is missing or has no JavaScript compiler API, as TypeScript 7 does, the `@typescript/typescript6` it installs): a documented prop the code lacks, a prop the package declares that the doc omits, a wrong `required`, or a type that does not match. A type is judged only when it reads exactly: the same text as the source, once whitespace, quotes and union order are set aside (exactly, if it contains `readonly`), or primitives, literals, arrays and unions of those, or a name for one, on both sides, a field such as `status.type` included, and for a union of props types, the type of any one member. A field the prop's variants give different types is listed when the doc gives only some variants' types. A mutable array type matches a readonly one, because callers can pass it; a readonly one documented for a mutable array is a mismatch. `Name = …` with a union after it must match in both parts; one value after it (`Size = 'md'`) is read as a default. A name only TypeScript's own libraries declare is not resolved, and `React.X` resolves through React where the prop is declared. Every other type is listed as not compared, never reported, and so is a name an index signature takes unless exactly one the package declares takes it; with a TypeScript older than 4.8 no type is judged. Those findings are warnings in `propDrift`; without TypeScript it is `skipped` with a reason.

Unified ranked search across components, hooks, docs, templates, and themes.

The single "I'm looking for X" entry point across every content domain. Matching and scores are keyword + fuzzy (not embeddings). Between score bands results keep the lexical order, whose domain priority can put a weaker component, hook, template, or theme above a stronger doc, and a query that is an entry's exact name answers with that entry first. Inside a band, fixed weights order the matches, so a description match can lead a keyword match in the same band (55–99 holds both). A component's usage guidance (its best practices) is indexed one tier below its description, so the words a reader types still find it. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, items from integrations installed next to this CLI package globally are searched too, and theme results name no step that adds a theme to an app; inside a project, only the project's own integrations count. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs global/computer-integrations`.

Directory to resolve @astryxdesign/core from: the project's installed Core, else, outside a project or in a project with nothing installed, the Core of the release that answers, installed into the per-user cache first when needed. A docs-only or themes-only search (`type: 'doc'` or `type: 'theme'`) does not need it. A search with no `type` covers the docs and themes alone only when that Core cannot be obtained, and then says so in `meta.partial`.

The query echoed back, `matchCount` (how many candidates matched in total, before `limit`), plus a ranked SearchResultEntry[] bounded by `limit`: each has domain, name, score, reason, description, and follow-up command, plus `import` for components and hooks, `title` for docs, `displayName` and `kind` for templates, and `displayName` for themes. A deprecated component's result also carries `deprecated`, `{replacement, description}` from its doc: the name of the component to use instead and the modernization route. A doc result is the smallest part that answers: one section (with `section`, and a command that reads only it), one docs-tree route, or a topic, whose command lists its sections. `parent` is the command that opens the level above it: the section list of its topic, the namespace a tree node sits in, the topic level (Guides or Foundations) for a flat topic, or the topic list for a top-level namespace. Every doc result also carries `package`, the npm package that authored it (for a section, the package its file came from). A theme result is one theme you can import: `name` is its slug, its command is `astryx theme add <slug>` (outside a project, where there is no app to add it to, `astryx theme eject <slug>`), and `package` is the npm package that ships it (`@astryxdesign/cli` for the CLI's own themes). When a search with no `type` could not obtain @astryxdesign/core, `meta.partial` is `{skipped, reason}`: the domains it skipped (`component`, `hook`, `template`) and why; the results are the docs and themes, and text mode prints one line on standard error.

Validate a single Astryx integration package and report its issues.

Validates exactly ONE integration at a time: the local package rooted at cwd (no `pkg`), or an installed package resolved from cwd/node_modules (`pkg` given). It loads and schema-checks the manifest, verifies each declared contribution root exists, and runs the codemod/template/component/docs/theme validators, returning every finding as an AstryxIntegrationIssue. A missing local manifest is guidance (name null, no issues), not an error, so callers can stay exit-0 in a non-integration directory. It also checks every doc the package ships under its roots (component, template, docs topic, theme, and translation, served or not) against the published authoring type for its kind, as `tsc` would, with the project's own `typescript` (or, where `typescript` is missing or has no JavaScript compiler API, as TypeScript 7 does, the `@typescript/typescript6` it installs): an unknown field, a missing required field, or a value outside a field's type is a warning in `docTypes` naming the field and a fix. A test fixture under `__tests__` in the components or docs root is counted, not checked. Without TypeScript, `docTypes` is `skipped` with a reason.
Installed package name to validate; omit to validate the package rooted at cwd.
Directory to resolve the local package / node_modules from.

The result envelope: `data.validated`, false when nothing was validated — with no `package.json` at all, `data.issues` carries one `no_package` error-severity issue so the command exits 1; with a `package.json` but no integration manifest, `data.issues` is empty, which means "not looked at", not "healthy"; `data.name` and `data.version` of the validated package (both null when `data.validated` is false; `data.name` is `(local package)` when the local package.json has no readable name), plus `data.issues`, an AstryxIntegrationIssue[] of {code, severity: `warning` | `error`, message, fix?, file?, line?}: `fix` is the change that resolves the issue, and `file` and `line` where it is, relative to the package, when the check knows them; and `data.notes` when there are any: {code, message, next?} information beside the issues; a note fails nothing by default, and one with `next: true` counts as a warning under `integration check --next`, fails `integration check --strict --next`, and fails `--strict` from the next minor release. Notes include `invalid_cli_command` for a `cliCommand` that was ignored as malformed and `cli_peer_version` when the running CLI is outside the `@astryxdesign/cli` peer range of the package, and the package layout findings added after the last minor release, each with its fix in the message: `duplicate_component_doc`, `symlinked_root`, `unreadable_file`, `invalid_package_json` (no `name` or `version`), `no_provider_id`, and `source_without_component_doc` for a doc whose file name differs from its source only in letter case where the two still pair; and `doc_name_mismatch` and `unknown_block_component` (see `docNames` and `blockComponents`); they become warnings in the next minor release. For the commands a topic writes, `runner_command` (written with a package runner), `plain_command` (written bare), `package_manager_command` (written for one package manager) and `doc_token` (a token that does not parse) notes each give the file, line and the token to write. A `doc_target_not_found` note names a doc whose `replaces` or `extends` names no topic and no guide of the CLI's docs or the package's own (such as a namespace, with the guides below it), so it changes nothing unless an app also installs a package that provides it, and a `doc_section_unplaced` note a section whose `before` or `after` names no section of the topic or guide it extends, so it is added at the end, and a `duplicate_guide_replacement` note two docs of the package that replace one guide, of which only the last is read; they become warnings in the next minor release. When the manifest loads, `data.docTypes` holds the doc type check: `status` (`checked` | `skipped`), `reason` when skipped, `typescript`, `docs` (doc values checked), `findings` ({doc, line, export, type, field, problem: `unknown_field` | `missing_field` | `wrong_type`, severity: `warning`, message, fix}), `unchecked` ({doc, reason}: a doc that could not be fully checked, or a root its reader cannot read), and `fixtures` when the components or docs root holds test fixture docs under `__tests__`: how many, none of them checked. When the manifest loads, `data.docNames` lists the component doc names it could not judge: `status` (`checked`), `findings` (always empty; a doc name the module its import names provably does not export is a `doc_name_mismatch` note, with its fix in the message) and `unchecked` ({file, name, reason}: a doc whose `name` differs from the name it is listed under and whose source exports cannot all be read, such as a re-export from another package). When the manifest loads, `data.blockComponents` lists the component names templates give in `exampleFor` or `componentsUsed` that could not be judged: `status` (`checked`), `findings` (always empty; a name neither the package nor Core has, and the template does not import, is an `unknown_block_component` note, with its fix in the message) and `unchecked` ({file, name, reason}: a name the template may reach through anything other than named imports and re-exports from Core, React, StyleX, local helpers or the entry of the package itself, such as an import from another package, a default or namespace import, an alias of or member read off an imported binding, require() or a dynamic import(), or a local module that cannot be read, or any name Core would have to resolve when Core is not installed). Since 0.7.3 each import apps cannot use is a note in `data.notes`, its fix inside the message, listed only: it does not fail this command or `integration check --strict`, and fails `--strict` from the next minor release. The codes are `component_import_not_exported`, `component_import_other_package`, `component_import_missing_name`, `example_import_not_exported`, `example_import_missing_name`, `template_import_not_exported`, `template_import_outside_root`, `template_private_import`, `template_import_missing_name` and `template_no_default_export`. Since 0.7.4 the examples a package ships are checked the same way: `component_without_example` (a published component no block template shows with `exampleFor` and `isShowcase: true`, or names in `alsoShowcaseFor`), `template_category` (a template category written as a path, such as `components/X`), `showcase_not_standalone` (a showcase that imports server-only code or reads `process.env` past `NODE_ENV`) and `template_asset_not_packed` (a `new URL(…, import.meta.url)` asset that is missing, or that `npm pack --dry-run` leaves out of the package). When npm cannot list the package's files, an asset no `files` entry can reach is still a note, and any other is listed in `data.exampleAssets` (`{status: 'checked', findings: [], unchecked}`, present only when it lists any) as {file, asset, reason}; `integration check` counts them as not compared. When the manifest loads, `data.publicImports` is `{status: 'checked', findings: [], unchecked}`: `unchecked` lists each import the check could not judge, as {file, specifier, reason}, the reason starting `example <label>:` for an import in a component example: an `exports` target not built yet; a module whose export list cannot be read in full (CommonJS, or a declaration file it cannot read); a root import in a package with no `exports` (the root module `main` names is not read); every name an import (other than a component doc's own component) names that its module does not export, while a TypeScript file in the package has a `declare module` block for a relative path or the package's own name or a subpath of it, which can add names to that module (a `declare module` in a comment, `declare global`, a wildcard such as `'*.css'`, and another package's name do not count; a file whose text has `declare module` but that cannot be parsed counts); the same for every such name when the package has more than 5,000 files to search for that block; a deep path into build output not built yet in a package with no `exports`; a template import of Core when `@astryxdesign/core` is not installed beside the package (a `packages/core` of the workspace under another name does not count); every import of the package's own name when package.json has no `name` or a `name` that is not a bare package name; one entry for the whole check when package.json cannot be read; and an import of a subpath whose `exports` entry has only a `types` target, unless it is `import type`, every binding is an inline `type`, or every name it imports is a type its types file declares: a value import of a name that file does not declare as a type, a namespace or side-effect import, or any import when the types file cannot be read (it may be build output). `integration check` counts the unchecked as not compared; they never fail it. `data.olderCliNotes` ({file, kind: `template` | `namespace`, field, message}), for the local package, lists each descriptor field a release before 0.7.4 refuses while the package's CLI peer range admits one, such as `stability` on a template or namespace doc; it is present only when it has entries, is never counted, and never fails a check.
`astryx doctor integration validate` runs it. Read it with `astryx docs cli/commands/doctor-integration-validate`.

The single JSON envelope every command emits under --json. Success is { apiVersion, type, package?, data, meta? }; failure is { apiVersion, error, code, suggestions? }. Discriminate by checking whether `error` is present.

{ apiVersion: number; type: string; package?: string; data: unknown; meta?: { answeredBy?: { cli: string; core: string | null; copy: "project" | "starting" | "matched" | "carried" | "fallback" } } & Record<string, unknown> }
Emitted for every successful command in --json mode: a type discriminator, the package that owns what the response is about, its data payload, and an optional meta object beside data.
Version of the JSON envelope contract. Bump on breaking shape changes so consumers can negotiate. Currently 1. Example: 1.
Names the payload shape. Every value is listed in the response-types enum.

The npm package that owns the one thing the response is about: `@astryxdesign/core` for a Core component, hook, or template, `@astryxdesign/cli` for a doc the CLI ships, or the integration package that contributed it. Absent when the response lists things from more than one package; each listed item then names its own `package`. Example: '@astryxdesign/core'.
The command's payload; its shape depends on `type`.

Optional, emitted as a sibling of data (never merged in). `answeredBy` is on every successful result of a release that has it: `{cli, core, copy}`, the answering CLI version, the Core it pairs with (or null), and which copy answered: `project` (the project's own CLI), `starting` (the copy that started the run, in a project with no CLI of its own), `matched` (the release equal to the project's Core, when the project's own CLI cannot start), `carried` (outside a project), or `fallback` (the matched release could not be obtained, so the starting copy answered). A `deprecations` field is an array of `{id, replacements}` entries; each stable lifecycle id names the replacement commands without changing the command data. Other fields may be added (spec:AST-017 FR13).
{ apiVersion: number; error: string; code: ErrorCode; suggestions?: Suggestion[] }
Emitted for every failure in --json mode, including uncaught throws and command-line parse errors, which are converted to this shape.
The same contract version carried on the success envelope. Example: 1.
Human-readable message. It is for people and changes freely, so never branch on it.
Stable, machine-readable identifier; always present, append-only, and never changes meaning. Branch on this. Example: 'ERR_UNKNOWN_COMPONENT'.
Optional "did you mean..." hints, present only when candidates exist.
The suggested value (e.g. a candidate component name).
Optional per-item explanation; some call sites emit a bare name with no reason.
The human-readable (text) output is a deterministic projection of this same JSON: --json exposes the structured source of truth, and the default format is rendered from the same data.
`code` is the stable contract; see the error-codes enum (ErrorCode) for the full append-only list. Branch on `code`, never on the `error` prose, which can be reworded or localized at any time.

The process exit code is part of the contract too. Exit 0 means success, and every error envelope exits 1. Some commands also exit 1 with a success envelope when what they report failed: a failed check (doctor and its integration subcommands, integration verify, theme build --check), a gap report that was not delivered, an upgrade left incomplete, or init agent docs refused for a path outside the project. Read the envelope, not the exit code, to tell them apart.

The CI check for an integration package's own build: every source check, run in continuous integration or a typecheck script, against the package in the current folder

Takes no package argument: it runs the four `doctor integration` checks, `validate`, `components`, `templates`, and `docs`, against the integration package in the current folder, which is where its own build runs it. It prints each result as that check prints it, then a summary with the errors, warnings, and skipped work of each, and exits 1 when any of the four would exit 1 on its own. With `--strict` it also exits 1 on any warning and on any check, or comparison within a check, that did not run, such as a package with no `astryx.integration.*` or a comparison skipped because the project has no TypeScript, or prop types not judged because its TypeScript is older than 4.8: it adds no check, and lists each of those again as an error, after the checks, in their own issue format. That is the line for the package's own build, so its docs, types, and links stay in sync: run it as a `ci` step, or add `"typecheck": "tsc --noEmit && astryx integration check --strict"` to the scripts in package.json. Its exit codes and JSON are a contract for the builds that run it: a new check, or a new failure code, joins only in a minor release that names it in the release notes. A patch can still ship a Core component, template, or CLI topic whose name conflicts with one of yours. Run `integration check` on every build; run `integration verify` before you publish, to check that the packed package works in an app. To check an installed integration by name, run the `doctor integration` subcommands with its package name. Outside a package, it writes nothing, `validate` reports one `no_package` issue, and it exits 1.

Also exit 1 on any warning and on any check that did not run. A new check or failure code joins only in a minor release, named in the release notes; until then, a malformed `cliCommand` is reported as a note (`invalid_cli_command`) that fails nothing.

Also count the findings the next minor release turns into warnings (the notes marked `next`) as warnings now, so `--strict --next` fails on them. Run it to fix them ahead of the release; every run says how many there are.

integration check --strict --next

# Before you publish: check that the packed package works in an app
integration verify

A CLI older than your Core

Core codemods ship inside the CLI, so a CLI older than the installed @astryxdesign/core has none for the releases after its own version. upgrade then says it cannot finish, never reports your code as up to date, and prints the same upgrade pinned to the CLI release that matches your Core, such as `cd <project> && npx @astryxdesign/cli@<core-version> upgrade --from <old-version> --path <source-dir> --apply`. It changes to the folder this run used and names the directory it scanned as an absolute path, both with symbolic links resolved, so pasted from any folder it upgrades the same code. It is written for a POSIX shell (sh, bash, zsh), or for PowerShell on Windows, with each argument quoted for that shell; cmd.exe is not a target. The codemods this CLI has still run. It exits 0, so a script checks the JSON: the result carries `cliBehindCore` with `cliVersion` (the newest release this CLI has codemods for) and `command`.

Codemods never write to a file your project marks as generated, vendored, or ignored. upgrade reads these marks from the files on disk, so the answer is the same with any version control, or none. A file is protected when:
its leading comment says `@generated`, `@partially-generated`, or `Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.`
a `.gitignore`, or the `.hgignore` at the project root, excludes it
it is an installed dependency (such as anything in `node_modules`), is inside `.git`, `.hg`, or `.sl`, is a symbolic link, or is outside the project

upgrade does not scan installed dependencies or version-control folders at all, including through a symbolic link: a symlinked `node_modules`, or a link whose target is inside one or inside a package store such as `.yarn/cache`, is skipped. Other symbolically linked folders are scanned so a change they need is reported, but nothing is written through them.

Rules work as they do in Git: a later rule wins, so `linguist-generated=false` or a `!` line in an ignore file returns a file to normal handling. A folder name such as `dist` or `generated` protects nothing by itself. If a protection file cannot be read or parsed, upgrade stops with ERR_CODEMOD_PROTECTION_SOURCE before it writes anything.

# .gitattributes
generated/** linguist-generated=true
vendor/** linguist-vendored=true

# A later rule returns one authored file to normal handling
generated/hand-authored.ts linguist-generated=false

When a codemod would change a protected file, upgrade makes the change only in memory and leaves the file as it is. The rest of the upgrade goes ahead. With --apply, your other files are written, then upgrade runs the `hooks.postCodemod` commands from astryx.config (see `astryx docs authoring config`) and checks the protected files again. If one still needs the change, the run is incomplete: it exits 1, prints ERR_CODEMOD_PROTECTED with each file and the rule that protects it, and does not refresh the agent docs. Regenerate or edit those files, then run the same upgrade again. A dry run reports the same files and writes nothing.

With --json, the receipt says `complete: false` and `errorCode: "ERR_CODEMOD_PROTECTED"`. `modifiedFiles` lists the files upgrade changed (or would change), and `protectedFiles` lists each blocked file with its `reasons`, `declarations` (the rules that protect it), `codemods`, and `commands`. A generated file can name the command that rebuilds it on a `Command:` line in its header, such as `// Command: pnpm run gen:panel`; upgrade prints it as `Regenerate with: <command>` and lists it in `commands`.

A protected file a codemod cannot parse, such as a vendored bundle written for another toolchain, cannot need a change the codemod can prove, and upgrade never writes it. upgrade skips it, lists it under `declinedCandidates` with the parse error and where it occurred, and carries on; on its own it does not fail the run. If another codemod in the same upgrade still requires a change to that file (the 0.6.0 theme selector migration, for one, adds a TODO comment above a selector it cannot parse), the file is listed once, under `protectedFiles`, and the run is incomplete as for any protected file. A file upgrade owns that does not parse still fails the run with ERR_CODEMOD_FAILED.

Some changes a codemod can find but not make. upgrade lists them in the result, so a script can keep the rest of the run and act on each. Code a codemod can identify but cannot migrate safely is a manual migration: upgrade lists each file with its line, the codemod and what to change, finishes the run, and exits 0. With --json they are in `declinedCandidates`, one row per file (each finding in `reason` starts with `manual migration needed (<codemod>):`, and a file with several findings lists them all, joined by `; `), and `complete` stays true. A generated file that must be rebuilt is listed in `regenerate` with the command that rebuilds it, such as `astryx theme build`: a protected generated file a codemod still needs to change (also in `protectedFiles`), or a generated output a codemod found out of date (also in `protectedFiles`, with the rule that protects it, when the project marks it generated). With --apply, upgrade runs your `hooks.postCodemod` commands and checks again. If a protected file still needs rebuilding, the run is incomplete exactly as for any protected file: it exits 1 and the result says `complete: false` and `errorCode: "ERR_CODEMOD_PROTECTED"`. If a file nothing protects still needs rebuilding, no protected file is in the way: the codemod could not make a required change, so it is also in `errors` and the run fails with `ERR_CODEMOD_FAILED`, as described below. Either way, rebuild it, then run the same upgrade again. When a codemod also failed, the failure is reported as below, and the receipt it carries still lists `declinedCandidates` and `regenerate`, unless a protected file to regenerate also remains, in which case the run returns `ERR_CODEMOD_PROTECTED` with the failure in `errors`.

When a codemod or a `hooks.postCodemod` command fails, upgrade still makes every other change, exits 1 with ERR_CODEMOD_FAILED, and does not refresh the agent docs. With --json, the result is the usual error, `{"error": ..., "code": "ERR_CODEMOD_FAILED"}`, plus a `receipt`: the same fields a finished run returns, with `complete: false`, each failure in `errors`, and every file upgrade changed (or would change) in `modifiedFiles`, so a script can review, keep, or revert them. An error that stops the run after codemods have written files, such as an astryx.config that fails validation, carries a `receipt` too. Rerun past a failed codemod with --skip-codemod.

Every icon definition: what an icon stands for, and the shared name icon sets map their icons to.

An icon definition is one thing an icon stands for, such as `close` or `delete`. Every icon set registers its icons against definitions in its data file's `map`, and templates are written against definitions, so a project that switches icon sets gets the same definition from the new set. Built-in definitions, marked [built-in], are the shared names Core renders (the semantic icon names in `astryx docs icons`); every set maps them, and `integration check` fails until it does. The others are optional: map each one your library draws. `map` keys a definition by its camelCase name, shown after the id (`eyeSlash`); `experimental icon map` and `--pairs` take either spelling. A set may add its own definitions; in a project that sets `experimental.iconSet`, they are listed here with the package that ships them. `astryx experimental icon <definition>` finds the icon each installed set draws for it.
