Motion duration primitives. Three bands: fast (micro-interactions), medium (entrance/exit), slow (continuous). Min/max variants derive from base × ratio. Of a theme's two `motion` knobs, `tempo` (0.75–1.5) scales every duration here; `character` leaves durations alone. A duration scale beats `tempo` for the bands it sets, and explicit `tokens` beat both. `tempo` leaves these unscaled: finger tracking, momentum, the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard, the press's onset delay, cancel distance and tap flash, hover-intent delays, gesture thresholds, Spinner's and Skeleton's loops, and the 200 ms Reduce Motion cap.

Easing curves for animations and transitions. Of a theme's two `motion` knobs, `character` sets `--ease-entrance` and `--ease-move`: `crisp` decelerates without overshoot, `expressive` overshoots slightly, and at `standard` both equal `--ease-standard`; `--ease-exit` keeps its own curve at every character. `tempo` leaves curves alone. A duration scale's own fields win over the knobs, and explicit `tokens` win over everything. No curve here shapes motion that follows a finger or the system (dragging, momentum, the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard), and the press's clocks, hover-intent delays and gesture thresholds keep their timing whatever the character.

Use an installed built theme as the base for ordinary customization. Import it into your source and pass it as `extends` to `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`. Build the result, then add the local slug. Only eject when you need to own and maintain a full source fork.

A local theme is a folder in `src/themes/<slug>/` holding a `<name>Theme.ts` source that exports `<name>Theme`, and a same-stem `<name>Theme.doc.mjs` descriptor that `theme add` reads. The stem must be a valid export name, so a hyphenated slug drops the hyphen: `brand-dark` lives in `src/themes/brand-dark/brandDarkTheme.ts` exporting `brandDarkTheme`, beside `brandDarkTheme.doc.mjs`. The descriptor's `name` is the folder's slug, and it must declare its type or `theme add` and `theme list` refuse it. `astryx docs authoring theme-doc` lists every field.

astryx theme list
astryx theme add stone
astryx theme eject stone
astryx theme build src/themes/stone/stoneTheme.ts
astryx theme add stone
Add to use, eject to fork

# Write palette + receipt, and open a visual preview
astryx theme palette generate palette.config.json \
  --out src/themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.ts \

The command writes a `.ts` file exporting 21 shades (stops 0–100) for both light and dark, plus a `.receipt.json` to regenerate later. Point your theme's tokens at the palette, then run defineTheme (see below).

For the full palette config fields and CLI flags, run `astryx docs cli/commands/theme-palette-generate`. For the integration-authoring walkthrough of connecting a palette to theme tokens, run `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/themes/generate-a-palette`.

defineTheme creates a theme from explicit token overrides and optional scale configs. Existing themes may use `color` to expand an accent seed into neutral, surface, text, border, and related values; it is not an accent-only edit. Keep that configuration when preserving existing output. For new complete palettes, generate and review a committed palette module, then import its `palette` export and reference stable stops from semantic tokens. This keeps mapped roles coherent when the accepted palette is regenerated; generation itself does not rewrite the theme. Other scale configs generate typography, radius, and motion values from parameters. Explicit token overrides always take precedence over scale-generated values, token by token. When an existing `color` config is in use, overriding `--color-accent` in `tokens` re-points `--color-accent-muted`, `--color-text-accent`, and `--color-icon-accent`, but `--color-on-accent` stays baked from the `color.accent` seed. Prefer a `[light, dark]` tuple for `color.accent` over overriding `--color-accent` alone. localTokens accepts any valid CSS custom-property name; prefixes do not establish ownership.

`extends` lets you derive a new theme from an existing one, inheriting its tokens, component overrides, icons, and fonts. Only specify what you want to change; everything else carries over from the base theme.
Base tokens are copied first, then child tokens override on top.
Deep-merged: child component rules override matching keys from the base.
Shallow-merged: child icons override matching names from the base.
Replaced, never merged: a child that sets iconVariants replaces the base list; a child that omits it inherits the list.
Merged by slot: a child entry replaces the base entry for that slot whole; an omitted or undefined entry keeps the inherited one.
Shallow-merged: child indicators override matching names from the base.
Deep-merged per surface: the base's resolved surface first, then the child's overrides.

Field by field: the child's `fast`, `medium` and `ratio` regenerate the fast and medium duration tokens; `slow` and `easing` left unset keep the base theme's tokens, so an inherited slow band stays at the base's ratio. Each knob (`tempo`, `character`) the child leaves unset keeps the base's.
Child config replaces base entirely (these are scale inputs, not additive).
Width-breakpoint overrides merge by fixed name. Inherited ordered rules keep their relative order; child rules append and re-resolve against the child root axes.

Inheritance is resolved when the theme is defined, so an extended theme is flat: `astryx theme build` emits one self-contained stylesheet holding everything the child inherited, and the base theme's CSS does not need to be loaded next to it. A base that is not a theme (most often an import that missed) throws when `defineTheme` runs, rather than producing a theme that silently inherits nothing.
For the integration-specific guidance on mapping a palette to tokens when extending, see `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/themes/define-the-theme`.

The `components` field in defineTheme uses semantic component keys and style keys, not raw CSS selectors. Use `base` for all instances, `variant:value` or `stateName` for specific props/states, and let the theme pipeline choose the underlying selector. For raw external CSS escape hatches, prefer the data-attribute selector surface documented in `astryx docs styling/styling-advanced`.

Themes can add new prop values to any component. Any `prop:value` key where the value isn't a built-in gets treated as a new variant. Use `astryx theme build` to generate TypeScript augmentations for type safety.
Custom variants only work when the theme that defines them is active. The component's variant map is extended via module augmentation, with no changes to the component source needed.

Use `adaptations` for opt-in token, theme-local token, and component changes under viewport width, primary-pointer precision, contrast preference, or motion preference. Conditions in one `when` are ANDed. Rules are ordinary ordered objects, and later matching writes win.
`widthBreakpoints` are fixed named start points. Defaults are 640 / 768 / 1024 / 1280 / 1536 CSS pixels. `from` includes its point; `below` excludes it. Breakpoint configuration alone emits no CSS.

Precedence follows rule order. Root theme values apply first, then every matching rule in declaration order. A later rule may deliberately restore a root value. `onDark` and `onLight` media-surface overrides apply after adaptations and win on the same leaf.
`extends` preserves the base rule order and appends child rules. Inherited conditions use the child's effective breakpoint map. An empty child rule is a no-op, not a removal operator.

A rule may replace a theme-local token only when the exact name is already enrolled by root `localTokens` or an enrolled base. Component writes in a rule are validated exactly like root `components`: same targets, axes, and value domains. The one addition is that a rule may not be the only place a custom value is enrolled: a value that is valid only because a theme enrolls it generates unconditional type augmentation, so declare it on the root theme first and let rules restyle it. Built-in values need no root declaration. When rules can match together, their ordered portable and local token writes are validated as one effective graph; any reachable cycle fails before CSS is emitted.

Adaptations compile to CSS media queries with no resize listener or styling rerender. Runtime and `astryx theme build` use the same compiler, but only a built theme is present at first paint in an SSR app.
`astryx theme build` compiles a defineTheme file into production-ready artifacts. Recommended for SSR apps (Next.js, Remix) where styles must be present on first paint.

Built themes with an icon registry

`theme build` emits an icon import when it detects a named import used by the theme's `icons:` field. It does not compile that registry module. Move the registry to a separate module and use a named import.

# Emit the built theme
astryx theme build ./src/themes/ocean.ts -o dist/theme.css --icons-specifier ./icons.mjs

# Compile the icon registry alongside it
esbuild src/themes/icons.tsx --bundle --format=esm --outfile=dist/icons.mjs \
  --external:react --external:lucide-react --jsx=automatic

In the example above, the generated theme imports `./icons.mjs` from `dist`. If the second command is skipped, `theme build` can still succeed, but loading or bundling the generated module fails because `dist/icons.mjs` is missing. `--icons-specifier` changes the emitted import; it does not create or verify the target file. Match the specifier to a module that resolves from the generated JS file.

Without `--icons-specifier`, the detected source import specifier is emitted unchanged. In the default flow without `--out`, a bundler can resolve an extensionless `./icons` to the neighboring `icons.tsx` source, but Node ESM does not perform that lookup and reports `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. Moving the output with `--out` also changes where relative imports resolve from.
Keep `react` and the icon library external so the registry does not bundle its own copies of those dependencies.

A registry entry can be a function of `{size, variant}`. The built theme keeps the function, so `Icon` asks it for the size and variant it renders, as the runtime theme does, including for entries inherited from a built or package theme. The built theme's `icons` field and the registry its module re-exports are React nodes, with each function read at size `md`. A function written in the theme file itself cannot be carried, so the build fails; move it into the registry module.

A theme that lists `iconVariants` also writes an `IconVariantMap` augmentation into `<theme>.variants.d.ts`, so `Icon`'s `variant` accepts those names wherever the theme's types load. Its declaration carries the list too, so a theme that extends the built theme types `variant` in its icon entries by that list.

A built theme keeps its `componentIcons`. Names, `null` values, and static requests are written into the module. A slot function stays a function: the module imports it from the module the theme source imports it from, so component slots resolve the same for the built theme as for the runtime theme. The built theme's `componentIcons` field leaves out slot functions, as the runtime theme's does. A slot function defined in the theme file fails the build: move it to its own module and import it. In `--family` output, a member supplies its own slot functions through a named import of its whole `componentIcons` map. The module keeps each slot import as the theme source spells it, and `--icons-specifier` does not change it, so with `--out` in another directory, make a module answer to that specifier from the output directory, as for the icon registry.

Use family mode when an app switches among one base theme and its selected descendants. The build writes one keyed CSS file containing every member, plus one keyed JavaScript module and one declaration file, beside the root source.
The family stylesheet eagerly downloads every selected member so first paint is complete. Switching members changes only the theme identity; it does not add, remove, or reorder stylesheets.

Use `tokenVar()` when a non-StyleX styling library wants a CSS variable reference, and `resolveThemeTokens()` when JavaScript needs token values for a specific theme and mode without React context. Themes are registered by name when created with `defineTheme()`; call `registerTheme(theme)` for prebuilt or object-literal themes that need name-based SSR lookup.

Astryx is built on modern web platform features: the [`Popover`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API) API, CSS anchor positioning, and CSS `light-dark()`. These let components stay small, accessible, and dependency-free, but they also set a floor on which browsers render everything correctly.

A design system does not own its traffic; the products built on it do. Their audiences range from evergreen-Chrome-only internal tools to public sites with meaningful older-Safari share. So Astryx does not declare a single hard browser floor the way an app would. Instead it defines tiers that describe what works at each level, and hands the final decision to you. Pick the tier that matches your audience.
Astryx officially supports Tier 1 and Tier 2. Tier 3 is best-effort: components will not crash, but positioning and theming may degrade.
Everything works, including CSS anchor positioning. This is the reference target.
Components open, dismiss, and are fully usable. Only anchor positioning is missing, so layered surfaces (tooltips, menus, popovers) may not be positioned next to their trigger.
Best-effort. The only guarantee is "does not crash." `light-dark()` is unavailable, so theme colors may fall back to defaults.

Only three modern features carry a browser requirement. Everything else Astryx uses (`:has()`, `color-mix()`, container queries, the `<dialog>` element) has been widely available since 2023 or earlier and needs no special handling.
Positions layered surfaces relative to their trigger (tooltips, menus, popovers, dropdowns).
Opens, stacks, and light-dismisses layered surfaces via the top layer.
Compiles every theme color tuple into a single value that responds to color scheme. Underpins the whole theming system.

The gap that matters is between Tier 1 and Tier 2: the `Popover` API and `light-dark()` reached wide availability well before anchor positioning. So in Tier 2 browsers, layered surfaces open and dismiss correctly; they just are not positioned. This is the one feature most consumers will need to reason about.
Any component that opens a menu, popover, tooltip, or dropdown carries the browser requirement: it renders that surface in an overlay positioned against its trigger. That includes:
Tooltip, HoverCard, and Popover, and any prop that shows one (such as the Button `tooltip`)
Selector, MultiSelector, ComplexSelector, Typeahead, and PowerSearch (dropdown surfaces)
The overflow and flyout menus in Breadcrumbs, TabList, TopNav, and SideNav

If your product opens no menus, popovers, tooltips, or dropdowns, it has no anchor-positioning requirement; it needs only `light-dark()` (Tier 2 and up) for correct theme colors. Page layout, typography, forms, buttons, cards, and tables work down to Tier 2 with no special handling.
Components never throw on missing platform APIs. Where a browser lacks the `Popover` API, layers fall back to plain visibility instead of crashing.
Tier 1 and Tier 2 are officially supported and tested.
Non-layered components render correctly down to Tier 2.
Astryx does not guarantee correct layer positioning below Tier 1 (anchor positioning). Closing that gap for a Tier 2 audience is a consumer choice; see below.
Astryx does not ship a `light-dark()` fallback, so theme colors are not guaranteed below Tier 2.

On a phone, the components that respond to the on-screen keyboard, a fully expanded `height='tall'` BottomSheet and ChatLayout's composer, measure it the same way: the layout viewport's height minus the visual viewport's height times its scale. Where the visual viewport shrinks for the keyboard, as in Safari on iOS in the browser and as a home-screen app, in Firefox for Android and in Chrome on Android, they keep the focused field and the surface around it above the keyboard and leave the page where it was. If Firefox for Android pans to the field, they put the page back within a couple of frames.

In Chrome on Android, ChatLayout’s composer rides the keyboard as Gboard slides it up and down. A Tall BottomSheet’s focused field rides the keyboard as Gboard slides it up, and as Gboard slides it down after the field loses focus. The scroll room stays until the keyboard is down. A hide Chrome reports late, such as Back, which keeps the focus, rides down from Chrome’s report. When the keyboard is reported, the sheet places the field just above it in that same frame, so Chrome has no covered field to pan to; if Chrome pans anyway, the sheet puts the page back when that pan ends. Chrome follows your viewport setting, which Astryx documents and never sets: your app owns its viewport `<meta>` element. By default (`interactive-widget=resizes-visual`) Chrome lays the keyboard over the page and pans to a focused field elsewhere on the page. With `interactive-widget=resizes-content` it shrinks the layout viewport instead, so content anchored to the bottom sits above the keyboard, and those components measure no keyboard and change nothing: the browser has already made the room.
Chrome on Android resizes the page for the keyboard

If your audience includes Tier 2 browsers and you need correct layer positioning, you have three options, cheapest first. All of them are decisions you make for your audience; Astryx does not impose one.

Polyfill anchor positioning. Load a CSS anchor positioning polyfill conditionally behind an `@supports` check so it costs nothing on Tier 1. This is the lowest-effort way to get correct positioning; polyfills may not cover every position-fallback feature.

Provide a JS positioning fallback. Detect missing support with `CSS.supports("anchor-name", "--x")` and position layers with a measurement-based library (e.g. a floating-element positioner) when it returns false. More code, full control.

Accept degraded positioning. Document for your users that on Tier 2 browsers, layered surfaces open correctly but may not sit next to their trigger. Cheapest, and often fine for internal tools on evergreen browsers.
Feature-detect at runtime rather than sniffing user agents:
How These Tiers Move Over Time
The tiers are rolling, not frozen to specific versions. They track the Web Baseline year:
Tier 1 tracks the current Baseline year.
Tier 2 tracks Baseline minus two years.
Tier 3 is everything older, and remains best-effort.

This is not an arbitrary window: Baseline − 2 is close to where anchor positioning stops being available while the `Popover` API and `light-dark()` still are, so the tier boundary tracks a real capability edge, not a guessed date. The version floors above are reviewed and advanced roughly once a year as new Baseline years land. Always feature-detect rather than hardcoding version numbers, so your app adapts automatically as the platform moves.

Layered surface hierarchy: body → surface → card → popover. Each level sits visually above the previous one.
Status roles: pick the token by the surface. `<status>` is info, success, warning, or error.
Status text on the page or a card (4.5:1 or more).
Status icons and marks on the page or a card, such as a StatusDot. Defaults to the text colour.
Status borders on the page or a card, such as an invalid field. Defaults to the text colour.
Strong status fill, such as a Badge.
Text and icons on the strong fill (4.5:1 or more).
Pale status fill, such as a Banner.
Text and icons on the pale fill (4.5:1 or more).
Import the typed color tokens and use them in `stylex.create()`; they resolve to the active theme and color mode.
Use semantic tokens (--color-text-primary) instead of raw hex values.

Use status colors (success, error, warning) only for their semantic meaning.
Hardcode hex values, since they won't adapt to dark mode or custom themes.

semantic colors, support light-dark() auto switching.

Elevation tokens create depth through box-shadow. Three levels (low, med, high) establish a visual hierarchy for floating elements. Inset shadows provide focus and selection rings for interactive components.
Each level adds stronger offset and spread. Shadow color adapts to dark mode automatically via light-dark().

Pick the level by how far the surface sits from the page, not by how much shadow you want. Elevation encodes stacking order: a higher level means the surface is layered over more of the UI. Use exactly one level per surface, and only raise a surface above `none` when it actually sits above other content.
The component is flat and embedded in the surface; it is part of the page, not layered above it. This is the default for every surface except ChatComposer.
A Card in a grid, an inline Banner, a standard Button

The component is in the normal page flow but should read as distinct from the background. Use for emphasis or to separate the component from the surface behind it; the component still sits on the page, it is not floating over other content.
A raised Card that needs emphasis, a ChatComposer
The component sits over other content on the same page; it floats above nearby elements but not the whole screen.
A Popover, a floating Banner, a floating action Button
The component is placed over the entire UI; it is the topmost layer and typically has a backdrop or takes focus from everything else.
A modal Dialog, a full-screen overlay surface
If two surfaces overlap, the one on top takes the higher level. If a surface does not overlap anything, it is `none` or `low`; never `med` or `high`.

Configurable surfaces expose a single `elevation` prop instead of asking consumers to hand-write a box-shadow. It takes the graded enum `none | low | med | high`, narrowed per component to the steps that surface needs: Card, ClickableCard, SelectableCard, Button, IconButton, ButtonGroup, ToggleButton, and Banner expose the full scale, while ChatComposer exposes only `none | low`. `none` is a flat literal (`box-shadow: none`); the other levels map to the `--shadow-*` tokens above, so a surface stays theme-agnostic.

Prop defaults preserve current appearance: every surface defaults to `none` except ChatComposer, which defaults to `low` to keep its raised look. Set `elevation="none"` to flatten it; the flat composer draws a border with the same rest / hover / focus treatment as a text input.
Raising a surface with the elevation prop

Always float; no prop: intrinsic overlays (Dialog, Popover, Tooltip, Toast, HoverCard, DropdownMenu, and the components that compose them) bake their elevation in and never expose the prop. Flow content (inputs, Text, layout) is never elevated; input fields use inset rings, which are a separate concept from elevation.
When building a custom surface, read elevation from the token scale rather than a hand-rolled shadow; the same tokens the elevation prop resolves to.
Reach for the `elevation` prop on a configurable surface before writing any custom shadow.

Choose the level by how far the surface sits from the page: `none` when flat/embedded, `low` when in-flow but distinct, `med` when over page content, `high` when over the whole UI. See "Choosing a level".
Use inset shadows for input focus/selection states; they compose better than outlines.
Hand-write a `box-shadow` in app code; set the `elevation` prop or read `shadowVars` instead.
Raise a surface that does not sit above other content; a non-overlapping surface is `none` or `low`, never `med` or `high`.
Stack multiple elevation levels on the same element.
Use elevation shadows for decorative borders. Use --color-border tokens instead.

Install @astryxdesign/core, @stylexjs/stylex, @astryxdesign/theme-neutral, and @astryxdesign/cli in this project, then run `astryx init` to set up agent docs. Read the generated files to learn the conventions.
Then give it a look. Every app gets a theme whether or not anyone picks one, so it is worth one question at setup rather than revisiting screens later that were built around the wrong look:

Ask me what look and feel this app should have. Run `astryx theme list`, install the closest theme package, and run `theme add <slug>`; use `--package` when owners share a slug. Import `themes` and `defaultThemeSlug` from the generated module once and pass `themes[defaultThemeSlug]` to `<Theme>`. Customize with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`. Use `theme eject` only when I ask for an independent source fork. Default to neutral if I have no preference, and show me the result before moving on.
Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
Add the core package and its `@stylexjs/stylex` peer dependency, plus a theme and the CLI.

Then run `astryx init` to install the AI agent cheat sheet (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md). It's non-interactive; no prompts; so it's safe for AI agents, CI, and scripts. Add `--all` for pointers to the theme and page-building workflows.

Upgrade every Astryx package your app lists in one command, to the same release. Each theme names the exact Core release it works with, so a theme left on an older release no longer matches the new Core.

npm install @astryxdesign/core@latest @astryxdesign/theme-neutral@latest @astryxdesign/cli@latest
astryx upgrade --from <old Core version> --apply

Add every other Astryx package your app lists to the same command, and pass the Core version you had before to `--from`. If your package manager holds new releases back, exempt the whole `@astryxdesign/*` scope; in pnpm, `minimumReleaseAgeExclude: ['@astryxdesign/*']`. Exempting only some of its packages installs packages from different releases side by side.

Install the CLI once for your computer too, and the astryx command works in any folder, for you and for any coding agent, even before a project exists. Inside a project, the project's own version still answers, so a global install never changes what your team and CI get. Keep it in the project as well; that is the recommended setup.
Project, global, or both: `astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`. Everything else about global mode: `astryx docs global`.

Components that accept an icon prop use IconType: either a semantic name string or a direct SVG component. The semantic names below are resolved through the global icon registry.
Jump to first, skip to start
Jump to last, skip to end
For icons not in the semantic list, pass an SVG component directly. Any ComponentType<SVGProps<SVGSVGElement>> works; Icon applies size and color styling automatically.

Themes can replace the default SVGs for any semantic name with the `icons` field in `defineTheme()`. This lets you swap the icon set (e.g. heroicons → lucide) without touching component code, and keeps lookup scoped to the active theme instead of mutating global defaults.

An entry can also be a function of the request, so the theme maps Icon's size to its icon library's own props or artwork. `Icon` calls it with `{size, variant}`, where `size` is the size it renders at (`xsm`, `sm`, `md`, or `lg`: an explicit `size`, else the owning component's default, else `md`). Reads that return one node — `getIcon()`, `useIcon()`, `getIconRegistry()`, and the theme's `icons` field — call it with `{size: 'md'}`. The same entry shape works in `registerIcons()`.

Keep the function pure and synchronous: it computes its result from the request only, with no hooks, DOM or SVG measurement, browser globals, network access, mutable module state, or side effects. Its result is final. Returning `null` draws no glyph instead of falling back to a registered or built-in icon, while a `null` or `undefined` node entry still falls back. A child theme that sets an entry for a key replaces the inherited entry for that key.

A theme lists the icon variant names it supports once, with `iconVariants` in `defineTheme()`. The list belongs to the whole theme, never to one icon, and Astryx defines no names of its own. Inside `defineTheme`, an entry function receives `variant` typed as the listed names, or `undefined`, so a misspelled name is a type error. An entry that receives `undefined` draws its normal artwork.
Listing variants and mapping them to artwork
A theme that `extends` another inherits its list unless it sets its own; a list it sets replaces the inherited one instead of merging with it.

Request a variant with `Icon`'s `variant` prop. The entry receives it only when the active theme lists it; an entry the theme inherited also needs the theme that defined it to list it. Otherwise the entry receives `undefined` and draws its normal artwork, so an unlisted variant never breaks rendering. A `registerIcons()` entry receives the variants the active theme lists, and a node entry draws the same node for every variant. An icon component passed directly to `Icon` never receives `variant`, and `variant` is never written to the DOM: it selects artwork, so there is no theming selector for it.

<Icon icon="info" variant="filled" />  // brandTheme: the filled artwork
<Icon icon="info" />                    // the normal artwork

An application declares the variant names it uses by augmenting `IconVariantMap` from `@astryxdesign/core/Icon`. `IconVariant` is those names, and an entry passed to `registerIcons()` receives `variant` typed as `IconVariant`. `astryx theme build` writes this augmentation for a built theme's list.
Declaring the variant names an application uses

A glyph that belongs to one component or library gets a namespaced key (`numberInput:stepperDown`, `richtext:bold`) instead of a new semantic name. It resolves through the same registry and a theme overrides it the same way, but the shared IconName list stays reserved for glyphs the whole system uses, so adding one does not make every downstream icon registry grow a key.
Owning and theming a namespaced icon
Outside core, pass a fallback to `getExtendedIcon(key, fallback)` so the glyph renders with no theme.

A component icon slot names why an icon appears in one component, such as `code-block-copy` for CodeBlock's copy button. `defineTheme({componentIcons})` maps a slot to one of the shared icon names. A theme can then change the icon one component uses without changing that name's artwork everywhere; `icons` still chooses the artwork for each name. Each component's docs list its slots, their state, and their fallbacks (`astryx component CodeBlock`).
Mapping a slot, with its state

A slot value is a shared icon name, `null` to hide the icon, or a partial request of `icon`, `variant`, and `size`. A field the request leaves out keeps the component's own value. A slot with state also accepts a pure, synchronous function of that state that returns a request: returning `null` hides the icon, and returning `undefined` changes nothing. A request `size` changes only the icon, never the control around it. Icon content a component's caller passes wins over the slot.

An unknown icon name, a variant the theme does not list, or a size other than `xsm`, `sm`, `md`, or `lg` is ignored for that field, with one development warning. A theme that extends another merges `componentIcons` by slot (`astryx docs author-a-theme`). `theme.componentIcons` reads back names, `null` values, and static requests, and leaves out the slots a function resolves.

Do not judge a file or surface in isolation. First learn the app context that makes a pattern correct, inconsistent, or incomplete.
Name what the app is for, who uses it, and the task this surface helps them complete.
Trace where the surface sits: its route, entry point, navigation path, parent shell, and the page or block pattern it is meant to use.
Inspect sibling surfaces that do the same or adjacent jobs. Record their shared headers, actions, layout primitives, spacing, density, states, and narrow-screen behavior.
Read project guidance, including the root and relevant nested `AGENTS.md` files. Record app-owned wrapper components and intentional app conventions.

Record the installed `@astryxdesign/core`, `@astryxdesign/cli`, and integration-package versions from the project manifest and lockfile. Run the installed invocation of `astryx component --list` to see core and integration components, then inspect app-owned wrappers that do not appear in that catalog.
List the real data states, roles and permissions, supported locales and RTL behavior, and mobile or narrow-width needs that affect the task.

Keep this context with the review. Mark anything you could not learn as `not inspected`. Do not flag a documented, intentional app convention merely because it differs from a generic pattern; cite the convention and verify that the user task and accessibility requirements still work.
Review one exact revision and one named product surface, route, or component in its app context. Pick the smallest review that can answer your question.
A fast check for raw elements, direct icons, custom styles, and unsupported imports
Source findings plus app context visible in the project. It cannot call the rendered product good.
App fit and task completion plus source quality, rendered layout, states, assets, project checks, and accessibility evidence.
An integration template that people copy
The shared criteria plus versioned scoring, metadata, packaging, copy, and clean-app checks in `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/write-good-templates/grade-template-with-agent`.

If all you have is one source file, run the source check anyway and use any project context that is available. Report clear source blockers; list missing app purpose, route, sibling patterns, shell, theme and density, installed components and versions, real states and roles, locale and mobile needs, revision, runnable app, rendered states, and project checks; and do not call the full product good.

`astryx` in this guide means the project's installed CLI invocation, such as its local binary or existing package script. If the project has no installed invocation, report that evidence gap instead of downloading a different CLI version for the review.

A screenshot can prove a visible result, but it cannot prove which imports, components, or styles produced it. Source alone cannot prove responsive behavior, interaction, color modes, or whether an asset loads. Mark anything outside the supplied evidence as `not inspected`.

Mark each category `good`, `needs work`, or `not inspected`. Cite the route, sibling surface, project guidance, theme, component catalog, or user requirement behind every context-dependent result; cite a file and line for every source result; and name the rendered state for every visual result. Never turn missing evidence into a pass. A blocker is a finding that prevents the surface from building, rendering, operating, letting the target user complete the task, or meeting an accessibility requirement. Other departures from the rubric are `needs work`.

The surface uses the app's established shell, page pattern, theme, density, wrappers, integrations, and interaction conventions unless a deviation is intentional and evidenced. The target user can complete the surface's job across the real states and permissions in scope.
Astryx owns each visible or interactive pattern for which it has a suitable component. Raw elements remain only when their native semantics are necessary or Astryx has no equivalent.
Icons render through `Icon`, `IconButton`, or the receiving component icon prop, not as raw SVG or a library component used directly.
Component props and design tokens do the work before custom StyleX declarations, inline styles, or classes. Each custom rule has a reason because no supported Astryx surface fits.
Astryx layout primitives express the visible structure, hierarchy, spacing, and responsive behavior without rebuilding the same patterns in raw containers or CSS.
Every image, font, and other asset is intentional, accessible, stable, and working from the product build path.
Public imports resolve, client boundaries are necessary, reachable states are handled, and no dead code or wrapper hides a finding.

Before calling a pattern custom or wrong, compare sibling surfaces and the installed component catalog. Reuse an app-owned wrapper or integration component when it already owns the job. A documented app convention is not a finding merely because it differs from a generic pattern; cite the convention and verify the user's task and accessibility requirements.

Keep a native element when its semantics are necessary and Astryx has no equivalent. Common examples are a `form` that provides native submission, `input type="hidden"` for native form state, and an `img` when no general Astryx image component fits.
Compare the route with sibling surfaces that do the same job. Identify the app's shared header, actions, shell, page pattern, spacing, and density before judging the target.
Inspect every JSX opening tag. Moving raw HTML behind a PascalCase helper does not make the underlying pattern an Astryx component.

Count every raw SVG element used as an icon, including `svg`, `path`, `circle`, `rect`, `line`, `polyline`, `polygon`, `ellipse`, and `g`. For an inline SVG helper, count its raw SVG elements once in the helper definition, not again at each render. Count each icon-library component rendered directly outside an Astryx icon surface.
Look up a possible replacement with `astryx component <Name> --dense`. Do not invent a component or prop that the installed version does not provide.
Run the installed `astryx component --list` and inspect app-owned wrappers before rebuilding a pattern. Prefer the component the app or one of its installed integrations already uses for the job.
Inspect every `stylex.create` declaration, inline style, `className`, and `stylex.props` use. Look for a component prop or token first.

When replacing a literal spacing value, read `astryx docs spacing --full` for the matching step or token and the target component doc for the prop's accepted scale. Do not guess a pixel-to-step mapping.
Choose the root that matches the surface. Use `Layout` for a page, `Center` for centered content, and `AppShell` only when the surface owns global application chrome.
Render realistic empty, loading, error, long-content, and interactive states. Check narrow and wide widths plus each supported color mode.
Verify the target roles and permissions, supported locales and RTL behavior, and mobile needs. Follow the real task from entry to completion instead of judging only the static page.

This shared rubric has no numeric score. It answers whether ordinary product code uses Astryx well without pretending that an inapplicable template field or missing browser state earned points. Motion serves two purposes: it makes interfaces easier to understand, and it makes them more pleasant to use. A panel animating open helps the eye track what changed and where new content sits in the layout. These moments reduce cognitive load and make the interface feel responsive.
At the same time, well-tuned motion gives an application a sense of craft and polish that users notice, even if they can't name it.
The design system provides duration and easing tokens that keep these moments consistent across your application.
Nine duration tokens in fast, medium, and slow bands, and `--duration-exit`, the standard dismissal duration, which follows `--duration-fast`.

Four easing curves. `--ease-standard` decelerates, for state changes. `--ease-entrance` is for things arriving and `--ease-move` for things moving on screen; a theme's `character` sets both, and at `standard` they equal `--ease-standard`. `--ease-exit` accelerates, for things leaving: it moves off from rest and leaves fast, so the travel stays visible for the whole duration, and it is the same at every `character`.

Some parts of the interface benefit from animation. Panels, dialogs, and collapsible sections are disorienting when they appear instantly, so animation gives the eye something to follow. Toasts and notifications need just enough entrance to be noticed without startling. State changes like a switch flipping or a selection highlighting feel more intentional with a brief transition.
The common thread is that these are moments where the user needs to understand what happened.

Table row hovers. List item highlights. Anything the user does dozens of times per minute. Adding perceptible duration to these interactions makes the interface feel like it's catching up to the cursor. Keep these fast enough that the user never notices a delay.

Animations that block interaction are worse. If a user has to wait for a panel to finish sliding before they can click something inside it, the animation has become an obstacle. Motion should never stand between the user and their next action.

Not everything needs an animated exit. Elements the user is moving away from, such as tooltips, hover cards, and dropdown menus, can disappear instantly. The user has already shifted their attention. Animate the exit only when it helps orient the user, like a panel closing or a dialog dismissing to reveal what's underneath.
When you do animate exit, match the entrance. A panel that slides in from the right should slide back out to the right.

Direction should match the action. Navigating deeper into content should feel like moving forward. Going back should feel like returning. This keeps the user oriented in the structure of the application.

Contextual UI should feel connected to its trigger. A dropdown should expand from the button that opened it. A popover should appear near the element it describes. This doesn't apply to global UI like command palettes or toasts, which have their own fixed positions.

Some users experience motion sensitivity; animation that feels polished to one person can cause discomfort for another. When the OS reduced-motion setting is on, Astryx components change at once under a mouse or trackpad, and under a finger they cross-fade instead of moving: opacity only, in 200 ms or less. A value that changes in place, such as a progress fill, takes its new value at once under any pointer. Do the same in your own animations with `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`, adding `(pointer: coarse)` for the touch cross-fade.

Set transition durations and easing from the motion tokens, so a theme that retunes motion retunes your animations too. Ease something arriving on `--ease-entrance` and something moving on screen on `--ease-move`, so it follows the theme's `character`, and something leaving on `--ease-exit`, which stays the same at every `character`.

A theme sets how motion feels with two knobs in `defineTheme`'s `motion`. They drive the CSS motion tokens, and `tempo` also times the springs of touch motion; those springs don't follow `character` yet. Every theme follows each person's Reduce Motion setting; no theme loosens it.
`tempo` scales every motion duration: 1 is Astryx's own, 0.75 the quickest and 1.5 the slowest (values outside are clamped).

`character` sets how lively motion is: `'crisp'` decelerates without overshoot, `'standard'` is Astryx's own, and `'expressive'` overshoots slightly on entrances and moves. Exits and fades never overshoot.

Some motion never follows the knobs, because it tracks a finger or the system: finger tracking, momentum and the rubber band, the on-screen keyboard, the press model's onset delay, cancel distance and tap flash (its release fade follows tempo), hover-intent delays, gesture thresholds, the loops of busy indicators such as Spinner and Skeleton, and the 200 ms Reduce Motion cross-fade.

Precedence, lowest to highest: the knobs, then a duration scale (`fast`, `medium`, `slow`, `ratio`) for the durations it sets, then explicit `tokens`. A theme with no `motion` renders exactly as before.
Animate transitions that involve spatial change: panels opening, content expanding, elements entering the screen.
Use fast tokens for small, frequent interactions. Use medium tokens for larger transitions that rearrange the layout.
Honor reduced motion preferences at the OS level.
Let hover states or high-frequency interactions feel like they're lagging behind the user.
Let animation delay when a user can interact with new content. The transition should complete before (or not block) the next action.
Move elements in ways that contradict where they came from or where they're going.

A design system that prioritizes consistency, adaptability, and developer experience. Every decision flows from a few core ideas:
Components over primitives: use components for everything they cover before reaching for raw HTML
Semantic tokens over hardcoded values: colors, spacing, and radii are named by purpose, not appearance
Theme-agnostic code: your app code never references specific colors or measurements, so themes and dark mode work automatically
Open internals: every primitive is exported and composable, so you can build on top of it without fighting it
Eight rules that keep app code on-system.
Use components for everything they cover
Page layout is frame-first: pick the shell and budget regions before writing content (see `astryx docs layout`)
Dense data renders as rows (Table, List/Item), edge-to-edge with dividers; Card is for widgets, galleries, and settings groups
StyleX or Tailwind for custom styling; both are first-class (see `astryx docs styling`)
Semantic tokens, not hardcoded values (see `astryx docs tokens`)
CSS custom properties for colors, not hex values
Use useLinkComponent() for navigation so consumers can plug in their framework router via LinkProvider

The design system supports multiple styling approaches. Every component accepts an `xstyle` prop for StyleX style overrides via `stylex.create()`. For layout and wrapper styling outside of components, use StyleX or Tailwind utilities; both resolve to the same design tokens.
See `astryx docs styling` for the complete guide with examples.
Patterns that break theming, routing, or layout, and what to use instead.
Inline styles on raw elements. Use xstyle on components
Hardcoded colors (#fff). Use var(--color-*) or Tailwind semantic classes (text-primary, bg-surface)
Hardcoded spacing (16px). Use spacing tokens or Tailwind spacing utilities
Hardcoded <a> elements. Use useLinkComponent() so consumers can swap in their framework router via LinkProvider
Wrapping every list item or page section in a Card. Decide the frame first; dense data renders as rows (see `astryx docs layout`)
Badge as decoration. Reserve Badge for counts and enumerated states; use StatusDot or Token for status
Inventing props. Read component docs first

The radius scale uses a semantic naming system: inner → element → container → page. Each level fits a specific context. Themes can multiply the entire scale via a radius multiplier, with --radius-none and --radius-full as fixed anchors.
Inside a padded, rounded container, give nested elements a radius of outer radius minus padding so the curves stay concentric. Card does not do this for your content.
Use --radius-element for interactive controls (buttons, inputs, selectors).
Use --radius-container for content containers (cards, panels, dialogs).
Use --radius-full for pill shapes (badges, tags, avatar status dots).
Use --radius-page for small elements; it's meant for page-level containers.
Hardcode radius values; they won't scale with theme radius multipliers.

The design system uses a 4px base-unit spacing scale, written in rem so gaps and padding grow with the reader's browser font size the way text does: each step is 0.25rem, which is 4px at the default 16px root. Component gap props accept step values that map to these tokens. The scale provides fine-grained control at the small end (2px, 4px, 6px) and consistent rhythm at larger sizes (multiples of 4px).
Fifteen spacing tokens, from 0 to 3rem (0px to 48px at the default 16px root).

Stack, HStack, VStack, Grid, Toolbar, OverflowList, and ChatMessageList take a `gap` step: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, or 10 (×4px). Carousel takes the steps from 0 to 4. For custom layouts, use the spacing tokens in StyleX.

Use component gap props when available; they handle automatic spacing compensation.
Stick to the scale for consistency. If a value isn't on the scale, reconsider the design.
Use smaller steps (0.5–2) for tight internal spacing and larger steps (4–8) for section gaps.
Use arbitrary pixel values outside the scale.
Mix spacing tokens with raw px/rem values in the same component.

`astryx swizzle <Component>` writes an `astryx-swizzle.json` marker into an output folder it owns (one the copy creates, an empty one, or one it marked before); every module under that folder then compiles as Astryx source, so keep copies in a folder of their own, such as the default `components/astryx`. For a folder that already holds other files it writes no marker and says how to add one by hand. With `@astryxdesign/build`'s Babel, PostCSS and Vite integrations, or `withAstryx()` under webpack, a copy under that folder compiles into `astryx-base`, below `astryx-theme`, so theme component overrides reach it as they reach the package component. Under Turbopack, and with the stock StyleX plugins above, a copy's rules land in your own styles, above `astryx-theme`, and theme component overrides do not reach it.

`theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported theme becomes the default. `theme use <slug>` changes that default, and `theme remove <slug>` removes a non-default theme.

Customize a package theme with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`, then build and add that local theme. Use `theme eject` only when you want an independent source fork that no longer receives the package owner's updates. For the full authoring guide, see `astryx docs author-a-theme`.

A theme copied by the released `theme add` stays app source. The upgrade does not move, delete, or rewrite it. It only writes the missing same-stem descriptor with `maintained: false`, so the copy becomes a local theme.

Before the upgrade runs, theme commands skip a descriptor-less copy in `src/themes`. `theme list` and doctor name it as unmigrated and show the upgrade command. A script that meant to copy source now runs `theme eject` with the same arguments. A script that meant to make the app use a theme runs `theme add`.

`ASTRYX_THEME` is no longer read. Run `theme add <slug>` and `theme use <slug>` to choose the default in a generated app theme module. When that module exists, component metadata reads its recorded default theme. Without the module, the released `package.json#astryx.theme` lookup keeps its meaning.

The design system is built to be AI-friendly: consistent naming, predictable prop patterns, and a CLI that feeds structured documentation directly into AI context windows. But models still need the right context to avoid falling back to generic React patterns or inventing props.
The CLI includes a built-in agent docs system that generates context files for your AI tool of choice. One command sets up everything your AI needs to write correct component code.
Tell your AI to install the CLI and set itself up:
Install @astryxdesign/cli and run `astryx init --features agents` to set up your Astryx context. Read the generated file.

That's it. The `init --features agents` command generates everything your AI needs (component index, behavioral rules, CLI reference, and package guidance from configured integrations) from the installed project. After a dependency bump, `astryx upgrade --from <old version>` reports a stale block and adding `--apply` refreshes it.

By default this writes the instructions to `AGENTS.md` (the tool-agnostic standard most agents read), in the project root: the nearest folder whose `package.json` declares an Astryx package, else the nearest with any `package.json`. The search stops at the repository root. In the home folder, or in a settings folder in it outside a project, init writes no agent docs: every folder of the home folder whose name starts with a dot (`~/.claude`, `~/.gemini`, `~/.codex`) is a settings folder, and such a folder itself never counts as a project, even with a `package.json`; a project below it with its own `package.json`, such as an agent worktree, is set up normally. Claude Code skips `AGENTS.md` when the project has a `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so init also writes them to that file, even when it imports `AGENTS.md`: Claude Code does not follow that import in a session started in a subfolder. When both files exist, root `CLAUDE.md` gets the copy and a copy in `.claude/CLAUDE.md` is removed, unless the project ignores `CLAUDE.md`, in which case a `.claude/CLAUDE.md` the project commits keeps a copy. Gemini CLI reads only `GEMINI.md`, so init adds a one-line import of `AGENTS.md` there, unless `GEMINI.md` already imports it. `upgrade` keeps the copies in sync. The block between the Astryx markers belongs to Astryx: init and `upgrade` write, refresh, and remove it whatever the project's ignore rules or generated markers say, and never change the text around it. To target a specific tool's file instead:

astryx init --features agents --agent claude    # CLAUDE.md if present, else .claude/CLAUDE.md
astryx init --features agents --agent cursor    # .cursorrules if present, else AGENTS.md
astryx init --features agents --agent codex     # AGENTS.md (Copilot, Codex, etc.)
astryx init --features agents --agent hermes    # .hermes.md or HERMES.md if present, else AGENTS.md
astryx init --features agents --agent muse      # AGENTS.md (Muse)
astryx init --features agents --agent all       # every agent file present except GEMINI.md, else AGENTS.md and .claude/CLAUDE.md

With `--agent all`, `GEMINI.md` keeps its one-line import of `AGENTS.md`. With `--agent claude` or `--agent all`, as by default, when `CLAUDE.md` gets the instructions, `.claude/CLAUDE.md` gets none and a copy already there is removed, unless the project ignores `CLAUDE.md`: a fresh clone does not have it, so a `.claude/CLAUDE.md` the project commits gets a copy too, with `--agent claude` and `--agent all` alike. `init --remove-agents` removes them at the project root and in the folder it runs in.

For agents that work outside any one project, your global install keeps one short Astryx skill, `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, linked into the skill folders agent tools read, such as `~/.claude/skills/astryx`. It tells agents Astryx is there and when to use it; `astryx init --user` writes it now or, with `--remove-agents`, turns it off. Inside a project, agents follow that project's own agent docs. See `astryx docs global/computer-agent-guide`.
The generated context teaches your AI a 3-step workflow before writing any UI code:
`astryx build "<idea>"`: get the page template to start from (always one: the closest match, or the app shell), two other templates, and the blocks and components for the parts it lacks
`astryx template <name> <path>`: scaffold that template into the project, keep its frame and spacing, and replace its content
`astryx component <Name>`: read props and examples for every component used

It also includes rules that prevent common mistakes (start every page from a template, no raw divs, no style={{}}, use tokens not magic values), a CLI quick reference, and package-labeled integration guidance when a configured manifest declares `agentDocs`. After setup, you shouldn't need to manually correct your AI on these conventions; the agent docs handle it at the system level.

Cursor reads project rules from `.cursor/rules/`. To keep the Astryx context in a rule of its own, write it there. Give a path relative to the project root, such as `.cursor/rules/astryx.mdc`; an absolute path is refused.

AI agents frequently invoke the CLI with incorrect paths (e.g. node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/bin/docs.mjs instead of astryx.mjs), leading to silent failures. Adding an npm script alias with the correct path eliminates this entirely.
With this alias, agents run `npm run astryx -- component --list` instead of guessing the binary path. The `--` separator is standard npm convention for passing flags to scripts.

npm run astryx -- component --list
npm run astryx -- component Dialog --dense
npm run astryx -- docs styling --full --detail brief
npm run astryx -- docs tokens --dense

For a shorter read, add `--detail brief` (one line per section) or `--detail compact`. `--dense` swaps in a shorter text where a doc ships one. Use them when pasting CLI output into a web-based AI tool like ChatGPT or Claude.

astryx docs styling --full --detail brief
astryx component Dialog --detail compact
astryx docs principles --dense

Astryx ships a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that any MCP-compatible AI tool can connect to. Instead of manually pasting CLI output, the AI can query the Astryx design system directly, searching for components, reading full documentation, and pulling code examples on demand.
The MCP server exposes two tools: search(query) for discovering components, doc topics, and templates; and get(name) for retrieving full documentation with props, usage, and examples.

Add the server to your MCP config file. The entry is a remote HTTP server, and the exact shape differs per client, so use the snippet for the tool you run. An entry with an unrecognized transport is skipped with a warning rather than an error, which reads as a server that connects but exposes no tools.
Claude Code can also write that entry from the terminal:
claude mcp add --transport http astryx https://astryx.atmeta.com/mcp
Cursor (.cursor/mcp.json) - remote servers take no type field
Claude Desktop is the exception: claude_desktop_config.json holds local stdio servers, so a remote server is added through Settings, then Connectors, then Add custom connector, pasting the URL above.

Once connected, your AI tool can search for components by natural language (e.g. "dropdown menu", "success message") and retrieve full documentation without any manual CLI invocation. The server uses the same keyword index from component docs, so search quality improves automatically as component documentation is updated.

`integration add codemod` writes a codemod into a folder named after a version. Apps run it with `astryx upgrade` to migrate their code.

codemods/
  0.7.0/
    rename-delay.mjs         # the codemod
    rename-delay.test.mjs    # skipped: a test file
    __tests__/               # skipped: a test folder

The first add declares `codemods: './codemods'` in `astryx.integration.mjs`. The codemod's id is its path inside the version folder, without the extension: `rename-delay`. An id must be unique across all version folders in the package.

The loader skips `*.test.*`, `*.spec.*`, and `*.fixture.*` files and everything under `__tests__/` or `__fixtures__/`, so tests can sit beside the codemod. The folder name decides when an app runs the codemod; see "Choose when a codemod runs".
A codemod default-exports a plain object with a `type`, a `title`, and a `transform` function. `transform` returns the new source, or `null` to leave the file as it is.

`type: 'code'` rewrites the app's source files that match `fileExtensions`. `type: 'config'` rewrites the app's `astryx.config` file instead, and runs before code codemods. `title` shows in the upgrade output, and `api.jscodeshift` is a jscodeshift instance for the file. Every field is in `astryx docs authoring codemod`.
Two rules decide whether an app's `astryx upgrade` runs your codemods: the app's Core versions, and whether the app names your package.

Version folders are matched against the app's `@astryxdesign/core` versions, not your package's version. `upgrade --from <version>` runs each folder above `--from`, up to and including the Core version installed in the app. With Core 0.7.0 installed, `--from 0.6.3` runs `0.7.0/`, and `--from 0.7.0` runs nothing. A folder named after your own release, such as `1.0.0/`, waits until the app has Core 1.0.0.

`upgrade` runs your codemods only when the app lists your package in `integrations` in its `astryx.config`, or passes `--integration @acme/astryx-widgets`. Having your package installed is not enough: the run then skips your codemods with no warning.
An app previews codemods with `astryx upgrade` and writes the changes with `--apply`. Without `--apply`, nothing on disk changes.

# Preview each codemod and the files it would change
astryx upgrade --from 0.6.3 --integration @acme/astryx-widgets
# Write the changes
astryx upgrade --from 0.6.3 --integration @acme/astryx-widgets --apply

Integrations: @acme/astryx-widgets
<n> codemods to run (dry run)
Applying integration codemods...
  Rename AcmeCarousel delay to interval (v0.7.0, @acme/astryx-widgets)
!     ~ src/Hero.tsx (would change)
`<n>` counts Core's codemods for the same versions too: they run first and print above `Integrations:`. To run only yours, as when you test it, add `--codemod rename-delay`.

`--from` is the Core version the app had before it upgraded. The run scans `./src` unless the app passes `--path`, and it never writes a file the app marks as generated, vendored, or ignored; see `astryx docs cli/commands/upgrade`. `upgrade --list` shows only Core codemods.
An integration manifest has no `hooks` field. Commands that run after codemods, such as a formatter, are the app's to set, in `hooks.postCodemod` in its `astryx.config`.

In global mode: inside an app, `upgrade` runs with the release equal to the app's Core, whichever copy of the CLI the user starts, and only the codemods of integrations the app installs run. Outside a project, `upgrade` lists codemods and migrates nothing. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs cli/commands/upgrade`.

Apps copy the component doc's `import` field into their code, so that exact specifier must resolve from your packed package. `integration add` writes it together with an `exports` entry in package.json.
Add writes the entry only when package.json already has an `exports` map, so start every package with `"exports": {}`.

A file does not have to be named after its component. When `Slides.tsx` exports `AcmeCarousel` and nothing named `Slides`, keep the doc beside it as `Slides.doc.mjs` and set its `name` to `AcmeCarousel`: apps list, search and open the component by that name, and `integration verify` checks that its import exports `AcmeCarousel`. A file that exports its own name keeps that name. A package that names its files in kebab case works the same way: `acme-gallery.doc.mjs` beside `acme-gallery.tsx` sets `name: 'AcmeGallery'`.

The file name still opens the doc. A name that Core or another doc's file already has stays theirs, and so does a Core name your package replaces: with `Badge.doc.mjs` naming `AcmeBadge`, `astryx component Badge` opens Core's `Badge`, and `--package` with your package name reaches yours.

`integration verify` unpacks the packed package into a temporary app, resolves each documented import, and checks that the module exports the documented component name. Its `--json` output names each failure by code.
`component_import_unresolvable` means the exports map has no entry for the documented import.
`component_export_missing` means the module does not export the documented name, or package.json has no exports map.
`typescript_extension_in_specifier` means the public import ends in `.ts` or `.tsx`.
To import from the package root, set `import: '@acme/astryx-widgets'` and re-export the component from the file that `exports["."]` points to. See `astryx docs cli/commands/integration-verify`.

`doctor integration components` compares every props table in your component docs, hidden docs and every family entry included, with the props the component's TypeScript declares. Run it in your package after you change a component or its doc.

severity:  [warn]
component: AcmeCarousel
prop:      loop
kind:      not_in_code
message:   "loop" is documented, but AcmeCarousel's props have no "loop".
doc:       components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
source:    components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
docType:   boolean

1 prop(s) differ between the docs and the code in 1 of 1 component(s) compared (TypeScript 6.0.3). These are warnings: update the doc, or the code if the doc is right.
A doc's own `props` describe the export its `name` names. In a family doc, each entry describes its own export. A hook entry documents parameters and returns, so it is not compared.

It reads props with the `typescript` your package installs, and reads your package's `tsconfig.json` the way `tsc -p` does. It finds TypeScript the way the docs check does, TypeScript 7 included (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/check-your-docs`). Without a usable one it prints `[skip] Props not compared` and the reason.
Findings are warnings and leave the exit code at 0. Read them before you publish. With `--json`, they are in `data.propDrift.findings`.
Each finding's `kind` says what differs. Fix the doc, or the code if the doc is right.
The doc lists a prop the component's props do not have
Remove it from the doc, or add it to the code. A name an index signature takes, such as `data-*`, counts as present
Your package declares a prop the doc does not list, or builds one with a mapped type, such as `Partial<Record<'sm' | 'md', string>>`

Document it. Props from React, the DOM, or another package are never asked for, and neither are props whose keys another package defines (`keyof CSSProperties`, behind an alias or not), `className`, `style`, `xstyle`, `data-testid`, `ref`, `key`, or a prop whose JSDoc has `@internal`. A deprecated prop is still a prop: document it until you remove it. Write each fact in one topic. When two of your topics, or one of yours and a Core topic, repeat 10 or more words of prose word for word, the check lists the pair as a `copied_passage` warning. It names the topic that keeps the text (a Core topic, or of your two the one the passage fits) and the line in the other where to put the link instead (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/links`). Code and examples are not compared, and a topic may carry the text of the Core topic it replaces. A run with fewer than 4 distinct content words (words other than function words such as "the", "in" or "it"), or one that three or more topics share (a series lead-in), is not listed. Each listed pair is also a warning (`copied_passage`): `doctor integration docs` still exits 0, and `integration check --strict` fails until you fix it.

Keep docs dense. The check lists, as a `doc_fluff` warning, each padding phrase in your prose, with its file line and what to write instead, and each topic of 80 or more prose words in which fewer than half the words carry content (words other than function words such as the, and, in), with its measured share and the floor of 0.5. `doctor integration docs` still exits 0, and `integration check --strict` fails until you cut it. Code, examples, and quoted text are not read. The phrases: `it's important to note`, `it is important to note`, `important to note that`, `it's worth noting`, `it is worth noting`, `worth noting that`, `it should be noted`, `please note`, `note that` (opening a sentence), `as mentioned above`, `as mentioned earlier`, `as mentioned before`, `as noted above`, `as you can see`, `needless to say`, `in order to`, `due to the fact that`, `for the purpose of`, `at this point in time`, `in other words`, `basically`, `essentially`, `obviously`.

Set `replaces` to take over an existing topic, such as Core's `getting-started`. Readers who open the old name get your topic.

astryx integration add doc acme-getting-started --replaces getting-started
# The old name now opens your topic
astryx docs getting-started

The docs list shows your topic in place of the old one. Because your topic has its own `name`, the old name keeps resolving to it, so links and agents that learned the old name still land on your topic.
Set `extends` to merge sections into an existing topic instead of owning it. A section replaces the base section it matches, and a section that matches none is added at the end.

astryx integration add doc acme-theming --extends theme
astryx docs theme --index

Read the base topic's keys with `--index`, and give a section that replaces one that key as its `id`. A section that replaces one keeps its place. A section without an `id` matches only a base section with exactly its title, or one whose `id` is the key its title makes, so `Integration Themes` is added beside a base `Integration themes` that has no `id`.

A theme token is a named slot that Astryx components read for a value — `--color-accent` for the accent color, and so on. Components never read your palette directly; they read tokens. Defining a theme means pointing each token at a palette shade, so the components wear your colors.
Import the palette in `oceanTheme.ts` and point your tokens at its stops. Each token takes a `[light, dark]` pair — the shade to use in light mode and the one in dark mode.

Local imports must stay inside the theme folder. One that leaves it, such as `../../shared/colors`, fails with `invalid_theme`, and every theme in the package disappears from `theme list`. `astryx theme template` writes a file that explains every `defineTheme` field. For the full token set and component theming, read `astryx docs author-a-theme`.

To base a theme on an existing one, `extends` it: import the base theme and override only the tokens you change. Add the derived theme with `integration add theme ocean-contrast`, and import the base from its built package export, since local imports cannot leave the theme folder. The derived theme keeps a live link to the base and picks up its later changes when you rebuild it — unlike `--from`, which forks a copy (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/themes/add-a-theme`).

Each `[light, dark]` pair compiles to a `light-dark()` value, which switches only colors. Give it colors. For a value that is not a plain color — a gradient — put `light-dark()` on each color stop, not around the whole value: `light-dark()` takes two colors, so wrapping whole gradients makes the value invalid where the token is used, and `theme build` does not warn.

A theme names its typefaces in `typography`: `body`, `heading`, and `code`, each with a `family` and `fallbacks`. These set the `--font-family-*` tokens every component reads. Always give real `fallbacks` so text stays readable before the font loads, or if it never does. `heading` inherits `family` and `fallbacks` from `body` when you omit them.
The full type scale and font roles are in `astryx docs author-a-theme`.

Naming a family does not load it. When the theme uses non-system fonts, add `<slug>.fonts.css` beside the built module and production CSS, then export it as `./themes/<slug>.fonts.css`. `theme add` imports that stylesheet with the built theme.

The stylesheet can contain self-hosted `@font-face` rules or import a hosted stylesheet. A hosted `@import` is simple, but it delays loading compared with a preconnected `<link>`; choose that trade-off deliberately. Doctor warns when it cannot prove the loader — a hosted `@import`, or no font stylesheet while the app loads the family itself — but the warning does not fail the app.
Load every weight and style the theme uses. Do not let the browser synthesize bold or italic.
Include self-hosted font files and their licenses in the packed package.
Keep CSS and font assets side-effectful so a bundler does not remove the loader.
Run `integration verify`; it fails when an exported font stylesheet cannot resolve, but it does not check the font files the stylesheet names.

Before publishing, run `integration verify`. Then install the package in a clean app, run `theme add`, apply the generated theme, and open it in a browser. The source, packed exports, and applied result form one chain; check the last step too.
Text renders in the named families at every weight and style — the italic face resolves, not a synthesized slant.
Every font request succeeds; nothing silently falls back to a system font.
Color pairs still meet contrast in both light and dark mode.

A theme needs dozens of related colors — shades of each brand color for backgrounds, borders, text, and states, in both light and dark mode. A palette is that full set of shades. Rather than hand-pick every one, you name a few seed colors and generate the rest, so the shades stay consistent.

You write a short config naming each color family and its seed, then run `theme palette generate`. It expands each seed into a full light and dark ramp — the scale of shades — and writes the result into the theme folder, where your theme tokens point at it (see `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/themes/define-the-theme`). Keep the config and the generated palette together in that folder.
The smallest config is one color family: an `id` to name it and a `seed` color to grow it from. Save it as `themes/ocean/palette.config.json`:

# Print the palette without writing files
astryx theme palette generate themes/ocean/palette.config.json
# Write the palette and its receipt
astryx theme palette generate themes/ocean/palette.config.json \
  --out themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.ts

[ok] Wrote themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.ts

[ok] Wrote themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.receipt.json

Review and edit the candidate before adopting it as theme-owned palette data.

The command writes two files. `ocean.palette.ts` is the palette your theme tokens will read: it exports `black`, `white`, and `palette` — a ramp of 21 shades (stops `0` to `100`) for both `light` and `dark`. The `.receipt.json` beside it records the exact seeds and settings, so you can regenerate the same palette later. A second run leaves both files alone unless you pass `--overwrite`.

Add `--preview <file>.html` to also get a web page showing every shade, so you can eyeball the palette in a browser. Write it outside `themes/` so it does not ship in your package. Every option is in `astryx docs cli/commands/theme-palette-generate`, and the config it reads is described in `astryx docs cli/api/functions/generate-tonal-palette`.

Install the integration, then run `theme add` with its slug and package. The command records the package owner and regenerates one app theme module that imports the built theme, production CSS, and optional font CSS. Use `theme eject` only to copy source into an independent local fork.

npm install @acme/astryx-widgets
astryx theme add ocean --package @acme/astryx-widgets

`theme list` shows the available, added, and default themes. Use `theme use <slug>` to change the default, `theme remove <slug>` to stop importing one, and `theme eject <slug>` only when the app needs an independent source fork. Applying a theme — `mode`, SSR, and the production build — works the same for every theme; see `astryx docs use-a-theme`.

For ordinary customization, do not copy the package source. Import the built theme and derive a new one with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`, overriding only the tokens the app changes. Use `theme eject` only when the app must own an independent source fork. See `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/themes/define-the-theme`.

In global mode: install the theme package in each app that uses the theme; inside a project, the CLI ignores packages installed for the computer. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.
