The astryx.integration.* manifest that sits beside an integration package's package.json. It can preserve a stable provider identity across a package rename, and points the CLI at the package's components, templates, codemods, doc topics, source themes, managed agent guidance, issue tracker, and the command its users run the CLI with. Every field is optional.

The name that marks this package as the source of everything it contributes. Leave it out to use the package name from package.json. Set it to the old name only during a rename, so the IDs of what the package already contributed stay the same. If two packages use the same name here, the one you are working on wins; otherwise the one the CLI reads first wins, and the CLI warns about the other. Example: '@acme/widgets'.
The folder that holds your components and their docs, relative to package.json. Example: './src/components'.
The folder that holds your templates, relative to package.json. Example: './src/templates'.
The folder that holds your codemods, relative to package.json. Example: './codemods'.

The folder that holds your doc topics, relative to package.json. Every {topic}.doc.{ts,mjs,js} under it shows up in `astryx docs`: a flat topic next to the built-in topics, where it can set `replaces` or `extends` to take over a built-in topic or add to it, and a guide with `placement` at its own route in the docs tree, under a namespace doc of the same package. Example: './docs'.

The folder that holds your themes, relative to package.json, with one folder per theme. Each theme folder has the theme source and a matching .doc.mjs file with the same name. Installed themes show up in `astryx theme list`; `theme add` imports their built package exports, and `theme eject` creates an editable local fork. Example: './themes'.

Lines of guidance your package adds to the end of the agent instructions the CLI manages. The CLI owns the heading, labels, bullets, and which files it writes. Example: { append: ['Run acme verify.'] }.

Where people file issues for this package: an absolute URL, such as its GitHub issues page. A value that is not a URL fails the whole manifest; the scheme is not checked. Nothing warns when it is missing, but without it `astryx gap-report` about this package fails unless the project or a loaded integration has a gapReport handler, and `astryx swizzle` prints no feedback link for this package's components. When no handler is loaded, a github.com issues URL is filed with the GitHub CLI once the reporter passes `--confirm-public`; any other URL is returned for the reporter to open. Example: 'https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues'.
Link to this integration's docs site, such as its home page. Catalogs that list the package may show it. Example: 'https://widgets.acme.dev'.

The command your users run the Astryx CLI with, when it is not their package manager, such as a wrapper your company ships. Every command the CLI prints in an app that loads your package starts with it, in place of `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`: hints, errors, Doctor fixes, and doc text. One line, without a subcommand. If two loaded packages set different commands, neither is used and `astryx doctor` warns. An invalid value is ignored with an `invalid_cli_command` warning, and the rest of the manifest still loads. JSON output keeps commands bare. Example: 'acme astryx'.

In global mode: a manifest loads the same way when users install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI, and then applies in folders outside any project; inside a project, only if the project installs it. Peer ranges for `@astryxdesign/core` and `@astryxdesign/cli` are checked against the global CLI's release. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

The provider name defaults to the package name in package.json. During a rename, set `providerId` to the old package name so the IDs of what the package already contributed stay the same. The package version always comes from package.json.

`agentDocs.append` may contain at most eight lines. Each line is a trimmed, non-blank string of at most 240 Unicode code points with no line separators, control characters, NUL, or Astryx/XDS managed-marker text. The configured project may contain at most 32 integration lines total. Write each command in a line as a bare `astryx` command; the managed block says once, before your lines, how the app starts the CLI.

Set `cliCommand` only when your users run the CLI with a command other than their package manager's, such as `acme astryx`. The CLI picks the command it prints in this order: the `cliCommand` of the loaded integrations when they name one command, then the command a host tool names, then the package manager's. Two different `cliCommand` values cancel out, and `astryx doctor` warns in its `cli-command` check. See `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/configuration/cli-command`.

A themes root is version-gated: an older CLI lists and adds none of its themes. Depending on its age, that CLI ignores `themes` with an `unknown_manifest_key` warning and loads every other contribution kind, reports the root as invalid because it expects the earlier `manifest.json` theme catalog, or, if it is old enough to treat an unknown field as an error, rejects the whole manifest, so the package contributes nothing there.

Validate the manifest with `astryx doctor integration validate`. At the load boundary, a known field of the wrong type is an error, issuesUrl and docsiteUrl must be valid URLs, and unknown fields become warnings so an older CLI can still load the fields it understands. Before publishing, also run `templates`, `components`, and `docs` under the same `doctor integration` group. Those leaves compare authored identities with Core and explain whether an overlap is intentional or needs a rename.

The optional astryx.config.* file at your project root. Declares which integrations to load, where to route issue links, post-codemod hooks, local debug-log and gap-report handlers, a discover source, and experimental layout components. All optional; {} is valid.
Package names of Astryx integrations to load alongside core. Example: ['@acme/astryx-widgets'].

Where reports about Core go: `astryx gap-report` routes a Core report here when no handler is loaded, gapReport handlers receive it as `report.target.issuesUrl`, and `astryx swizzle` prints it as the feedback link for a Core component. A report or swizzle for an integration's component uses that integration's own issuesUrl, never this one. An absolute URL; a value that is not a URL makes the config invalid. Default: 'https://github.com/meta/astryx/issues/new'.

Commands to run after `astryx upgrade` changes files (e.g. re-run your formatter). Each hook is an object `{name?, buildCommand}`: buildCommand gets `{packageDir, files}` and returns `{command, args?, options?}` to run, or null to skip. A dry run prints each command instead of running it.

Record every command run. The handler is synchronous; promises are not awaited and output goes to stderr. Declare `debug` directly in this file so early commands can discover it. An integration can supply one too, as a `debug` named export from its manifest. Every handler runs: yours first, then each integration's in load order (the `integrations` list, then autolinked ones). A handler that throws is skipped; the others still run and the command's result does not change. Set `{"astryx": {"inheritDebug": false}}` in package.json to take only your own. Example: event => appendFileSync('runs.ndjson', JSON.stringify(event) + '\n').

Handle explicit gap reports in addition to every loaded integration handler. The project handler runs first. Public handlers require caller consent; internal handlers always run. Example: { audience: 'internal', async handle(report, {signal}) { return sendGap(report, {signal}); } }.

Tell `astryx discover` which integrations this project could add: an async function that returns a catalog. An integration can provide one too, as a `discover` named export from its manifest. Discover calls every source, yours first, and one that fails never hides the others. Discover only reads; your package manager installs. Example: async ({signal, package: name, version}) => fetchCatalog({signal, name, version}).
Unstable features; may change without a breaking bump.
Custom components for the removed layout expander, keyed by component name. The CLI still validates the field, so an entry without a string `from` makes `astryx.config` invalid, but nothing reads it.
Send every command run somewhere of your own

The config is validated at load with a strict schema: an unknown key, a misspelled one included, or a value of the wrong type makes the whole file invalid. `astryx gap-report`, `astryx discover`, and `astryx upgrade` stop with the error, and `astryx doctor` fails its `config` check (exit 1). Reads such as `component`, `docs`, `search`, `template`, and `theme` carry on silently as if there were no config and no integrations, and no debug handler runs, so run `astryx doctor` after editing the file.

One recorded CLI run: what a `debug` handler receives, whether it is set in astryx.config or exported by an integration manifest. There is exactly one event per run, and every field is present by the time a handler sees it.
Applies to: The argument of a `debug` handler
Version of the recorded shape: 1, 2, or 3. A field that changes meaning gets a new version, so switch on this.
Unique per run. Deduplicate on it.
When the run started, as ISO 8601.
When the run ended, as ISO 8601.
How long the run took, in milliseconds.
The full command name. Empty when astryx ran without a command. Example: 'theme build'.
The command name split into segments. Example: ['theme', 'build'].
The arguments after the binary, scrubbed.
Positional arguments, keyed by their declared names.
The command options, as the CLI resolved them.
Where each option value came from: 'cli', 'default', 'env', 'config', or 'implied'. The keys match `options`.
The root flags, such as --json, --detail, and --lang.
The process exit code. When a signal ended the run, 128 plus the signal number.
The signal that ended the run, such as 'SIGINT'. Null otherwise.
The failure: `name`, `message`, `code`, and `stack`. Branch on `code`, never on `message`. Null when nothing failed.
What the run answered with: JSON mode, the envelope types, the result count and kind, and the stdout and stderr it printed, scrubbed and cut at the capture limit.
Runtime facts: the CLI and Node versions, platform, CI, package manager, and whether a person, an AI agent, or automation ran the command. It never holds a hostname, a user name, or a raw session ID.
The project the command ran in, as flags and counts. It never holds package names.
Whether the values in the record were scrubbed. It is true on every event a handler receives. When it is false, treat the log as sensitive.
Keep a local log of the runs that failed

The shape only grows: fields are added, never removed or given a new meaning. When a meaning must change, `schemaVersion` gets a new value. In version 3, a null `output.resultKind` means the run never reached an answer, so do not count it together with a version 1 or 2 null.
The handler runs synchronously as the process exits, so a promise it returns is never awaited. It gets a copy of the event, and anything it throws is ignored.
Import DebugEventOutput, DebugEventEnv, DebugEventProject, and DebugEventError from @astryxdesign/cli/authoring for the fields of `output`, `env`, `project`, and `error`.

A handler for `astryx gap-report`: a plain object with an `audience` and a `handle` function. Set it as `gapReport` in astryx.config, or export it as `gapReport` from an integration manifest. Handlers add up rather than replace each other: the project handler first, then each loaded integration's in load order (the `integrations` list, then autolinked ones), whichever package the report is about.
Applies to: `gapReport` in astryx.config.*, or the `gapReport` named export of astryx.integration.*
Whether the destination is internal to your organization or public. A public handler runs only when the caller agrees; an internal handler always runs.
Gets the report and returns a receipt. It can be async, and the CLI waits at most 30 seconds for it. A throw, a timeout, or an invalid receipt is a failed delivery, and the other handlers still run.
The report. Each handler gets its own copy.
The component the gap is about.
A readable name for the category.
What the caller was trying to do.
More detail, when the caller gave some.
When the report was sent, as ISO 8601.
The package the report is about.
The integration's version from its package.json. Null for Core, and when the package.json has none.
Where the package takes issues. Null when it does not say.
Aborted when the handler runs past 30 seconds.
'filed': the handler created or queued the report. 'routed_only': it points to a place to file the report, and must return `url`. 'skipped': it chose not to act, for example on a duplicate.
An http or https URL. Required when status is routed_only.
A readable message of at most 2000 characters.
The receipt is strict: an unknown field, a URL that is not http or https, or a filed or routed_only receipt with neither `url` nor `message` is invalid.

A source for `astryx discover`: an async function that returns a catalog of packages a project could add, their versions, and what each version adds. Set it as `discover` in astryx.config, or export it as `discover` from an integration manifest. Discover calls every source, the project one first, and then reads the official list the CLI carries; another source's entry for an official package is kept. A source that throws, runs past 30 seconds, or returns an invalid catalog never hides the others; discover then uses the last good answer that source gave for the same request, or reports the source as failed when it saved none. Discover only reads: it prints the command that adds a package and never runs it.
Applies to: `discover` in astryx.config.*, or the `discover` named export of astryx.integration.*
The one argument the source is called with.
Aborted when the source runs past 30 seconds.
Set when discover shows one package: return that package with every version.
With `package`: return that version's contributions. Without it, the latest release's.
The catalog. Discover checks it, ignores fields and item kinds it does not know, and refuses any schemaVersion but 1.
Who answered, when the data was produced (ISO 8601), and false when the source knows its list is partial.
One entry per npm package. When two sources list the same package, the earlier source wins.
Shared by every npm name that publishes the same integration. Discover lists an integration once.
The integration's other npm names. Discover never offers a package the project has under another name.
One line, for the list and search.
The latest release. Null when there are only prereleases.
Every version, newest first: `{version, publishedAt, prerelease, status}`, where status is `ok` or why the version could not be read.

What the requested (else latest) version adds: `{kind, name, title?, summary?, keywords?}`, where kind is `component`, `template`, `doc`, `theme`, `codemod`, or `agent-doc` (a DiscoverKind) and name is the name the CLI uses for it.

In global mode: the discover source of an integration installed for the computer is called in folders outside any project; inside a project, only the sources of integrations the project installs are. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

A codemod module the CLI runs during `astryx upgrade`. Default-export a plain object with a `type` discriminant: 'code' rewrites source files, 'config' rewrites the astryx.config.* file. There is no factory to call.

Applies to: `<codemods>/<version>/<id>.{ts,mjs,js}` in an integration package: `<codemods>` is the codemods root of astryx.integration.*, and `<version>` is the exact @astryxdesign/core version (such as 0.7.0) whose upgrade runs the codemod. A file directly in the root never runs.
Short, human-readable title shown in upgrade output. Example: 'Rename Button prop kind to variant'.
When true, the codemod runs only when explicitly requested. Default: false.
File extensions this codemod applies to. Code codemods only; a config codemod always targets astryx.config.*. Default: ['.tsx', '.ts', '.jsx', '.js', '.mjs', '.cjs']. Example: ['.tsx', '.ts'].
(file: AstryxCodemodFile, api: AstryxCodemodApi) => string | null | undefined
The transform. Return the new source to rewrite the file, or null/undefined to leave it unchanged.
The source file presented to the transform.
Absolute path to the file being transformed.
The current source contents of the file.
Helpers and context passed as the second argument.
A jscodeshift instance configured with a parser for the file.
Accepted for jscodeshift parity. A call does nothing, and upgrade shows nothing for it.
Discriminant for the file-transforming variant. Use 'config' for a codemod that rewrites astryx.config.* instead (see notes). Example: 'code'.
The config-codemod variant (type: 'config') carries the same fields as a code codemod except fileExtensions: it always targets the astryx.config.* file rather than a set of source files.

Authors write a plain object and default-export it with the `type` discriminant; there is no factory. The CLI validates it at the load boundary via parseCodemod with a strict schema, and isOptional defaults to false.

Separates stable provider/artifact identity from package instances and runtime lifecycle state. Provider identity names integration manifests and settles provider conflicts. Docs-tree nodes are identified by doc identity; the tree covers the CLI's docs and each integration's. Artifact IDs for kinds outside the docs tree, provider instances, and compiler-input entries are defined for every provider-owned artifact; no command builds them.
Applies to: Integration manifests, provider conflicts, and docs-tree node ids.
Canonical logical provider ID. It defaults to the lowercase npm package name; Core uses the same model without publishing an integration manifest.
Versioned serialization of provider ID, contribution kind, and stable artifact name. Every segment uses RFC 3986 escaping.
Artifact ID restricted to one authored doc kind. Navigation changes do not change it.
One immutable package version and source/content digest. It carries no installed, configured, loaded, selected, or healthy state.
{ id; provider; kind; stableName; source; authored }

Normalized compiler input. `stableName`, the key in its doc ID, is given separately from the authored display name; source paths remain package-relative, and provider provenance plus the authored snapshot are immutable.
Provider package renames require an explicit mapping: a ProviderInstance may retain its stable providerId while packageName changes. Silent identity changes are not inferred.

Fields every authored doc kind can declare for the docs tree: `placement`, `stability`, and two reserved fields, `aliases` and `audience`. The docs tree reads `placement` for every guide and namespace doc, the CLI's and each integration's. Nothing reads `aliases` or `audience` today: a reference topic that sets one fails to load, placed in the docs tree or not, and other doc kinds accept them and ignore them.
Applies to: Every authored doc kind's .doc.mjs object. Theme descriptors take none of these fields.

Names the doc's one parent in the docs tree: a namespace of the same package, one of its slots, and an order. Read for every guide, the CLI's and each integration's, and for every namespace doc: a guide with `placement` gets a route in the tree instead of a flat topic name, and cannot also set `replaces` or `extends`; a namespace doc with `placement` nests under that parent. In the CLI's own topic directory a topic that sets it fails to load: the CLI keeps its guides in its docs tree directory. Commands, API functions, schemas, and enums do not set it: the tree adopts each by its `namespace`.
The parent namespace: `namespace:<name>` in the same package.
A slot the parent namespace declares; it must accept this doc's kind. Optional when the parent has one slot.
Integer sibling order within the slot. Docs without an order come after the ordered ones, sorted by title. The same order sets each doc's Previous and Next links.
Reserved: prior names or routes the docs tree will keep resolving to this doc, without creating another identity. Nothing reads it today, and a topic that sets it fails to load.
Reserved: which docs bundle includes this doc ('public' when omitted). Nothing reads it today, and a topic that sets it fails to load. Default: 'public'.

Marks the doc of an experimental surface: one whose shape can still change, or disappear, in any patch release. A command's help shows it as `[experimental]`. The doc's own text still says so. Omit it for a stable surface.

Unknown fields: `component`, `function`, `generic`, `schema`, `command` and `enum` docs accept a field they do not know, and nothing reads it, so a doc written for a newer CLI still loads here. `page`, `block` and `namespace` docs refuse one, as do `theme` descriptors. Sections and content blocks refuse one in every doc.

The doc-type for a component directory's {Name}.doc.mjs. A discriminated union of SingleComponentDoc (props on the doc), MultiComponentDoc (a `components` array), and SubComponentDoc (a `subComponentOf` pointer). All three share the ComponentBaseDoc fields below; the variant is chosen by which of props / components / subComponentOf you set.
Doc-kind discriminant for the stamped default-export format. Optional: legacy `export const docs = {...}` docs omit it and the parser falls back to shape-sniffing.

Stable machine identity without the Astryx prefix, PascalCase. e.g. 'Button', 'TextInput', 'AppShell'. For an integration component it is the export apps import: the doc sits beside the file that exports it, and when that file exports nothing under its own name, `name` may name the export it does have. Change `displayName`, not `name`, to edit the visible label; registry URLs derive from this identity by default.
Human-readable display name with spaces between words ('AppShell' → 'App Shell'). Drives the docsite gallery and sidebar label.
Optional public registry identity. The converter derives a stable kebab-case slug from `name`; set `slug` only to override it, and keep prior relative paths in `aliases` after a published rename.
Exact public package specifier consumers use to import an integration-owned component. The packed-package gate resolves this specifier and verifies it exports the component name.

Integration components only: the exact `name` of the Core ComponentDoc this component takes over for unqualified lookup, so every app that loads the integration gets it from component detail, component lists, search, `swizzle <Name>`, and issue routing; `swizzle --list` keeps listing Core names. The Core original stays reachable with `--package @astryxdesign/core`. It takes effect only when the package's peer range starts at the release that applies it, `"@astryxdesign/cli": ">=0.6.7"` or later; with a lower range nothing changes and `doctor integration components` warns (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components/replace-a-core-component`). Set it only to intentionally own a Core identity; give an alternative or variant its own name instead.

Marks a deprecated component: it keeps working and stays documented, labeled with what replaces it. `replacement` is the `name` of the documented component to use instead; `description` is the modernization route in a sentence or two. The docsite shows a Deprecated badge in the component's page header and index tile, labels its search result, and adds a notice that links the replacement; `astryx search` results and `astryx build` kit entries carry the field. Omit it for a component that is not deprecated.

Search keywords for CLI discovery: synonyms and related UI concepts from other design systems (MUI, Chakra, Radix, and others). Lowercase. `astryx search` matches them; `astryx component <term>` also suggests Core components by keyword.

Sub-component names to hide from human-facing UI (CLI listings, docs catalogs). They stay public and importable; agents and tooling can still discover them via source. In an integration it hides only full entries in this doc's `components`, which the CLI then neither lists nor opens; hide a sub-component that has its own doc with `hidden` in that doc.
Hide this entire component from human-facing UI. It stays public and importable. Use for a shared primitive that only makes sense inside its parent.
Optional sidebar/docs group. Clusters related components; ungrouped components appear flat in alphabetical order.
Overview-gallery category representing the component's functional role. Independent of `group` (which is for the sidebar). `Data Input` is a deprecated compatibility alias for `Form Controls`.
Exclude from the categorized overview page while keeping the component in the sidebar and CLI. Use for sub-components or internal primitives.
{ container?: boolean; targets: ComponentThemingTarget[]; vars?: ComponentThemingVar[]; derived?: ComponentThemingDerivedVar[]; componentIcons?: ComponentIconSlotDoc[] }
Theming configuration: the stable selector surface (astryx-* classes + data-attribute reflections) that themes target via @scope selectors in defineTheme.
Marks a container component. Nothing reads it today: the theme pipeline maps `padding` to container tokens from a `theming.derived` entry `{property: 'padding', expand: 'container'}`.
Selector targets rendered by this component. Each entry corresponds to a themeProps() call in the source.
CSS custom properties exposed for theming.

Maps standard CSS properties to internal vars for theme-pipeline expansion. Ordered by priority: earlier entries emit first. The pipeline reads only Core components' entries, so an integration's have no effect.

The component's icon slots, which a theme maps through `defineTheme({componentIcons})`: each slot's name, role, fallback per state, the state a slot function receives, and what `null` does. Each entry corresponds to a slot in `ComponentIconSlotMap`.

Component usage documentation: concise summary, best practices, component-specific accessibility requirements, and optional visual anatomy. Required on a component doc; optional on a sub-component doc (`subComponentOf`), which uses its description instead.
What the component is and when to use it, in 2-3 short sentences.
3-4 do/don't design-guidance items ({guidance: boolean, description: string}). Never start the description with 'Do' or 'Don't'.

Component-specific requirements rendered in the shared Accessibility tab. Write at about a grade-7 reading level with short sentences, common words, and active voice. For color contrast, put the ratio in `requirement`; name the exact foreground, background, state, and any overlay in `description`; explain exceptions in plain language; and give a human or agent enough detail to reproduce the check. Keep repository audit procedures in the wiki rubric.

Verified per-theme accessibility measurements rendered in the shared Accessibility tab. Record light and dark mode separately, include rendered color pairs, and mark failed measurements. Put visuals excluded from the audit in `notMeasured` with a short reason; do not add them as table measurements. Each theme declares `applicability` for measured values, informed by the component contract and never inferred from the ratio: `Conditional` is required only in some contexts, `Supplemental` adds another meaningful cue, and `Decorative` has no required meaning. These values do not change row status. Provide a complete breakdown when one cell summarizes multiple combinations, and protect derived values with an automated audit.
Structural/visual parts in reading order ({name, required, description}).
Short code examples ({label?, code}) rendered by the CLI after the props table.

Interactive-preview config: initial prop `defaults`, `overlay` for modal-only components, `appShellMobile` for components gated on AppShell mobile context, and a `wrapper` for context-dependent sub-components.

SingleComponentDoc variant (required there): all public props for the one primary component. Each prop is {name, type, description, default?, required?, slotElements?, stability?}. Skip styling props like xstyle/className/style. Also present on SubComponentDoc.

MultiComponentDoc variant (required there): one entry per public component/hook exported from the directory. Each entry is a full ComponentEntry (inline: name, displayName, description, props | params+returns) or a name-only ComponentRef pointing at a sibling {Name}.doc.mjs. In an integration, each full entry the module named by `import` exports is a component under its own name.

SubComponentDoc variant (required there): the parent component's `name` (e.g. 'Chat'). Marks this file as a sub-component doc. The CLI does not copy family fields (group, category, keywords, theming, playground) from the parent to an integration's sub-component: its detail, list group and search use only what its own doc sets. Set any the child needs in its own doc.

SubComponentDoc variant (required there): one-sentence description of the sub-component's role within the parent composition. Single/Multi docs have no top-level description; they derive their summary from `usage`.

When it loads, a stamped component doc is checked about as loosely as an unstamped one, so adding `type: 'component'` to a doc that follows the type never breaks it: `displayName` may be missing, `category` may be any string, `usage`, `theming` and `playground` are not checked, and `examples` need only be an array. Unlike an unstamped doc, each entry in a group doc's `components` must have a `name`, and `import` and `replaces`, when set, must be non-empty strings. Write to the type anyway; it is the contract.
ComponentDoc is a discriminated union of three shapes that all extend ComponentBaseDoc. Pick the variant by which key you set: `props` (single), `components` (multi), or `subComponentOf` (sub).
SingleComponentDoc: one primary component; put props directly on the doc via `props`. Use for Switch, Badge, Spinner, TextInput.
MultiComponentDoc: a directory exporting several components/hooks; list them in `components` (inline ComponentEntry or name-only ComponentRef). Use for Table, Dialog, TabList.

SubComponentDoc: a single sub-component in its own {Name}.doc.mjs inside the parent directory; set `subComponentOf` to the parent name. It does not take the parent's family fields, and it may omit `usage`.

The stamped format is `export default { type: 'component', ... }`, which `astryx integration add component` writes; legacy docs use `export const docs = {...}` and omit `type` (the parser shape-sniffs). A hook that is part of a component API is listed in a MultiComponentDoc `components` array: inline as a ComponentEntry (with `params`/`returns`), or by name with its own SubComponentDoc file, as Core's useTableSelection is.

The doc-type for a standalone React hook (e.g. useMediaQuery, useFocusTrap, useOverflow) that gets its own `.doc.mjs`. Hooks that are part of a component API (e.g. useImperativeDialog) belong in that component's MultiComponentDoc `components` array instead. `HookDoc` is the hook-flavored view of the shared `type: 'function'` kind. `astryx hook` reads Core's hook docs only; an integration lists its hooks in a component doc's `components` array.
Doc-kind discriminant (shared with FunctionDoc). Legacy `export const docs = {...}` docs omit it.
Stable hook name exactly as exported, e.g. 'useMediaQuery', 'useFocusTrap'. Change `displayName`, not `name`, to edit the visible label; registry URLs derive from this identity by default.
Human-readable display name. Hooks read better as the raw identifier ('useMediaQuery') than spaced, so keep the identifier verbatim.
Optional group for sidebar/docs organization; same as ComponentDoc.group.
TypeScript type signature as a string.
Default value as a string, if optional with a default.
True if required. Omit if optional.
Return value documentation. For object returns, list each field; for primitive returns, use a single entry.
Field name on the returned object, or 'value' for primitive returns.
Usage documentation: description and best practices.
What the hook is and when to use it, in 2-3 short sentences.
3-4 do/don't design-guidance items ({guidance: boolean, description: string}).
Accessibility requirements specific to using the hook ({name, description}).
Structural/visual anatomy elements (rarely used for hooks).
Component names this hook is commonly used with. Enables cross-referencing (e.g. `astryx hook useToast` links back to Toast).
Other hook names this hook is commonly used with.

`parseDoc` accepts a stamped hook doc without `displayName` and does not check its `usage`, and `astryx hook` prints a hook doc without checking it at all. Write to the type anyway; it is the contract.
A hook's discriminant is `type: 'function'`: HookDoc and FunctionDoc share the generalized function kind. HookDoc is the hook-flavored view: named `returns` fields and a required `usage` block.

A hook that is part of a component API is listed in that component's MultiComponentDoc `components` array: inline with `params`/`returns`, or by name with its own SubComponentDoc file, as Core's useTableSelection is.

The generalized `type: 'function'` doc-type covering both React hooks and CLI/API functions. A hook (HookDoc) is the hook-flavored view of this same kind; FunctionDoc adds the fields an API function needs (a {type, data} return envelope, thrown error codes, the wrapping CLI command). The CLI binding itself lives in a separate CommandDoc.
Which flavor. Nothing reads it today: no reader sections docs by it or infers it from `importPath`. The CLI's API function docs set 'api'.

Optional in the type, but every doc the CLI ships declares it. The group that reads this doc. The CLI's API functions use 'cli/api', which the docs tree adopts by kind: each is the leaf `cli/api/functions/<name>`, the name in kebab case (`themeUse` is `theme-use`). Every function doc the CLI ships declares one, and `astryx doctor` fails on one that is missing or that nothing reads.
Reserved: other names for this doc. Nothing reads it today, so they do not resolve to it.
Full signature as a string, e.g. 'search(query, options?): Promise<SearchResponse>'.
Return documentation. Hooks list named return fields (`name` set); API functions list {type, data} envelope entries where `type` is the response discriminant and `name` is omitted.
Field name (hooks); omit for API envelope entries.
TS type (hooks) or response-type discriminant (API), as a string.
What this return value / envelope entry provides.
Errors the function throws (API functions), keyed to ERROR_CODES.
The condition under which it is thrown.
Optional heading shown above the snippet.
Usage documentation (hooks): description, best practices, accessibility requirements, and anatomy. Same shape as HookDoc.usage.
The CLI command that wraps this function, e.g. 'search'.
Related function names; the CLI links each to its doc. Name the CLI command with `command`, not here.
Component names this is commonly used with (hooks).
Other hook names this is commonly used with (hooks).
An API function doc (envelope return, no field name)

`parseDoc` accepts a stamped function doc without `displayName` and does not check its `usage`, and the CLI reads its own function docs without checking them. Write to the type anyway; it is the contract.
The `type` discriminant is 'function' for both flavors. `kind: 'hook'` or `kind: 'api'` names the flavor; nothing reads it today.

The two flavors differ in `returns`: a hook lists named fields (`name` set), while an API function lists {type, data} envelope entries whose `type` is the response discriminant and whose `name` is omitted. `throws` (keyed to ERROR_CODES) applies to API functions.

The function does not know it has a CLI. The terminal binding (args, flags, exit codes) lives in a separate CommandDoc that references this function via `fn`; here you only note the wrapping command name via `command`.

The doc-type for a CLI command: the terminal binding of an operation. A command is not its own behavior; it is a FunctionDoc exposed on the CLI, referenced via `fn`, carrying only CLI-surface facts (args, flags, subcommands, examples, exit codes). A `defineCommand` converter turns it into Commander config + `--help`.
Doc-kind discriminant. Marks the file as a command doc.
One-line summary → Commander `.description()` + the docs listing.
Longer body / when-to-use. `astryx docs` prints it after the summary; `--help` shows only the summary.

Optional in the type, but every doc the CLI ships declares it. The group that reads this doc. The CLI's commands use 'cli/commands', which the docs tree adopts: each is the leaf `cli/commands/<name>`, spaces as hyphens (`theme build` is `cli/commands/theme-build`). Every command doc the CLI ships declares one, and `astryx doctor` fails on one that is missing or that nothing reads.
Name of the FunctionDoc (and `@astryxdesign/cli/api` export) this command wraps. Example: 'search'.
FunctionDoc param this arg binds to; `astryx docs` shows that param's description when the arg has none.
Override description. `--help` shows an argument's description only when it sets this.
Whether the positional argument must be supplied.
Whether the argument collects a variable number of values.
FunctionDoc param this flag maps to (inherits its description).
Override/explicit description. Nothing requires it: a flag with neither this nor `param` shows no description.
Default value: a string, a boolean, or a list of strings.
True for CLI-only flags with no function param (e.g. --verbose). Nothing reads it.
Optional heading shown above the invocation.
A full terminal invocation, e.g. 'astryx search button --json'.
The condition that produces this exit code.

What the command does outside a project. `same`: the answer it gives in a new project. `refuse`: it writes nothing and fails, naming the app project or integration package it needs. `own`: something else. Every `refuse` and `own` command also carries an `In global mode:` note in its `notes` that tells readers exactly what it does. Every command and subcommand declares one, and `astryx manifest` publishes it; a command that only groups subcommands declares none. The CLI tests run every command in an empty folder and check what it does against this value; `astryx doctor` does not check it.
Deprecation notice — a DEP-* id and the replacement.
A command that wraps the search() function
A command carries only CLI-surface facts. Behavior, parameters, returns, and thrown errors live in the FunctionDoc it points at via `fn`; the function does not know it has a CLI.

Bind an arg/option to a function param via `param` so it inherits that param's description: an option's in `--help` and `astryx docs`, an arg's in `astryx docs` only. Mark a flag with no function param (e.g. `--verbose`) `cliOnly: true` and give it its own `description`; nothing checks either. `--json` is a global flag, so a command doc does not declare it.

The doc-type for a closed vocabulary: a fixed set of literal values such as error codes or response-type discriminants. Colocated as a `.doc.mjs` next to the source of truth it documents. Only the CLI reads enum docs, from its own source: one in an integration's docs directory fails to load, and so do that package's other docs.
Doc-kind discriminant. Optional in the type, but the CLI reads a doc as an enum doc only when it is set; without it the doc drops out of the docs tree.
URL-safe identifier, used as the docs slug within its namespace. Example: 'error-codes'.

Optional in the type, but every doc the CLI ships declares it. The group that reads this doc. The CLI's enums use 'cli/api', which the docs tree adopts by kind: each is the leaf `cli/api/enums/<name>`. Every enum doc the CLI ships declares one, and `astryx doctor` fails on one that is missing or that nothing reads.
Reserved: alternate slugs for this doc. Nothing reads it today, so `astryx docs <alias>` does not open it.
The enumerated members: one entry per literal value.
What the value means / when it occurs.
An enum doc is the human-readable mirror of a closed vocabulary defined elsewhere in source (e.g. an ERROR_CODES map or a response-type union). Keep the members in sync with that source of truth.
Mark a value with `deprecated` (a migration hint) rather than deleting it, so old codes stay documented while readers are pointed at the replacement.

Declares one level of the docs tree: named slots, and adoption rules for already-discovered docs. It never scans folders, lists its children, or copies child documents: a child names its parent with `placement`, or a namespace adopts a discovery group. `astryx docs <route>` lists each slot's children one level down. The CLI keeps its namespace docs in its docs tree directory; an integration ships its own in its docs directory, and they appear in `astryx docs` beside the CLI's.
Stable provider-local identity. Moving the namespace does not change this value.
One-line summary used in listings and search results.

Optional canonical parent: {parent, slot?, order?}. `parent` names a namespace of the same package as `namespace:<name>`. An invalid placement withdraws the namespace with a diagnostic; it never falls back.
Prior names or routes the docs tree will keep resolving to this doc. Not read yet.
Reserved: bundle audience. Nothing reads it yet: a namespace that sets 'internal' still shows in `astryx docs`. Default: 'public'.
Search terms not already present in the title or summary.
Named placement and collection targets. Each slot declares a title and the doc kinds it accepts. `accepts.providers` is not read yet: only docs of the namespace's own package can be placed in a slot.
Provider-local rules that adopt otherwise-unplaced docs from a logical discovery group. They never scan a folder.

Ordered layout content for the namespace page. Graph-only workflow, collection, and reference blocks are available here without widening the stable ReferenceContentBlock union used by existing topic renderers. `astryx docs <route>` prints the prose, heading, code, table, and list blocks above the slots, and `--json` returns every block with its links resolved. A collection block is not rendered yet, and `astryx doctor` warns on one.
A CLI namespace with one adopted source group

The docs tree reads namespace docs from the CLI and from every configured integration. An integration's namespace doc without a `placement` is a top-level level of the tree, and its guides name it with `placement`; a doc can be placed only in a namespace of its own package. When two packages claim one route, the CLI's own docs win, then integrations in configured order, and `astryx doctor` names the loser.

Child docs request one canonical home with placement. A collection block refers to those docs by stable reference and never creates a second identity or parent. It is not rendered yet: `astryx doctor` warns on one.
Use a directory as implicit navigation.
Put JSX, HTML, ANSI, callbacks, or custom renderer code in a doc.
Use choice, callout, or checklist blocks before the full block-extension contract exists.

The doc-type for a reference/topic doc: tokens, principles, theming, patterns, accessibility, migration guides. Unlike ComponentDoc it is not tied to a component: drop a `.doc.mjs` in the docs directory and it shows up in `astryx docs`. Content is built from ordered sections of mixed content blocks.
Applies to: <topic>.doc.{ts,mjs,js} in the folder the integration manifest's `docs` names
Doc-kind discriminant. Stays 'generic' (the reference/topic discriminant). Legacy `export const docs = {...}` docs omit it.
URL-safe identifier, used as the CLI topic name. e.g. 'tokens', 'principles'.
Human-readable title. e.g. 'All Tokens'. (Reference docs use `title`, not `displayName`.)
One-line summary shown in topic listings.

Words a reader may search for that the title and sections do not use: a synonym, a task, or another library's name for the same thing. `astryx search` matches each as a keyword of the whole topic, so an exact one ranks the topic like its own title does. Example: ['dark mode', 'color scheme'].

Name of an existing topic this doc takes the place of. Authored by an integration that serves its own guide instead of the built-in one: on a doc of the same name it swaps the content, and on a doc of another name it also leaves the old name as an alias so `astryx docs <old>` still resolves. Exclusive with `extends`. Example: 'getting-started'.

Name of an existing topic this doc merges onto, section by section. A section replaces the base section with the same `id`, or else the one with exactly its title when either of the two has no `id`. A key derived from a title counts only against an `id`: a section without an `id` also matches a base section whose `id` is the key its title derives, and a section with an `id` also matches a base section without one whose title derives that `id`. Two different `id`s never match, two sections without an `id` whose titles differ only in case or punctuation stay separate, and a section that matches none is appended. The topic keeps the base's title and description. For correcting or adding to a topic rather than owning it. Exclusive with `replaces`. Example: 'theme'.
Ordered sections that make up the doc. Each becomes an h2 in full output and can be retrieved via `astryx docs <topic> <section>`.

Stable section anchor. New docs should set this instead of relying on a mutable title. Published @astryxdesign/cli 0.6.3 and earlier reject the field and hide every doc topic the package ships, so `astryx integration verify` fails an integration that sets one until it declares an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer of `>=0.6.4`.
Navigation category ('guide' | 'foundations'). Mirrors the parent doc's category so sections can be grouped independently.

Ordered content blocks: prose, heading, code, table, list, token-ref, and reference. A `reference` block (`{type: 'reference', target, projection?, presentation?}`) includes another doc from its canonical source instead of a copy: a schema, command, function, or enum doc as `astryx docs` prints it, then the command that opens it. `projection.fields` keeps only those fields of a schema; `presentation` is `full` (the default), `compact` (no code blocks), or `summary` (only the doc's title, summary, and command). Any other doc shows as a summary. Graph-only workflow and collection blocks are available through GraphContentBlock on NamespaceDoc, without widening the stable ReferenceContentBlock union. Inside text, `{@link <target>}` links another doc by identity (`[<provider>:]<kind>:<name>`): the CLI prints the command that opens it, and `astryx doctor` warns on one that names no doc.
Preview type for token tables in this section. The CLI rejects a value not in the list below and returns the value in `astryx docs --json`, but draws no preview from it. Omit for non-token sections.
Token category for foundational docs that map to a token section (e.g. 'color'). `astryx docs --json` returns it as authored; no tokens page links to the doc through it.
A reference doc with one section

A stamped generic doc without `title`, `description` or `sections` still loads, as older codemod output does; its title falls back to `displayName` or `name`. Without a description and sections it is not a usable topic, and `astryx doctor` reports it.

Each `sections[].content` is an ordered array of ReferenceContentBlock, the stable discriminated union of prose, heading, code, table, list, and token-ref, plus the reference block (ReferenceDocBlock). A read inlines a reference block the way it inlines a token-ref, so `astryx docs`, in text and in `--json`, returns only the stable block kinds. Docs-graph-only workflow and collection blocks are exported separately as GraphContentBlock and accepted by NamespaceDoc. choice, callout, and checklist remain invalid. ReferenceContentBlock is also reused by the `notes` field on SchemaDoc and CommandDoc. Inside text, `{@link <target>}` links another doc by identity (`[<provider>:]<kind>:<name>`): the CLI prints the command that opens it, and `astryx doctor` warns on one that names no doc. Write a CLI command in text, shell code, or a table cell as a bare `astryx` command: a text read adds the runner the reader uses in front of it, and `--json` returns it as written.

A reference block includes content, where a link only points at it: `astryx doctor integration docs` fails when its target names no doc, when `projection.fields` names a field the schema does not have, or when the doc cannot take the projection or presentation it sets, and a read marks the missing content. A target without a provider names a doc of the package that wrote it, so an integration names the CLI's docs with the CLI's provider, as in `@astryxdesign/cli:schema:integration`.
A section that includes two fields of the integration manifest

A `token-ref` block (e.g. {type: 'token-ref', topic: 'tokens', section: 'Color Tokens'}) references a token table in another topic; the CLI resolves and inlines it at read time so the docsite can render live theme values.

A section may set `previewType`, a hint for previewing its token table, to one of 'swatch' | 'shadow-box' | 'radius-box' | 'spacing-bar' | 'size-bar' | 'border-line' | 'duration-bar' | 'easing-curve' | 'font-sample'; the CLI rejects any other value.

The doc-type for documenting an authored/received OBJECT shape (astryx.config, a codemod payload, the doc-types themselves). Colocated as a `.doc.mjs` next to the schema it describes. Fields nest recursively, so a whole shape is one tree.
Doc-kind discriminant. Marks the file as a schema doc.
URL-safe identifier, used as the docs slug within its namespace. Example: 'config'.

The group that reads this doc: 'authoring' for a file an author writes (a section of `astryx docs authoring/field-reference`), or 'cli/api' for a shape the CLI returns (the docs tree adopts it by kind, as the leaf `cli/api/schemas/<name>`). Every schema doc the CLI ships declares one, and `astryx doctor` fails on one that is missing or that nothing reads.
Reserved: alternate slugs for this doc. Nothing reads it yet: `astryx docs` finds a schema doc by its `name` only.
What this schema applies to, e.g. 'astryx.config.{ts,mjs,js}' | 'AstryxConfig'.
The fields that make up the shape. Object-typed fields nest their members recursively via each field's own `fields`, so the whole shape is one tree.
Field name, or a dotted path for a nested field (e.g. 'hooks.postCodemod').
TypeScript type signature as a string, e.g. 'string[]' | "'a' | 'b'".
What the field is for, in 1-2 sentences.
True if the field must be provided. Omit (don't set false) if optional.
Default value as a string, if any.
Deprecation reason, if the field is deprecated.
Nested object fields, for object-typed fields. Recursive.

Freeform prose/notes rendered after the field table and examples. The stable ReferenceContentBlock union (prose, heading, code, table, list, token-ref), without the reference block a ReferenceDoc section also takes; a token-ref note is accepted but not rendered.
A small schema doc with a nested object field

SchemaFieldDoc is recursive: an object-typed field lists its members in its own `fields`, so an entire nested shape (including paths like `hooks.postCodemod` or `experimental.xle.components`) is documented as one tree.
Name nested fields with a dotted path from the root (e.g. `hooks.postCodemod`) so readers can see where each field sits in the shape.
Set `required: true` only for mandatory fields.
Keep `type` close to the real TS type; use single quotes for string-literal unions.
Set `required: false` for optional fields; omit `required` entirely instead.

The doc-type for template metadata. A discriminated union of PageTemplateDoc (type: 'page') for full page templates and BlockTemplateDoc (type: 'block') for editable compositions. A block can stand alone or use `exampleFor` to attach to one component; `isShowcase` requires that component ownership.
Discriminant selecting the variant: 'page' for a full page template, 'block' for an editable composition that may be standalone or component-owned.

Stable identifier for block templates; change `displayName`, not `name`, to edit their visible label in the gallery. For page templates it is a human-readable label, while the existing template-directory/CLI slug owns the default registry path. `astryx template --list` and `astryx search` print `name` as the label of both, and `astryx template <id>` finds a template by its id, never by `name`: an integration template's id is its path under the templates folder without the `.doc.*` suffix.

Human-readable label for the gallery. The CLI prints `name` instead; `astryx template --list --json` also returns an integration template's `displayName`. Spaces out block names that mirror a PascalCase component ('ChatMessageMetadata' → 'Chat Message Metadata').

Optional public registry identity. The converter derives a stable kebab-case slug from `name` (or the existing page-template slug); set `slug` only to override it, and keep prior relative paths in `aliases` after a published rename.
One-sentence description of what the template provides.

Search keywords for CLI discovery: the ideas, domains, and other names a builder might use for what the template serves (e.g. ['monitoring', 'uptime', 'on-call'] for a service-health dashboard). Lowercase. `astryx search` matches them as it matches the description and `astryx build` ranks page templates on them, so keep them out of `description`. Integration templates need @astryxdesign/cli 0.6.6 or later: earlier CLIs reject the field and drop that template, and CLIs before 0.6.4 also hide the package's doc topics.

Integration templates only: the exact id of the Core template this one replaces for unqualified lookup. First: your peer ranges must include the global CLI's version

Your `@astryxdesign/core` (and, if you use it, `@astryxdesign/cli`) `peerDependencies` ranges must include the version of the CLI installed globally. If they do not, Astryx skips your package outside projects, and `astryx doctor` warns and names the range.
Inside a project that does not install your package, `astryx discover` offers it, with the command that adds it to that project, once your peer range admits the project's release.
Installed in an app: it works in that app, as always, whichever `astryx` the person runs, because the app's version of Astryx answers there.

Installed next to the global install (`npm install -g @astryxdesign/cli your-package`), or in the same folder as the CLI by a tool that installs them together: it works in every folder outside a project. People and agents there see its components, templates, docs, themes, codemods, and discover source.

Installed only globally, inside an app that does not install it: it adds nothing there. When it supports the app's version and loads, `astryx discover` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command.
Installed both ways: the app's copy is the one used in that app. In your own package folder, your working copy is used.
Astryx loads a global integration with the same loader and checks as an app's, so nothing extra goes in your manifest.

Declare the `@astryxdesign/core` (and, if you use it, `@astryxdesign/cli`) `peerDependencies` range your package really supports. Outside a project, Astryx skips your package when that range leaves out the global version, and `astryx doctor` says why: too narrow, and global users lose it after an upgrade; too wide, and it loads against a Core it may not build with.
Keep imports in your docs and templates to packages an app installs with yours, since outside a project there is no app to check them against.

If you set `cliCommand`, know that outside a project it starts every command Astryx prints, and that two global integrations naming different commands cancel out, falling back to `astryx` (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/configuration/cli-command`). Inside an app, only the app's integrations count.

`No package.json found. Run this command inside an integration package.`
Run `npm init -y` (only with npm: writes package.json) and `npm pkg set name=@acme/astryx-widgets` (only with npm: edits package.json) first, in the package folder.
Component commands read Core. Run `npm install -D @astryxdesign/core` in the package.
`core_not_found`: `Could not resolve @astryxdesign/core, so component names could not be checked.`
`Error: unknown subcommand 'integration verify'`, or `Error: Pass --check to verify the integration tarball.`
Your CLI is older than `integration verify`. Run `npm install -D @astryxdesign/cli@latest`. On the older CLI, the same check is `integration pack --check`.
The old name still runs the same check. Switch to `astryx integration verify`; the old name will be removed in a later release.
`astryx integration verify` prints each failure as a `[fail]` line. Add `--json` to see its issue code, such as `component_export_missing`.
`component_export_missing`: `Component "AcmeCarousel" advertises import "@acme/astryx-widgets/components/AcmeCarousel", but that packed module does not export "AcmeCarousel".`

package.json has no `exports` map, or the module does not export the name. Keep `export function AcmeCarousel`, and add the entry: `npm pkg set 'exports[./components/AcmeCarousel]=./components/AcmeCarousel.tsx'` (only with npm: edits package.json). When the quoted name is a file name, such as `acme-carousel`, set the doc's `name` to the component the file exports. A type-only export does not count.
`template_export_missing`: `Template "acme-dashboard" public import "@acme/astryx-widgets/templates/acme-dashboard" does not have a default export.`

Run `npm pkg set 'exports[./templates/acme-dashboard]=./templates/acme-dashboard.tsx'` (only with npm: edits package.json), and keep `export default` in the source. Start new packages with `"exports": {}` so each add writes these.
`component_import_unresolvable` or `template_import_unresolvable`: `…Package subpath './components/AcmeCarousel' is not defined by "exports"…`

The `exports` map has no entry for it. Run `npm pkg set 'exports[./components/AcmeCarousel]=./components/AcmeCarousel.tsx'` (only with npm: edits package.json), or `'exports[./templates/acme-dashboard]=./templates/acme-dashboard.tsx'` for a template.
`component_import_unresolvable`: `…but a consumer cannot resolve it: Cannot find package '@acme/old-name'`
You renamed the package after the add wrote each doc's `import`. Change `import` in every component doc to the new name.
`Declared templates root "templates" has 0 of 2 expected files in the pack list. Add "templates" to "files" in package.json.`
Run `npm pkg set 'files[]=templates'` (only with npm: edits package.json).
`docs_tree_needs_cli`: `The package ships a namespace doc or a placed guide but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.`

Run `npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.4'` (only with npm: edits package.json) and `npm pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json` (only with npm: edits package.json).
`replaces_needs_cli`: The package has a template that sets `replaces` but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.

Run `npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.4'` (only with npm: edits package.json) and `npm pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json` (only with npm: edits package.json). A stable CLI before 0.6.4 rejects `replaces`, drops that template, and hides your doc topics.
`component_replaces_needs_cli` (a warning): The package has a component that sets `replaces` but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer, or a peer range that admits an earlier CLI.

Run `npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.7'` (only with npm: edits package.json) and `npm pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json` (only with npm: edits package.json) to turn the replacement on. Until then apps see no change (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components/replace-a-core-component`).
`keywords_needs_cli`: The package has a template that sets `keywords` but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.

Run `npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.6'` (only with npm: edits package.json) and `npm pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json` (only with npm: edits package.json). What an older CLI does with the field is in `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/document-the-template/template-doc-overview`.
`themes_need_cli`: The package ships a theme but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.

Run `npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.6.4'` (only with npm: edits package.json) and `npm pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json` (only with npm: edits package.json). A CLI older than published 0.6.4 cannot read typed theme descriptors, so it drops your themes and can hide your doc topics.
`section_ids_need_cli`: The package has a doc section that sets `id` but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer.
The same fix as `themes_need_cli`, or drop the section `id`s: a CLI older than published 0.6.4 rejects them and hides your doc topics.
`doc_tokens_need_cli`: The package writes doc tokens (`{@command …}`, `{@pm …}`, `{@pm-only …}`) in its docs, but its @astryxdesign/cli peer admits a CLI before 0.7.4.

Run `npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/cli=>=0.7.4'` (only with npm: edits package.json) and `npm pkg set 'peerDependenciesMeta.@astryxdesign/cli.optional=true' --json` (only with npm: edits package.json). A CLI before 0.7.4 prints each token as written, so readers see raw tokens.
These appear in an app that installs your package, or in the doctor checks that predict them.
`Error: No component named "AcmeCarousel"` for a component your package documents.

Its doc still names its file. Set `name` to the export, such as `name: 'AcmeCarousel'` in `acme-carousel.doc.mjs`. A family member is listed only when the module its family doc imports exports it (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components/describe-the-component/component-family`).
`astryx component Dialog` opens Core's `Dialog`, not yours.
A name that Core, a legacy docs package, or another package's file already has stays theirs. Run `astryx component Dialog --package @acme/astryx-widgets`, or give your component a name of its own.
`Error: Template "dashboard" is ambiguous — narrow it with --type and/or --package.`
Your template id matches a Core id. Rename it, such as `acme-dashboard`, or set `replaces: 'dashboard'` to take its place. `astryx doctor integration templates` warns about this before you publish.
The guide stays hidden until its `placement` names a namespace and slot your package declares. For `"…" names no doc`, fix the link target.
Error: Unknown topic "acme". The docs of @acme/astryx-widgets did not load; run `astryx doctor integration docs` in that package to see why.
One invalid doc hides all of your docs. Run `astryx doctor integration docs` in the package and fix the `invalid_doc` it names.
`cli-command` warns: `Loaded integrations declare different CLI commands`

Two packages the app loads set different `cliCommand` values, so the CLI prints the package manager's command. Agree on one command, or remove the package that does not belong. See `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/configuration/cli-command`.
Your `cliCommand` is not one line of plain text of at most 120 characters, so it is ignored. Fix the value; the rest of the manifest still loads.
`astryx upgrade` runs none of your codemods

The app must list your package in `integrations` in `astryx.config`, or pass `--integration @acme/astryx-widgets`. It runs a codemod folder only when its version is after `--from` and at most the installed `@astryxdesign/core`.
Your docs section, templates, or themes are missing only in some apps

Those apps run a CLI too old to read them (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks` lists which field needs which CLI). Update `@astryxdesign/cli` there, and keep your optional `@astryxdesign/cli` peer so npm checks the app's CLI against it when the app installs your package.
What each check catches is in `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.

An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.

mkdir acme-widgets && cd acme-widgets
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
npm pkg set name=@acme/astryx-widgets type=module  # only with npm: edits package.json
npm pkg set 'exports={}' --json  # only with npm: edits package.json
npm install -D @astryxdesign/cli @astryxdesign/core typescript@6

Set `"type": "module"`: the `.js` files the CLI generates, such as a built theme, are ES modules, and Node fails to load them in a package marked `"type": "commonjs"`, which `npm init -y` (only with npm: writes package.json) writes on npm 11.
Start with `"exports": {}`: each component and template you add then writes the public import that `integration verify` resolves.
Run the CLI as `astryx`, which runs the `@astryxdesign/cli` you installed as a devDependency.
Component commands read Core, so they need `@astryxdesign/core` installed.

The checks compare your docs with your code through TypeScript's JavaScript compiler API, which `typescript` 5.0 through 6 has. TypeScript 7 does not ship that API: on TypeScript 7, also install `@typescript/typescript6`, its TypeScript 6 API package, and the checks use it.
An integration can ship several kinds of items. Start with a component named `AcmeCarousel`.

`integration add` creates the component source, its `.doc.mjs`, the package export, and `astryx.integration.mjs`. Update the generated doc so the CLI understands the component, then write the component itself.
Read it back the way an app will.
You now have an integration package with one exported component.

Run `integration check --strict` in every build (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`): a doc, prop, template, or link that drifts from the code then fails your build, not your users' apps. Set it up now, as the `typecheck` script, and run it.

npm pkg set scripts.typecheck="astryx integration check --strict"  # only with npm: edits package.json
npm run typecheck
[ok] 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped. Every check passed.
Run `typecheck` in CI and before every publish. When you add a `tsconfig.json`, put `tsc --noEmit && ` in front of the check so the same script checks your types.
What each check covers, and what `--strict` adds: `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.

Run `integration verify` to check that an app would see the component, then make the `.tgz` file you install next. `--pack-destination ..` writes it beside the package folder, so the next pack does not ship it.

astryx integration verify
npm pack --pack-destination ..  # only with npm: builds the publish tarball

Integration package ready

[ok] @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

4 packed files; 3/3 required files present.

`integration verify` installs the packed package in a temporary app and confirms the component resolves through its public import there (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`). It publishes nothing and leaves no `.tgz` file, so `npm pack` (only with npm: builds the publish tarball) writes `../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz` for the next step.
Install Core, the CLI, and your `.tgz` file in a new app. The app loads your package because it is a dependency, with no config.

cd ..
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
npm install @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli ../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz
astryx component AcmeCarousel

An integration is an ordinary npm package. These six fields control how it is named, developed, checked, and published.
`peerDependencies` are packages the app supplies. `devDependencies` are packages you use while building the integration.
Each add writes it into the `import` of the doc it generates. Rename before you add, or update each `import` after.
The release you publish, such as `1.0.0`
Apps see it; `astryx.integration.mjs` never repeats it.
Each component and template add writes its public import here, and `integration verify` resolves it.
Keeps private files out. When the list exists, each add appends its root and `astryx.integration.mjs`.
`@astryxdesign/core` when your code imports it; `@astryxdesign/cli`, optional, when you ship a feature that needs a newer CLI (`astryx docs authoring/ship/versioning`)
The app supplies these packages for your integration.

Peer ranges and releases are covered in `astryx docs authoring/ship/versioning`; `files` and publishing in `astryx docs authoring/ship/publishing`. Add `"typecheck": "tsc --noEmit && astryx integration check --strict"` to `scripts` so each run checks your types and that your docs, props, and links still match the code. It needs `typescript` and a `tsconfig.json`; see `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.
The first `integration add` creates `astryx.integration.mjs`, and each later add updates it. You do not need to write or edit this file during the quick start.
`package.json` defines the npm package, including its name, version, dependencies, published files, and exports.
`astryx.integration.mjs` tells the CLI where the package keeps each kind of integration item.
The integration item files live under those roots. For example, a component can have `AcmeWidget.tsx` for its source and `AcmeWidget.doc.mjs` for its documentation.

The file tells the CLI where this package keeps its integration items. Edit it only when you want a custom root or another optional setting. Paths are relative to package.json, and later adds keep a custom path you already set.
Every field is in `astryx docs authoring integration`.
You can edit the package files by hand, but the CLI handles the normal workflow. These links always open the canonical command docs.
astryx integration add: Add one working contribution to an integration package. Read it with `astryx docs cli/commands/integration-add`.
astryx integration verify: Check the package the way npm will publish it, before you publish. Read it with `astryx docs cli/commands/integration-verify`.
astryx doctor integration: Check an integration package while authoring it. Read it with `astryx docs cli/commands/doctor-integration`.

It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs it. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

The manifest loads, each root holds contributions the CLI can read, and each doc matches its authoring type. Notes list a malformed `cliCommand` (`invalid_cli_command`) and, for each topic, a command written with a package runner (`runner_command`), bare (`plain_command`) or for one package manager (`package_manager_command`), and a token that does not parse (`doc_token`; see `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/doc-syntax`). Notes fail nothing by default; `integration check --strict --next` fails on the ones marked `next`, and the next minor release counts them

A declared root is missing (`missing_root`), a contribution does not load (`invalid_doc`, `invalid_component`, `invalid_theme`), or two templates in the package replace one Core id (`ambiguous_template_replacement`)

The manifest has a key this CLI does not know (`unknown_manifest_key`), or a doc field does not match the doc's authoring type: a field the type does not have, a missing required field, or a value outside the field's type. It also warns on what no reader can serve: a prop listed twice (`duplicate_prop`), a `propDescriptions` key that names no documented prop (`unknown_translated_prop`), a section with no content (`empty_section`), two sections of a topic with one key (`duplicate_section_key`), or a `.doc.zh.mjs` or `.doc.dense.mjs` overlay beside no topic file (`orphan_doc_overlay`). Since 0.7.3 it also lists, from source and without failing, what the package tells apps to import that they cannot: a component's import (the doc's `import`, or the one the CLI derives) or a template's public import whose subpath package.json `exports` does not declare (`component_import_not_exported`, `template_import_not_exported`) or that names another package (`component_import_other_package`); an example that imports an undeclared subpath (`example_import_not_exported`); a template that imports a path outside the templates root (`template_import_outside_root`) or a path its package or Core does not export (`template_private_import`). It lists the same way a component's import whose module does not export the component (`component_import_missing_name`), an example or a template that imports a name its package does not export (`example_import_missing_name`, `template_import_missing_name`), and a template source with no default export (`template_no_default_export`). Each is a note, printed with its fix, that fails `--strict` from the next minor; an import it cannot judge, such as an `exports` target not built yet or a deep path into a `dist/` not built yet, is listed under `publicImports` as not checked. It checks docs with your installed `typescript`, or, where that is missing or has no JavaScript compiler API (TypeScript 7), with an installed `@typescript/typescript6`; without either, it prints `[skip] Docs not type-checked`. With no `astryx.integration.mjs` it prints a hint and exits 0
No component name clashes with a Core component, each `replaces` names one Core component, and each component doc's props match the component's TypeScript props

`Calendar` shows the Gregorian calendar unless you choose another one. Pass `calendar` to `<InternationalizationProvider>` to set it for a subtree. A locale on its own never changes the calendar: `fa-IR` shows Gregorian dates in Persian until you pass `calendar="persian"`. Calendar and language are independent: `locale="en" calendar="hebrew"` shows Hebrew dates in English. `Calendar` also takes its own `calendar`, which wins over the provider. Use it when one screen shows two calendars side by side.

Values never change with the calendar. `value`, `defaultValue`, `onChange`, `min`, and `max` stay Gregorian ISO dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`) in every calendar, so your data, server code, and existing handlers keep working.
Any other identifier, such as `islamic`, shows Gregorian dates and warns once in development.
Load Temporal where the runtime lacks it

Calendars whose months are not Gregorian use the runtime's `Temporal` for their month lengths, leap months, and years. Chrome and Edge 144 and later, Firefox 139 and later, and Node.js 26 and later ship it. Safari and older runtimes do not. Astryx bundles no polyfill, so Gregorian applications pay nothing.

Where `Temporal` is missing, load the full build of `temporal-polyfill` before your app renders. The default build has no non-ISO calendars. Load it only where `Temporal` is missing: a native implementation is more accurate for the lunisolar calendars.
Load the polyfill only where Temporal is missing

If you render on the server, load it there too. `Calendar` resolves its calendar during render, so a server without `Temporal` renders Gregorian dates, and a browser with it renders Persian ones: hydration then fails. When both have `Temporal`, or both lack it, they render the same markup.

Without a `Temporal` that supports it, a calendar that needs one shows Gregorian dates and warns once in development, on the server and in the browser. The Gregorian-aligned calendars (`buddhist`, `roc`, `japanese`) work everywhere without it.
In the lunisolar calendars, months start on new moons computed from astronomy, and runtimes do not all agree on a few of them. Astryx follows the runtime's `Temporal` and does not correct it.
Native `Temporal` in Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Node.js 26 agrees with official observatory data from 1900 through 2100.

A polyfill reads the platform's `Intl` data instead. Under a polyfill, Node.js 24 starts nine `chinese` and four `dangi` months in that range one day apart from the native result: the first month of the 2027 `chinese` year starts on February 6 with native `Temporal` and on February 7 under the polyfill. Safari uses the same kind of `Intl` data, so expect the same differences there.
Within one browser, the day numbers a person sees, the dates a screen reader announces, and the value they pick agree. Only two different runtimes can disagree.

If you render on the server, a server and a browser that use different implementations can disagree on one of these month starts. The browser then renders that month differently from the server markup, and React renders that part again on the client during hydration. The `temporal-polyfill/full/global` import keeps a native `Temporal` where one exists, so on its own it leaves Chrome, Edge, and Firefox on native `Temporal` and a Node.js 24 server on the polyfill. When identical server and browser markup for these calendars matters more than matching official data, call `installImplementation()` from `temporal-polyfill/full/shim` on the server and in the browser before rendering: it installs the polyfill even over a native `Temporal`. A server runtime with native `Temporal`, such as Node.js 26, also matches native browsers. Otherwise, do not replace a native `Temporal`: that makes native environments less accurate.
