A function in the package, `(source) => Component`, that turns a library export that is not a component (icon data, an SVG string or URL) into one. `module` is a `./` path from the package root. Example: {module: './src/adapt.js', export: 'adapt'}.
The named looks the set offers, in lower-kebab case, such as `outline` and `solid`. Icon size is never a variant: CSS sets it. Omit it when the set has one look. Example: ['outline', 'solid'].
The variant each icon's own `export` draws; one of `variants`. Example: {variant: 'outline'}.
The export that maps each built-in icon definition to its artwork, keyed by exactly the built-in definitions in `map`. Example: 'themeIcons'.

Which of this set's icons draws each icon definition: definition name to icon `id`. Keys are Astryx's definitions (`astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-definitions`) or ones the set declares in its `definitions` folder, one file per definition. One icon may draw several definitions; each definition maps to one icon. Every built-in definition must be mapped. Example: {"close": "x", "delete": "trash", "remove": "trash"}.
Lower-kebab identity, unique in the set. Example: 'trash'.
The named export that draws the icon's default variant, named `<Name>Icon`: a React component that takes SVG props and draws with `currentColor`. Example: 'TrashIcon'.
The import specifier, when it differs from the set's `module`.

Lower-case terms a person might search for, the words of the icon's own name included; at least one. Do not copy the words of the definitions `map` names the icon for: search already matches the icon by them. Example: ['trash', 'delete', 'remove', 'bin'].
Other variants of the icon: each names one of `variants`, never the default, and the export that draws it. At most one export per variant.

Reviewed equivalents of this icon in other icon sets or libraries, such as `{set: 'lines', export: 'CrossIcon', variant: 'solid', confidence: 'exact'}`. When a copied template imports a matched icon from that installed set, `exact` and `strong` matches are used before any other rule; a `likely` match is only suggested. A match never names this set itself.

A file that fails this schema, repeats an id, gives an icon no words, has a `map` key that is not camelCase or a `map` value that is not an icon id in the file, or names a variant `variants` does not declare is invalid, and its set is withdrawn from every surface until it is fixed. `astryx doctor` names the reason.

A template declares the icon definition each icon it imports draws. With a project icon set, each declared icon maps to the icon whose `matches` name it with `exact` or `strong` confidence (for an icon another installed set ships), else to the icon this file's `map` names for its definition. Nothing is guessed from names or words.

Write it with the CLI: `astryx experimental icon add` registers one icon and its `map` entry, `astryx experimental icon map` changes an entry, and `astryx experimental icon new-set --from` wraps a whole library.

Experimental: may change or be removed in a patch release. One thing an icon can stand for, such as `close` or `delete`. Astryx ships one file per definition; an icon set adds its own in the same format. A set's data file `map` registers which of its icons draws each definition.
camelCase identity: the key a data file's `map` uses. Must match the file name. Example: 'delete'.
One sentence: what an icon with this definition is for. Example: 'Delete something permanently.'.
Lower-case terms a person might search for; at least one. Example: ['trash', 'bin', 'discard'].
Only on Astryx's own definitions: the definition is a shared icon name Core renders, so every icon set maps it.
Marks the definition as experimental: the icon-definitions listing shows it as `[experimental]`. Omit it for a definition you mean to keep.

A set's own definitions sit in a `definitions` folder in the set's directory, one file per definition. Its `map` registers icons for them like for Astryx's. `astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-definitions` lists every definition: Astryx's, and, in a project that sets `experimental.iconSet`, those of each installed set. A definition file refuses a field it does not know.

IconDefinitionDoc is static metadata: one default-exported object of literal fields directly under a `/** @type {import('@astryxdesign/cli/authoring').IconDefinitionDoc} */` comment. Discovery reads it without executing it.
To share a definition with every set, copy its file into Astryx's definitions folder in a pull request.

Icon sets are experimental: the `astryx experimental icon` commands, the `experimental.iconSet` key in astryx.config, the `experimental.iconSets` key in an integration manifest, the data file, icon definitions, and the output and JSON of all of them can change, or go away, in any patch release without a deprecation period. A project that does not set `experimental.iconSet` sees no change in any stable command, apart from: the marked `experimental` group in help and in `astryx manifest` (its command, and its `responseTypes` and `jsonSupported` entries); the marked experimental entries in the CLI reference listings; and a search for "experimental", which also finds the stable `stability` field of the field reference. Templates, discover, and doctor answer as they do with no icon set installed. With a package that ships icon sets installed and no opt-in, the warnings an older CLI gives about the manifest key `experimental` (in `astryx doctor` and `astryx doctor integration validate <package>`, and the one-line nudge other commands print to stderr) are gone. `astryx search` never returns icons or these docs; to find an icon by meaning, use `astryx experimental icon <words>`.

Astryx keeps a list of icon definitions: one file per meaning, like `close` or `delete` (`astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-definitions`). An icon set registers which of its icons draws each definition, in the `map` of its data file; one icon may draw several definitions (`file` and `document` can both be your `document` icon). Templates say which definition each of their icons draws, so a project that uses your set gets your icon for every definition you map. Every set maps the built-in definitions, the names Core renders itself.
The CLI knows no icon library. You, or your agent, pick each icon from the library you wrap; the commands below verify it, write the files, and check the set.

`outline.doc.mjs` is the descriptor: name, display name and description (`--display-name`, `--description`), and `license`, the SPDX license of the artwork (it starts as your package's own). `outline.icons.json` starts with no icons and an empty `map`; its `module` is your package name. `outline.generated.js` is the set's generated module, with its declaration file `outline.generated.d.ts`: the CLI writes both, and every icon and the theme map are exports of it. Every field is in `astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-set-files icon-set-doc` and `astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-set-files icon-set-data`.

The set's icons import from your package by name, so your package's entry must re-export the generated module. The command writes only the set's own files: your entry, `exports`, `main`, `types`, `files`, peers, and scripts are yours, and the receipt names each change to make as text to copy. For an entry file in the package (and the declaration file package.json names) that is the line `export * from './icon-sets/outline/outline.generated.js';`, relative to it; for a package with no entry, `index.js` and `index.d.ts` with that line and the package.json `main`, `types`, and `exports` that name them; for a built or CommonJS entry, the line to add to the source it is built from. `integration check` names the same change until you make it, and the receipt also names the peers and the `typecheck` script to add. `integration check --strict` type-checks the set's doc files with your package's TypeScript; the receipt says when it is missing (`npm install -D typescript@6`).
Add icons one at a time

Pick an icon from the library and ask which definitions fit it. Nothing is written yet. To read every icon a set already has, one line each with its words and the definitions it draws, run `astryx experimental icon --set <set> --all-icons`; `astryx experimental icon <set>/<id>` reads one, or says the id does not exist:
Each row is an Astryx definition (or one your set declares) with the exact command that adds the icon for it. Run one:
astryx experimental icon add Bin --from @acme/glyph-library --definition delete

The CLI reads the library's exports without running them and refuses a name the module does not export, suggesting close names. It adds the icon as `BinIcon` (id `bin`, words from its name), writes `export {Bin as BinIcon} from '@acme/glyph-library';` to the set's generated module, and sets `map.delete = "bin"`. Running it again changes nothing. Do not copy the definition's words into the icon: `astryx experimental icon` matches an icon by its own words and by the name and words of every definition it is mapped to.
When no Astryx definition fits, add your own in the same command. It needs no pull request:
astryx experimental icon add Dice5 --from @acme/glyph-library --new-definition random --description 'Pick something at random.' --words dice,shuffle,chance

`experimental icon map <definition> <icon>` points a definition at an icon the set already has (a definition is named in camelCase, `eyeSlash`, or by the kebab id the definitions list shows, `eye-slash`; an icon by its id, its export name in any case, or another name its library exports it as, such as `trash-2`, never by one word of its id), `experimental icon map --pairs close=x-mark,search=magnifying-glass` writes many entries at once (checked together, all or none; an entry the map already has is replaced, and the receipt shows what it was), and `--remove` drops an entry. `experimental icon new-definition <name> --description ... --words ... --icon <id>` adds your own definition for an icon you already have. `experimental icon --definitions` lists every Astryx definition, built in or not, with its words (`--json` for a script).

Every component the library exports becomes an icon (an alias of one component is recorded once), named `<Name>Icon`, with an id from its name (`Squares2X2Icon` is `squares-2x2`: a dimension stays one word). `map` is filled only where a definition's name is an icon's id (`delete` → icon `delete`), and the receipt lists those entries under Mapped by name: a library can draw another meaning under the same name (one library's `delete` is a backspace key), so check each. An icon whose id is only one of a definition's words (`trash` for `delete`) may mean something else in this library, so the receipt lists it under Suggestions, with the `experimental icon map <definition> <icon>` command for each, and writes nothing for it: check the meaning, then run the ones that fit. Run it again after a library release to refresh the icons that library supplies; `map` entries whose icon still exists are kept, and the receipt names any icon the library dropped, any icon `--exclude` left out, and the `map` entries each took with it. Icons you added from your own files or another library are left as they are. Icons you added one file at a time from the same package (`--from <package>/dist/XIcon`) move to the root import when you refresh from the package root and the root exports the same icon; each keeps its id, export, `map` entries, variants, and words on that refresh and every later one, and the receipt lists it under `moved`. A library icon whose id or name a moved icon already has is left out. When another icon of the set already reads the same root export, the icon stays on its own file, and the receipt says why. An icon you already have is known by the library export it re-exports, so it keeps its export name exactly, its `map` entries, variants, and words, even when a newer CLI spells its id differently or your `--exclude` lets a library prefix come off new ids; the receipt lists each changed id under `renamed`. An id you chose that is not a spelling of the library name (`dismiss` for `XIcon`) is kept. A refresh with `--dry-run` writes nothing and prints the Mapped by name and Suggestions lists again; `--display-name` and `--description` on a refresh rewrite the descriptor. Variants added with `add --variant … --all` are kept too; run that `add` again to pick up icons the release added. `experimental icon --list` shows how many definitions the set maps.

With a package or package subpath, it also records the installed library and version as the data file's `source`, so `integration check` warns when your dependency moves to another version; copies the library's LICENSE (and NOTICE) files into the set directory; and sets the descriptor's `license` to the library's. A set you started without `--from` gets the same the first time a refresh records its source, unless you already changed `license`: a `license` you set is kept (the receipt names the library's), and every later refresh keeps it too. Your package.json `license` is never changed. Edit `license` when the artwork's license differs from the library's package license. When the library ships no license file to copy, the receipt says so under `licenseNoticeMissing` and in its notes, and the CLI writes nothing: add a `NOTICE` file to the set directory (`icon-sets/<set>/NOTICE`) that names the library, its version, and its license. `integration check` accepts a file named `LICENSE`, `LICENCE`, `NOTICE`, or `COPYING`, in any case and with an optional suffix such as `NOTICE.md` or `LICENSE-MIT`, in the set directory or the package root; without one it reports `icon_license_notice_missing`.
A library with a module per style supplies variants. Declare them when you create the set, then add a variant for every icon in one run:

astryx experimental icon new-set heroicons --from @heroicons/react/24/outline --variants outline,solid --default-variant outline --description 'Heroicons, outline and solid.'
astryx experimental icon add --variant solid --from @heroicons/react/24/solid --all

A library that redraws its artwork for small sizes (Heroicons' 20px mini and 16px micro) ships each of those as its own set in its own package (their export names match the 24px ones), not as variants: a variant's size comes from CSS. `--variants` lists the variants; `--default-variant` names the one each icon's own export draws (when omitted, the look a library that names its looks draws; otherwise the set's current default, else, on a set without icons, the first variant; a set with icons changes it only with `--from`, and only in a library that names its looks). `--all` adds the variant for every icon whose id an export of `--from` has (`TrashIcon` in the solid module becomes `TrashSolidIcon`, the solid variant of `trash`), and the receipt lists the icons the module has no export for. Running it again changes nothing.

A library whose icons are data (objects or SVG strings) has no components to find: create the set, declare an `adapter` in its data file (see library shapes), and run the command again; every data export then becomes an icon through the adapter. When every icon export shares a leading word, such as `feather` in `featherEye` and `featherSun`, ids and export names leave it out: `featherEye` becomes id `eye`, exported as `EyeIcon`. The prefix is read over icon-like exports only: SCREAMING_CASE constants (`README`, `VERSION`), number and boolean exports, and, next to components or icon objects, plain strings are never icons. Components named `…Provider` or `…Context` are never icons either. Leave out any other export that is not an icon with `--exclude meta,version`: the data file keeps the list in `exclude`, so a refresh leaves them out too. When a library exports one icon under several names (`Trash2` and `Trash`), the icon is recorded once and its other names become words, so `experimental icon trash-2` finds it and `experimental icon map delete trash-2` maps it. `experimental icon add` reads the prefix the same way, and reuses the icon an export already has, so its commands need no `--id`.
Every icon is a named export of your package's public entry, so apps, templates, and theme maps all import components from one place:
The data file's `module` is your package name or one of its package.json `exports` subpaths, never a file path. `integration check` fails otherwise.
A variant is a named look the set supplies (for example outline or solid); size comes from CSS. List the names in `variants` in the data file and the one each icon's own export draws in `default`.
Each export is named `<Name>Icon`, and a variant `<Name><Variant>Icon`, such as `TrashSolidIcon`. `experimental icon add` names them that way; `integration check` warns on another name.
Each export is a React component: a function, a class, `forwardRef` or `memo`, or what your adapter returns. `integration check` fails on a plain object or string.

It accepts SVG props (`className`, `style`, `aria-*`, `width`, `height`), draws with `currentColor`, and fills its box (`1em` or `100%`), so `<Icon icon={TrashIcon} size="sm" />` sizes and colors it like a built-in icon. The CLI cannot check this statically; the test below can.

`experimental icon add` writes the set's generated module (`generated` in the data file) and its declaration file, which re-exports each component's own types and types each adapted icon as `ComponentType<SVGProps<SVGSVGElement>>`. Add this line to your package's entry and its types; `experimental icon new-set` names the exact line and file in its receipt (see add an icon set):

An optional render test you can copy. Save it inside your package directory and run it there, since it imports your package by name through its `exports`, and install `react-dom` first (`npm install -D react-dom`). A library may add its own classes beside yours, so it checks the class list. A component that writes its own `width` and `height` attributes (24, from a `size` prop, say) still fills its box when it passes `style` through to its svg: the `Icon` component and `themeIcons` size the svg with CSS, which overrides size attributes. The test checks that too.
`--from` is any import specifier: a package, a package subpath, or a `./` path inside your package. Use the row that matches the library:

`experimental icon add --variant solid --from @acme/glyph-library/solid --all` for every icon at once, or `experimental icon add Bin --from @acme/glyph-library/solid --id bin --variant solid` for one (the set must declare the variant: `new-set --variants`)
Every look in its export names (`XOutline24WGHT500Icon`, `XFilled24WGHT500Icon`)

`experimental icon new-set meta --from @acme/vector-icons` wraps each glyph once as `x` (`XIcon`), in the look `--default-variant` names or the library's usual default (outline, the middle weight). For another look: `experimental icon new-set meta --variants outline,filled` declares it in place, then `experimental icon add --variant filled --from @acme/vector-icons --all`
One file per icon, default export
Declare an `adapter`, then `experimental icon add Rocket --from @acme/glyph-data --definition rocket`
Declare an `adapter` that renders them, then `experimental icon add` as above

`experimental icon add Rocket --from ./src/icons/rocket.js --definition rocket`, and `--id rocket --variant solid` for its other looks. The file exports a component named as written (no library prefix is taken off), with a declaration file beside it (`rocket.d.ts`) or written in TypeScript, since the set's types re-export its own; when package.json lists `files` and none covers it, the receipt names the `files` array that publishes its folder.

An export that is not a component goes through your adapter: a function in your package that turns it into one. Declare it in the data file, `"adapter": {"module": "./src/adapt.js", "export": "adapt"}`, and `experimental icon add` writes `export const RocketIcon = adaptIcon(RocketIconSource);`:

The generated module also exports `themeIcons`: one entry per built-in definition in `map`, each an element of your own icon, hidden from assistive technology and sized `1em` by its attributes and by CSS (its `style`), so it fills the theme's icon box even when your component writes its own size attributes. The CLI rewrites it on every `experimental icon add` and `experimental icon map`, so you never write it by hand, and `integration check` proves it matches `map`. A theme uses it in one line:

`astryx integration check` reads the set without running your icons. An unmapped built-in definition is an error that names the definition's description and words and the `experimental icon map <definition> <icon id>` command that fixes it, so you or your agent can pick the icon. It names a search of your set (`experimental icon <word> --set <set>`) only when that search finds icons, and suggests one icon: the first of the suggestions `experimental icon new-set` gives for that definition. It never matches part of a word, and never writes a suggestion. Its icon-set codes:

`invalid_icon_set` (error): the descriptor, data file, or a definition file is invalid, for example a repeated `id`, an icon with no words, or a `map` key that is neither an Astryx definition nor one in your `definitions` folder. The set is withdrawn: apps do not see it.
`icon_builtin_definition_missing` (error): a built-in definition is not in `map`.
`icon_definition_unused` (warning): a definition you declared is not in `map`.
`icon_definition_shadowed` (warning): a definition you declared now exists in Astryx; map to Astryx's and remove yours.
`icon_export_missing` (error): an export, the generated module, or the adapter does not exist.
`icon_module_invalid` (error): the set's module, a file it re-exports, or the generated module does not parse; reported once, instead of a missing export per icon.
`icon_generated_types_mismatch` (error): the generated module's declaration file is missing or does not match it.
`icon_theme_map_mismatch` (error): the theme map disagrees with the built-in entries of `map`.
`icon_source_version_drift` and `icon_license_notice_missing` (warnings): the data names another library version than the package depends on, or a set with an upstream ships no license notice.

The other Astryx definitions your set leaves unmapped are not issues: a library need not draw every definition. They are listed under "Unmapped icon definitions (optional)", and in the JSON as the validate result's `iconSets`: for each set, `unmappedDefinitions` (each `{name, description, words}`) and `suggestions` (each `{definition, icon}`, for any unmapped definition one of your icons fits). They are never counted and never fail a check.

An export fails only when the reader proves it absent; what it cannot judge it does not fail either. An icon export whose module is an `exports` target you have not built yet; an icon or adapter export it cannot prove either way (behind a re-export it cannot follow, bound to a default or namespace import, or imported from a package that is not installed); and a theme map or theme-map entry it cannot read are listed under "Not checked", and in the JSON as each set's `unchecked` (each `{icon}`, `{adapter}`, or `{entry}`, with its `reason`). Build the package, install the package it imports from, export the icon by name, or write the entry as a binding or element to have it checked. An export your built module lacks is still an error.

Errors fail the check. Warnings fail only with `--strict`. A set that maps every built-in definition and every definition it declares passes `--strict`, which integrations run in their build (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`). The flow, start to finish: `experimental icon new-set` → `npm install -D typescript@6` when the receipt asks → `integration check` → `experimental icon add` (or `experimental icon map`) for each definition it lists → `integration check` passes.
Run `astryx integration verify` yourself before publishing. Do not put it in `prepublishOnly`: under `npm publish --dry-run` its own `npm pack` becomes a dry run too, and it checks nothing.

Declare `@astryxdesign/cli` as an optional peer (`peerDependenciesMeta`). A required peer an app cannot satisfy makes npm remove the app's CLI without a word. Icon sets are experimental, so no version range promises them, and the format may change in a patch release. A CLI reads a set only when it knows every key the set's data file uses: a key it does not know withdraws the set, naming the key. `exclude` is read only by a CLI whose data-file reference lists it (`astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-set-files icon-set-data`); a set without `exclude` is read by every CLI that has `astryx experimental icon`. A CLI without it reads `experimental` as a manifest key it does not know: `astryx doctor` there warns that your package was published against a newer Astryx CLI, other commands print a one-line nudge to run it, and your icons, icon definitions, and template icon mapping do not appear (`astryx docs authoring/ship/versioning`).

Every built-in definition needs an icon, because Core renders it. When your library has no icon with that exact meaning, map the closest one, or add your own artwork as a component file in your package (`experimental icon add <Name> --from ./src/icons/<name>.js --definition <definition>`; a ./ path is named as written). Artwork you draw is yours: note its license beside the library's, for example in a NOTICE file in the set directory.
The generated declaration file imports React types, so declare `@types/react` as an optional peer for TypeScript users.

Keep the wrapped library in `dependencies`: your generated module re-exports its components, so apps get it with your package, and `integration check` compares its range with the version the data file records.
`integration check --strict` type-checks the set's doc files; it does not type-check the generated declaration file against React's types. Run `tsc` with `@types/react` installed to check those.

Your package needs `react` (the theme map and adapter use it) as a peer, as Core does. The `experimental icon new-set` receipt names the peers your package.json does not declare yet, as the JSON to add: `react` (`>=18`), and `@types/react` and `@astryxdesign/cli` (from the release that wrote the set) as optional peers; and the `typecheck` script (`astryx integration check --strict`) when there is none.
Share a definition with every set

Your own definitions need no change to Astryx. To share one with every set, open a pull request that copies its file into the CLI's icon definitions folder, with a description and words. Its name must not clash with another definition.

astryx experimental icon delete              # ranked matches with import lines
astryx experimental icon outline/bin         # one icon and every variant
astryx experimental icon --list              # installed sets and their definition coverage
astryx experimental icon use outline         # make it the project's icon set

A template declares, in its descriptor's `icons`, the definition each imported icon draws (`{TrashIcon: 'delete'}`). Once the project sets `experimental.iconSet` in astryx.config (`experimental icon use` writes it), each declared icon becomes the set's icon for that definition. An icon the set does not map keeps its original import, and the copy reports every icon as mapped or kept. Nothing is guessed from names. A mapped icon loses its library's sizing props (`size`, `strokeWidth`, `absoluteStrokeWidth`), since a set's icons take their size from CSS; the report names them as `dropped`. Comments on a rewritten import line are kept.

Each `icons` key is the name the template imports from its module, not a local alias. When a template imports the same name from two modules, such as `TrashIcon` from a library's outline and solid modules, one key covers both: both draw the same definition. Each then becomes the project set's variant of the same name when its module belongs to an installed set that declares the variant (so solid stays solid), else the set's default.

Every place the CLI reads or reports icon sets, all experimental. Outside `astryx experimental icon`, each appears only in a project that sets `experimental.iconSet`; `astryx search` never returns icons:

The project's icon set, by set name or as `<package>/<set>`, and the opt-in: templates, discover, and doctor read icon sets only when it is set. `astryx experimental icon` ranks its icons first, and without it treats the only installed set as the project's. `astryx experimental icon use` writes it.
The folder that holds the package's icon sets, relative to package.json. `astryx experimental icon new-set` declares it.

The icon definition each imported icon draws (`{TrashIcon: 'delete'}`): a named import by the name it imports, a default import by its local name. `astryx template`, shown or copied, then writes the set's icons and reports `icons` (status, set, mapped, kept): every key is mapped, or kept with why (no match, a namespace or type-only import, a re-export, an Astryx or project-set import, or no import at all). `integration check` notes a key the template's source never imports (`template_icon_not_imported`), never failing.
A package's sets (`iconSets`) and, for `@scope/name/<set>`, the set's display name, license, icon count, and definitions; `--type icon-set` keeps only sets.

Build the page with Astryx components as usual, then render it. The page module needs a default export; it renders on your machine with the React and Astryx packages your project installed. Outside a project (no Astryx Core or CLI installed or declared for the folder), it renders with the Astryx, React and StyleX that the CLI itself runs with, so a single page file renders anywhere, a React app included.

The result is ONE file with nothing beside it: the markup, only the CSS rules the page uses (from Core and from any stylesheet it imports, such as a theme), the page’s own StyleX styles, and local images as data: URIs. It runs no script and loads nothing from the network, so it opens from disk, attaches to a message, and displays inside a sandboxed frame that blocks network and script. Colors follow the viewer’s light or dark setting, and a `data-theme` of `light` or `dark` on the root element picks one. The file also carries the source of the page and of every local module, stylesheet, JSON file and image it imports, so whoever you share it with can read that code; keep secrets out of what the page imports.

What it cannot keep: anything that needs a browser while running. State, effects, click handlers and data loaded after the first paint are gone. Charts made with recharts are the exception: the render draws each chart and ResponsiveContainer a module of the page (not an installed package) imports from recharts by name (`import {LineChart} from 'recharts'`), inside the page, so a custom tick, label or shape sees the page's React context. A chart sized by its container scales to the width the page gives it, and its legend stays out of the picture: a horizontal legend takes its own row under it (above it when the legend asks for the top), and a vertical legend on one side sits beside it, on that side; in a chart of fixed size, a legend keeps the place its props give it. Charts show the data and props of the page's first render, before its effects run: when the page cannot be drawn again without a browser, or its effects change its charts or re-render the component that makes them, each chart is drawn by itself and its parts see React context defaults. A value a chart's parts read from a React context that an effect changes may still show its later value. A `chart-size` warning counts the charts the render cannot draw (one used through `import * as R`, say), and says when charts were drawn by themselves. Read browser-only values such as window inside an effect, or the render stops with ERR_RENDER_BROWSER_API.

Each warning names something that may look different from what you meant, and what to change. The most common is a component that ignores its children: `<ListItem>Save</ListItem>` renders an empty row because ListItem takes `label="Save"`. Others flag remote images (a sandboxed viewer cannot load them; save the image next to the page and import it), a `<script>`, `<link>` or `<iframe>` the page itself renders (the file promises to run and load nothing, so remove them), missing images, and output the page printed while rendering.

Every rendered file carries its source, so this writes the page back byte for byte; edit it and render again. A file whose source block was removed but whose markup came from Astryx components is rebuilt from that markup instead: the components, their recorded props and the text come back, while styling, icons and behavior do not, so treat it as a starting point. HTML that was never an Astryx page is refused with ERR_RENDER_NOT_ASTRYX; describe the page to `astryx build` to start one.

It writes the page, the modules, stylesheets and JSON files the page reaches through its own imports, and the images, fonts and media the render carried (however the page named them, as long as their bytes really are one): each goes where the page's relative imports find it from wherever you put the page, and a file the page imports through a path alias (`@/components/Header`) goes where your project's `tsconfig.json` or `jsconfig.json` alias points. Every file but the page goes inside the one new folder the restore creates (the topmost folder on the page's path that does not exist yet), never into a folder that already exists: a page that imports other files comes back into a new folder (`--out restored/app/page.tsx`), and a file it imports through a path alias comes back only when that alias points inside the new folder. Nor does it write a file that a test, story or benchmark runner would run by its default patterns (Jest, Vitest, Bun, AVA, Playwright, Storybook, Cypress and `node --test`: names such as `*.test.*`, `*.spec.*`, `*_test.*`, `*-test.*`, `*.bench.*`, `*.stories.*`, `*.cy.*`, and anything under `test/`, `tests/` or `__tests__/`), judged from the repository root (every folder above the file up to it), else the topmost folder with a package.json. Restored files are the sender's code: read them before you run or import them. Without `--out`, everything comes back into a new folder beside the HTML file, named after it (`page.html` comes back into `page-restored/`). A received file that carries anything else (a file the page never imports, a dotfile, `package.json`, a tool configuration, a path that leaves the folder) is refused with nothing written. A rendered file that lost its embedded source on the way (a sanitizer or an editor strips `<script>` blocks) and has no Astryx components to rebuild from is refused with `ERR_RENDER_SOURCE_DAMAGED`. An existing file is never replaced unless you pass `--overwrite`, and the refusal names every one; a generated, vendored or ignored file, and any path through a symbolic link, is not written even then. Add `--json` for the result as data: what was written, how big it is, and every warning.

Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once into its cache in the background after a command you run online (on Windows, the first component command downloads it), and a component command before that, offline, fails with `ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`. Once a day, never in your first day, your global install checks the registry's `latest` version in the background, without slowing the command. When a newer one exists, a command that succeeds prints two lines on standard error, at most once a day:

A new release of Astryx is available: 0.7.2 → 0.7.3
To upgrade, run: npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest

The command is the one for the package manager that installed your global install: `npm i -g`, `pnpm add -g`, `yarn global add`, `bun add -g`, or `volta install`. A global folder moved with the package manager's own setting (`BUN_INSTALL`, Yarn's `global-folder`, `PNPM_HOME`, or npm's prefix) counts while that setting names it; an app's own copy never runs the update check.
When the newest version needs a newer Node than your computer runs, the second line says which Node to install first.

Inside a project, the notice is about the project's version, and names the project's install and `upgrade` commands. The install command always adds the CLI next to Core, so a project that installed only Core gets its own CLI too, as recommended.

A new release of Astryx is available: 0.7.1 → 0.7.3
To upgrade, run: pnpm add @astryxdesign/core@0.7.3 @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.3, then pnpm exec astryx upgrade --from 0.7.1 --apply

No notice prints with `--json`, after a failed command, when the `CI` environment variable is set, or when `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER` is set; with either variable set, the CLI does not check the registry either. Unlike some CLIs, a notice prints even when standard error is not a terminal, because agents run the CLI without one.

In a project, the project's version

The project installs the CLI, as recommended: that CLI answers, whatever its version, as it always has. When you type the global astryx command instead, it passes the run to the project's CLI, with the same arguments, input, output, and exit status, so either command gives the same answer.

The project installs only Core, or nothing is installed yet, as in a fresh clone: the astryx command you started answers, as it always has. When its version differs from the project's Core, a hint after the command, once a day, names the command that adds the CLI at Core's version.

The project's CLI is installed but cannot start: the CLI version equal to the project's Core answers instead (from the installed Core, else the lockfile, else the newest one the declared range allows), installed once into a cache.

Components come from `@astryxdesign/core`, and templates, docs, and agent guides come from the CLI. In a project, that Core is the one the project installs, so component commands work offline once the project's dependencies are installed. Outside a project, or in a project with nothing installed yet (a fresh clone), they use the answering version's own Core, from beside the CLI or the cache; when that Core cannot be downloaded, the error says to install the project's dependencies. When the project's CLI and Core are different versions, `astryx doctor` warns and prints the command that brings them to one version.
Outside a project, your global install

In a folder that belongs to no project, your global install answers as a brand-new project on its version would, so you and your agents can read every component and doc. It never installs a newer version by itself.
A few commands work on your computer rather than a folder, such as `astryx init --user`: your global install answers them in any folder.

Using astryx with your own i18n library

Astryx components render astryx strings through astryx's provider. Consumer components render consumer strings through whatever i18n library you already use: react-intl, i18next, next-intl, LinguiJS, and so on. The two systems coexist and read from the same source of truth for the active locale.

Keep the two providers in sync on locale, and each library owns its own catalog. Astryx never sees your app strings, and your i18n library never sees astryx internals. Runtime locale swap works the same way: re-render both providers with a new `locale` prop and the whole tree updates live.

Single-catalog usage (where an external i18n runtime like react-intl or i18next resolves both your app strings AND astryx's strings through one provider) is on the roadmap via a `Translator` adapter. Track [meta/astryx#4029](https://github.com/meta/astryx/issues/4029). For now, run the two providers side by side as shown above.
Using astryx as your i18n library

For production apps with substantial localization needs, we recommend a dedicated i18n library such as react-intl, i18next, next-intl, or LinguiJS. If your app is small or you do not want another runtime, you can resolve your own strings through astryx too. Keep app keys in a separate namespace from `@astryx.*`, and include your own `en` catalog because astryx's built-in English fallback only contains astryx component strings.

`Catalog` types the rich `{defaultMessage, description?}` authoring shape. `RuntimeCatalog` types the generated key-to-message string map. `ProviderMessagesByLocale` accepts either shape for the provider, while `MessagesByLocale` keeps the original rich-only context shape.

Internationalization ships with `@astryxdesign/core`. There is nothing to install. Wrap your app in `<InternationalizationProvider>` and set the active `locale`; astryx components pick up localized strings from that provider.
The provider always has the built-in English catalog. Pass additional catalogs through `messages` when you enable another locale.

Astryx ships English and first-party translations for supported locales. Compact runtime modules from `@astryxdesign/core/locales/*.generated.js` contain only the messages apps need; the existing `@astryxdesign/core/locales/*.json` files retain translator context. Until a locale is available, apps can pass a local catalog in either shape. Missing keys fall back through the locale chain to English (for example, `pt-BR` walks to `pt`, then to shipped `en`).
Locale catalogs only affect astryx strings. Your app can continue using its own i18n system for product copy.
Re-render `<InternationalizationProvider>` with a new `locale` prop and every astryx string updates live. No reload, no separate API call.
Persisting the user's choice (localStorage, cookie, URL segment, account setting) is up to the consumer. Astryx reads whatever `locale` you pass in.

Astryx tracks text direction (`'ltr'` or `'rtl'`) alongside the locale. By default the direction is derived from the `locale` you pass to `<InternationalizationProvider>` via [`Intl.Locale.getTextInfo()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Locale/getTextInfo), so RTL locales such as Arabic (`ar`), Hebrew (`he`), Farsi (`fa`), and Urdu (`ur`) resolve to `'rtl'` automatically.

You don't wire anything per component. Once the direction is set, astryx components mirror on their own: layout and spacing flip via CSS logical properties, directional icons (chevrons, carets) flip in place, keyboard arrow keys swap left/right, and overlays position on the correct side. Set the direction once and the whole component tree follows.

Pass the optional `dir` prop to force a direction. This overrides the locale-derived default; useful for RTL layout testing under an English catalog, or to skip derivation when you already know the direction.

There's one more step: tell the browser about the direction too. Add a `dir` attribute to your page; usually on the `<html>` tag. This is what makes text align to the correct side, punctuation and mixed-language text flow correctly, and layouts mirror. The provider handles astryx components; the `dir` attribute handles everything else on the page.

Astryx doesn't set `dir` for you; you set it, alongside the same direction you pass to the provider. If your app is server-rendered (like Next.js), the `getLocaleDirection()` helper computes the direction from a locale so you can set it while the page renders:
Set <html dir> in a Next.js root layout

In a plain client app, set the same attribute on `<html>` whenever the locale changes. (`getLocaleDirection()` safely returns `'ltr'` for anything it doesn't recognize, so you can call it with any locale string.)

To make just one part of a left-to-right page right-to-left; say an Arabic quote or a comment thread; wrap that part in its own `<InternationalizationProvider dir="rtl">` and add `dir="rtl"` to the element around it. Pop-up overlays; menus, dialogs, popovers, tooltips; opened from inside that region mirror too: they position with logical CSS anchor placement, so they land on the correct side and inherit the region's direction automatically.

Astryx generates a `pseudo` locale that wraps every string in `⟦…⟧` and replaces letters with accented look-alikes. Turn it on in development to catch hardcoded astryx strings and layout issues caused by longer text.
Astryx component authors read strings with `useTranslator()` rather than hardcoding user-facing text.

Astryx's own strings live in `packages/core/locales/en.json`. New user-facing strings must go through `useTranslator`; this is enforced by the `@astryx/no-hardcoded-i18n-string` ESLint rule. See the AI contribution guide for the alias-and-resolve pattern used when adding new keys.
When you author a component that needs to respond to direction, resolve it from the DOM, not from a render-time JavaScript read, and reach for the lightest tool that works. In priority order:

Use `insetInlineStart`, `paddingInlineEnd`, `marginInline`, and friends instead of physical `left`/`right`. Most mirroring needs nothing more; the browser flips it from the ambient `dir`. The `@astryx/no-physical-properties` ESLint rule enforces this.
2. Directional icons: mirror with CSS, not a name-swap

Render one fixed glyph and wrap it in the shared `rtlStyles.mirror` (a `scaleX(-1)` that only applies under `[dir="rtl"]`). It flips from the ancestor `dir` through the cascade, so it works on the server with no hydration flash. Do not pick `chevronLeft` vs `chevronRight` in JS. This is how Pagination, Calendar, and Carousel handle their chevrons.
Mirror a directional icon with CSS
3. Behavioral logic: read the DOM lazily, on the event

For things CSS can't express; keyboard arrow-key mapping, drag/scroll math; read direction at interaction time with `isRtlElement(el)` (a `getComputedStyle().direction` check), never during render. The focus primitives (`useListFocus`, `useGridFocus`, `useTreeFocus`) already auto-detect direction from their container, so arrow keys flip for free; don't pass a direction flag to them.

Reach for it only when you genuinely need the direction value during render and none of the above fit. It's SSR-safe and returns `'ltr'` outside a provider (matching `useTranslator`'s silent fallback), but it's the one path that can mismatch on hydration if the provider's `direction` disagrees with `<html dir>`; so prefer the options above, which resolve purely from the DOM. As of the CSS-mirror migration, no astryx component reads direction from context at render time.

In a stylesheet with no layers at all, a zero-specificity reset like `* { padding: 0 }` loses to any class selector, so most developers treat resets as harmless. Layers change the rules twice: unlayered styles beat every named layer, and a later layer beats an earlier one, both regardless of specificity. The same reset therefore wins against every component style either by staying unlayered or by landing in a layer declared after astryx-base. Same CSS, opposite outcome, and no error or warning when it happens.

This is the most common way an adoption breaks, through one of two @import mechanisms. A top-level @import without the layer() keyword keeps the legacy reset unlayered, where it overrides every design system layer. And an @import nested inside a file that was itself imported into a layer inherits that surrounding layer, so a reset can silently land in a consumer layer above astryx-base. Either way the fix is the same: import the legacy reset into the lowest layer explicitly.

Astryx's theme defines its own CSS custom properties (color, spacing, radius, shadow, font, motion and more), and `astryx docs tokens` has the full list. An app token with one of those names collides in one of two ways. An app `@theme` key takes Astryx's value, because `astryx.css` sets the tokens on `:root` above Tailwind's `theme` layer: with `@theme { --spacing-4: 1.5rem }`, the app's `gap-4` stays 16px. Marking the block `@theme inline` keeps the app's value in its utilities. An app `:root` variable replaces Astryx's value, so Astryx's own components change: `:root { --spacing-4: 1.5rem }` widens Astryx's spacing step 4 from 16px to 24px. Where the root Theme component sets a token again, such as `--color-warning`, the app's own rules inside it read Astryx's value instead. Rename any app token that shares a name.

Put the `@layer` line above the app's `@import "tailwindcss"`, never below it. A `@layer` statement orders only the layer names the page has not seen yet, and the Tailwind import names `theme`, `base`, `components`, and `utilities` as it loads. Below that import, the statement can only add `reset`, `astryx-base`, and `astryx-theme` after Tailwind's `utilities`. That inverts the cascade: the Astryx reset then outranks every utility class in the app, and, for example, removes the borders and padding the app's utilities give its controls. Nothing reports it: the build and the browser console stay clean, and the `@layer` line still looks right in the source, so only the rendered page shows the problem.
The load-order rule from the Tailwind section still applies: `globals.css` must be the first stylesheet the page loads, so its `@layer` line names the layers first.

Complex components are composed from smaller components. Each sub-component accepts its own xstyle, className, and rest props. You style the parts individually; there's no single "drill into sub-part" prop.
The pattern: the parent component (Dialog) controls structure and behavior, child components (Layout, Header, Button) control their own appearance. Style each piece where it lives.

When external CSS needs to target an Astryx component by prop or state, combine the stable component class with reflected data attributes. The component class identifies the component (`.astryx-button`, `.astryx-card`); data attributes identify the axis and value (`data-variant`, `data-size`, `data-level`, etc.). This is the preferred selector surface for new CSS because it is explicit and collision-resistant.

For systematic theming, use defineTheme component overrides instead of raw CSS selectors. defineTheme keeps the higher-level `prop:value` API (`variant:primary`, `size:sm`) and handles selector generation for you. Run `astryx docs author-a-theme` for component theming.

Astryx 0.7 emits canonical `astryx-*` target classes and reflected `data-*` attributes only. Run `astryx upgrade --from <your 0.6 version> --apply --path .` to rename removed target keys inside theme `components` maps and to migrate CSS selectors. The CSS migration renames removed target classes and replaces target-qualified bare prop/value/state classes such as `.primary`, `.sm`, `.level-2`, and `.checked` with their reflected `data-*` selectors.

Removed target mappings: `base-table` → `table`; `checkbox` → `checkbox-indicator`; `codeblock` → `code-block`; `codeblock-copy-button` → `code-block-copy-button`; `codeblock-header` → `code-block-header`; `codeblock-title` → `code-block-title`; `date-input-clear-icon`, `date-range-input-clear-icon`, `multi-selector-clear-icon`, and `selector-clear-icon` → `input-clear-icon`; `hovercard` → `hover-card`; `navicon` → `nav-icon`; `popover-surface` → `popover`; `progressbar`, `progressbar-fill`, `progressbar-mark`, and `progressbar-track` → their hyphenated `progress-bar*` forms; `radio` → `radio-indicator`; `radio-dot` → `radio-indicator-dot`; `statusdot` → `status-dot`; `textarea` → `text-area`.

`input-clear-icon` styles the clear icon of every input. In CSS the upgrade keeps each old clear-icon rule on its component with `:where(.astryx-<component> *)`. A theme key cannot carry that scope, so the upgrade renames the key and adds a `TODO(astryx upgrade)` that names the CSS selector to use instead.

The upgrade treats a `components` map as a theme when it belongs to a `defineTheme()` call imported from Astryx, an object typed as an Astryx theme, or the theme object a same-stem theme descriptor (`<stem>.doc.mjs`) declares: the top-level binding exported as `<stem>`, with a static `name` and component entries that are style objects. A look-alike object anywhere else, such as a theme object from another library in the same file, is not an Astryx theme. It leaves computed theme keys, unqualified classes, unknown consumer classes, declarations, comments, and CSS inside JavaScript or TypeScript strings unchanged. It adds `TODO(astryx upgrade)` when a map has both an old and a canonical key, and when a bare class Astryx once emitted has no known meaning on the target it qualifies. Review each TODO by hand.

StyleX Build Setup (required for swizzled components)

Astryx components ship pre-compiled: `astryx.css` and each package's own stylesheet hold all of their styles, so consuming the published packages needs no StyleX setup. But `astryx swizzle <Component>` copies the raw StyleX *source* into your app, and StyleX source requires a build-time StyleX compiler to produce atomic CSS. Without one, importing the component throws an error that starts `Unexpected 'stylex.create' call at runtime`, and the page does not render. Typography is built on a geometric type scale: base size × ratio^step, with 14px and 1.2 as defaults. Every text style is a semantic token that composes font size, weight, and line-height, so components express intent (heading, body, label) rather than raw values.

Two layers work together: raw size tokens (--font-size-xs ... --font-size-5xl) form the geometric scale, and semantic type scale tokens (--text-heading-1-size, --text-body-leading, etc.) reference them by var(). Themes override the entire scale by adjusting base and ratio in defineTheme; all semantic tokens recompute automatically.

Three font roles: body (UI text), heading (titles and headings), and code (monospace). By default, body and heading share the same system font stack; code uses a monospace stack. Custom themes can assign different families per role; heading inherits from body when not explicitly set.

Astryx never loads font files. defineTheme and the built CSS only set font-family: naming a webfont (Fraunces, JetBrains Mono, and so on) makes every browser look for it, and quietly fall back when the app has not loaded it. `astryx theme build` warns when a theme names families that are neither CSS generics nor common system fonts and prints the snippet to add; loading the font is always the app's job.

Line heights are computed from a tiered target ratio and snapped to a 4px vertical grid. Small text (<20px) targets 1.5, medium text (20–31px) targets 1.4, and large text (≥32px) targets 1.25. A minimum gap of fontSize + 4px is enforced. The result is a unitless ratio stored in each --text-*-leading token.

The 4px grid matters: every line box aligns to 4px increments, which keeps baselines, spacing, and component heights predictable. The expandTypeScale utility computes these automatically when you provide a base and ratio, so you should never need to set line-height manually.

Semantic tokens that combine size, weight, and line-height into a single type style. Each token triplet (--text-*-size, --text-*-weight, --text-*-leading) is consumed by Text and Heading. Use the component props rather than composing raw font tokens.

Display variants (display-1, display-2, display-3) continue the geometric progression above heading-1, at steps +6, +5, and +4. They use normal weight (400) instead of semibold, and tighter line-heights (~1.2), since large text reads better with less leading. Use display types for hero banners, marketing headlines, and data callouts, not for document headings.

Runs a series of diagnostics: Node version, @astryxdesign/core install and version alignment with the CLI, installed themes and wiring, astryx.config validity, whether every integration astryx.config names loads (a failed one fails the run), integrations linked from package.json without a config entry, core peer dependencies, integration provider identity and contribution issues, agent docs, the detected package manager, and the health of the docs the CLI reads (authoring and CLI docs, the docs tree, doc size), and returns a structured report. Theme checks run when the generated app module exists; without one, doctor reports that the CLI manages no themes and names theme add, and the `themes` check counts a theme as wired when package.json `astryx.theme` names one or when the source of the app (JavaScript, TypeScript and CSS files, outside dependencies and build output; type-only imports do not count) imports the built module or stylesheet of a discovered theme, the same imports theme add writes, or passes one to Theme (followed through module-scope variables, defineTheme extends, re-exports and installed packages; only a theme whose package is installed, or a local theme, counts), naming the file; a theme passed to Theme that cannot be traced, such as a prop or a variable declared inside a component, is reported as unconfirmed (info), not as missing. Earlier descriptor-less copies are a non-failing upgrade warning. It never installs, writes, or mutates. It imports astryx.config, executes every added theme source while validating private inputs, and loads every recorded built theme module to prove its runtime imports work, including themes from installed packages. Local theme source also runs during build-freshness checks. Stylesheets are parsed without execution. Config and theme top-level code therefore run, so use doctor only with project code you trust. Outside a project it checks the computer instead: the Node version (`node-version`), the release that answered (`answering-release`), the newest release the computer knows of (`newest-release`), the astryx commands on the search path (`cli-on-path`), the integrations installed for the computer (`computer-integrations`: each one used outside a project, and a warning for one skipped because its peer range excludes the answering release or that fails to load), and the computer-level agent text (`computer-agent-text`): present and matching this release, present but different, edited, absent, or turned off, and where it is linked, with `astryx init --user` as the fix for the stale and absent cases. The agent-text check is always info. The newest-release check also runs inside a project: it names a newer release when the computer knows of one; inside a project whose release is older it names the install and upgrade commands; outside one, when the CLI installed for the computer is older, it names the command of the package manager that installed it, after the Node the newest release needs when the computer runs an older one. It is always info and installs nothing. The `cli-on-path` check also runs inside a project: it lists every astryx command on the search path in order, passes when the first is a release that hands each project run to the release of that project, and warns when the first is another program or a release that predates the hand-off, naming `pnpm add -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest`. Inside a project, `computer-integrations` lists, as info, the integrations installed for the computer that the project does not install, with its install command; they are not used there. It never fails a check because the folder has no project, and installs nothing. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, it checks the computer instead (the Node version, the version that answered, the newest version it knows of, the astryx commands on the search path, the integrations installed globally, and the agent guide for the computer) and never fails a check because the folder has no project. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs global/who-answers`.

Earlier descriptor-less copies are a non-failing upgrade warning. It never installs, writes, or mutates. It imports astryx.config, executes every added theme source while validating private inputs, and loads every recorded built theme module to prove its runtime imports work, including themes from installed packages. Local theme source also runs during build-freshness checks. Stylesheets are parsed without execution. Config and theme top-level code therefore run, so use doctor only with project code you trust. Outside a project it checks the computer instead: the Node version (`node-version`), the release that answered (`answering-release`), the newest release the computer knows of (`newest-release`), the astryx commands on the search path (`cli-on-path`), the integrations installed for the computer (`computer-integrations`: each one used outside a project, and a warning for one skipped because its peer range excludes the answering release or that fails to load), and the computer-level agent text (`computer-agent-text`): present and matching this release, present but different, edited, absent, or turned off, and where it is linked, with `astryx init --user` as the fix for the stale and absent cases. The agent-text check is always info. The newest-release check also runs inside a project: it names a newer release when the computer knows of one; inside a project whose release is older it names the install and upgrade commands; outside one, when the CLI installed for the computer is older, it names the command of the package manager that installed it, after the Node the newest release needs when the computer runs an older one. It is always info and installs nothing. The `cli-on-path` check also runs inside a project: it lists every astryx command on the search path in order, passes when the first is a release that hands each project run to the release of that project, and warns when the first is another program or a release that predates the hand-off, naming `yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli@latest`. Inside a project, `computer-integrations` lists, as info, the integrations installed for the computer that the project does not install, with its install command; they are not used there. It never fails a check because the folder has no project, and installs nothing. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, it checks the computer instead (the Node version, the version that answered, the newest version it knows of, the astryx commands on the search path, the integrations installed globally, and the agent guide for the computer) and never fails a check because the folder has no project. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs global/who-answers`.

Installed next to the global install (`yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli your-package`), or in the same folder as the CLI by a tool that installs them together: it works in every folder outside a project. People and agents there see its components, templates, docs, themes, codemods, and discover source.

npm pack  # only with npm: the tarball the registry receives
yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli ./your-package-1.0.0.tgz
mkdir -p /tmp/try-global && cd /tmp/try-global
astryx discover
astryx docs
astryx doctor
Remove it again with `yarn global remove your-package`.

In global mode: users can also install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI (`yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli your-package`). It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs it. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone; the guide says to run the command that installed the CLI, such as `yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli`, when that command is not found, and `astryx doctor` names the same step. To keep the CLI across restarts, install it into a folder in your home and put its `bin` folder on your PATH, as for a permission error (`astryx docs global/install-once`), or run that command when the machine starts.

yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli
# with Volta: volta install @astryxdesign/cli

yarn global remove @astryxdesign/cli
# with Volta: volta uninstall @astryxdesign/cli

The app holds a copy, not a link. After each change, pack again and run the same `bun install`.

# 1. Build and test against the new release
bun add -d @astryxdesign/cli@latest @astryxdesign/core@latest
# 2. Rerun the checks
astryx doctor integration validate
astryx doctor integration docs
astryx integration verify
# 3. Admit the new Core once the checks pass
npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/core=^0.6.0 || ^0.7.0'  # only with npm: edits package.json
# 4. Migrate apps across a change that breaks them
astryx integration add codemod rename-delay --to 0.7.0

Keep the CLI installed in each project too: that pins its version for teammates and CI (`astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`). Inside a project, whichever astryx command you type, the project's version answers. Outside a project, your global install answers with its own version, and a version you name, such as `bunx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.0`, answers as exactly that version.

In a project with nothing installed yet, such as a fresh clone, the same commands use that Core too, and offline the error reads `This project has no Core installed, and Core <version> could not be downloaded`: install the project's dependencies (`bun install`, or your package manager's), and the project's own Core answers from then on.

Commands the CLI prints for you to run start with a name that reaches the same version: the project's runner (such as `pnpm exec astryx`) in a project, `astryx` outside a project when your global install answered, and otherwise the CLI pinned to the version, such as `bunx @astryxdesign/cli@0.6.8`. An integration is a way to share things with Astryx users: a package you own and maintain, built on a framework Astryx gives you. Publish one, many, or any mix, and people install it in one step. It works with the Astryx CLI alongside Core. See each kind under {@link namespace:building-blocks}.
For example, ship a carousel as an integration. Any app that installs it can find it with `{@command search carousel}`, and the CLI uses it like any Astryx Core component.
An integration can also replace a built-in template or doc. To start, install `@astryxdesign/cli` and open {@link generic:quick-start}.
Every field of every file you write for an integration is in {@link generic:field-reference}.

Every integration runs `{@command integration check --strict}` in its own build: it is required, not optional, so a doc, prop, or link that stops matching the code fails your build instead of your users' apps. See {@link generic:checks}.

In global mode: every kind your package adds also applies outside projects when users install it for their computer, beside the global CLI; inside a project, only if the project installs it. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

`Calendar`, DateInput, DateRangeInput, and DateTimeInput show the Gregorian calendar unless the application chooses another one. Values never change with the calendar: they stay Gregorian ISO dates. {@link generic:i18n-calendars} has the short version.

In global mode: each command declares its behavior outside projects (`outsideProject`). Most answer like a new project; some write nothing and name the project they need; `doctor`, `init`, and `upgrade` behave differently. Commands with different behavior describe it in their `In global mode:` note, and CLI tests run each command in an empty folder against its declared value. Inside a project, the project's Astryx release runs every command, whichever astryx command you type. See {@link namespace:global}.

In global mode: components from an integration installed for the computer show up outside projects; inside a project, only components from integrations the project installs. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

In global mode: installed for the computer, beside the global CLI, your package's manifest is read as it is in a project and applies in folders outside any project; peer ranges are checked against the global CLI's release. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:global-integrations}.

Every file an integration author writes, field by field: the integration manifest, astryx.config, codemods, identity, and each doc type. The guides that use them are the rest of {@link namespace:authoring}.
Help people find a page: give it a category for `{@command search}` and template listings, and flag a sparse starting shell as a scaffold.

A codemod module the CLI runs during `{@command upgrade}`. Default-export a plain object with a `type` discriminant: 'code' rewrites source files, 'config' rewrites the astryx.config.* file. There is no factory to call.

A source for `{@command discover}`: an async function that returns a catalog of packages a project could add, their versions, and what each version adds. Set it as `discover` in astryx.config, or export it as `discover` from an integration manifest. Discover calls every source, the project one first, and then reads the official list the CLI carries; another source's entry for an official package is kept. A source that throws, runs past 30 seconds, or returns an invalid catalog never hides the others; discover then uses the last good answer that source gave for the same request, or reports the source as failed when it saved none. Discover only reads: it prints the command that adds a package and never runs it.

A handler for `{@command gap-report}`: a plain object with an `audience` and a `handle` function. Set it as `gapReport` in astryx.config, or export it as `gapReport` from an integration manifest. Handlers add up rather than replace each other: the project handler first, then each loaded integration's in load order (the `integrations` list, then autolinked ones), whichever package the report is about.
